passages.title: The spoils question and true believers defined
passages.tafsir:
Sūrat al-Anfāl opens in the aftermath of Badr — the first confrontation between Islam and disbelief — at the exact moment its victors began to argue over the spoils. Allah answers the dispute in ayah 1 by lifting the spoils out of everyone's hands entirely, then immediately, in ayat 2–4, redraws the picture of what a believer actually is. That sequence is the key to the passage: a question about property is answered with a definition of faith. The believers had asked "who gets what?"; the revelation replies, in effect, "first remember who you are."

## The story behind ayah 1

Ibn Kathir records from al-Bukhari that Ibn 'Abbas said, "Al-Anfal are the spoils of war," and that when Sa'id bin Jubayr asked him about Sūrat al-Anfāl he answered simply, "It was revealed concerning Badr." The sources preserve two scenes from that day as reasons for the revelation, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests it is not unlikely that both events took place and the verse came down in answer to both.

The first scene is intimate — a single fighter and a single sword. Imam Ahmad recorded that Sa'd bin Malik said: "O Allah's Messenger, Allah has brought comfort to me today over the idolators, so grant me this sword." The Prophet ﷺ replied, "This sword is neither yours nor mine; put it down." Sa'd put it down, but said to himself that the Prophet might give the sword to another man who had not fought as fiercely as he had. Then he heard a man calling him from behind, and asked, "Has Allah revealed something in my case?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "You asked me to give you the sword, but it is not for me to decide about. However, it has been granted to me, and I give it to you" — and Allah sent down, "They ask you about al-anfāl. Say: al-anfāl are for Allah and the Messenger." Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i collected this hadith, and At-Tirmidhi graded it "Hasan Sahih."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates another sword narration, also from the Musnad of Ahmad, narrated by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. His brother 'Umayr fell a martyr in the battle of Badr. Out of the disbelievers arrayed against him, Sa'd killed Sa'id ibn al-'As, took his sword, and presented himself before the Prophet ﷺ, wishing that the sword be given to him. But the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to deposit it with the spoils. He stepped forward to obey, though his heart ached with the thought that his brother had laid down his life in this jihad, and he had killed the enemy confronting him and taken possession of his sword — yet even that was taken from him. He had hardly gone far when this verse of Sūrat al-Anfāl was revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ called him back and let him have the sword. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that according to some other narrations — which it sources to Ibn Kathir and Mazhari — Sa'd had himself requested the sword, and the Prophet ﷺ had answered: "This is not my property which I could give to someone, nor is this owned by you. Deposit it with the rest of the spoils. This matter will be decided in accordance with what Allah decrees."

The second scene is the wider dispute. Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Umamah said, "I asked 'Ubadah about al-Anfal" — 'Ubadah bin as-Samit, a participant at Badr — and he said: "It was revealed about us, those who participated in Badr, when we disputed about the spoils and our dispute was not appealing. So Allah took al-Anfal from us and gave it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger ﷺ divided it equally among the Muslims." In a second report, Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Umamah said that 'Ubadah bin as-Samit described the day itself. When the two armies met and Allah defeated the enemy, the Muslims split into three groups: one pursued the fleeing enemy, inflicting utter defeat and casualties; one came to the battlefield to collect the spoils; and one surrounded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so that the enemy could not attack him suddenly. When night came and the groups returned to camp, the collectors said: we collected it, so none else will have a share in it. The pursuers said: no — you have no more right to it than us; we kept the enemy away from the spoils and defeated them. The guards said: you have no more right to it than us; we surrounded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for fear the enemy might make a surprise attack against him, and were kept busy with that. Then the ayah came down — "They ask you about al-anfāl. Say: al-anfāl are for Allah and the Messenger. So fear Allah and settle all matters of difference among you" — and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divided the anfāl equally between the Muslims. At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah collected a similar narration, and At-Tirmidhi said "Hasan." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that everyone was pleased with this decree of Allah and His Messenger — and naturally ashamed of what had passed between them.

Notice what the ruling actually does. It does not adjudicate between the three claims; it dissolves them. "Say: the spoils are for Allah and the Messenger" — meaning, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, real ownership belongs to Allah, and the right of disposal rests with His Messenger ﷺ, who distributes according to Allah's command. No one holds a prior claim at all. The moment nobody owns anything, there is nothing left to fight over.

## The word al-anfāl

The passage's first word repays attention. Anfāl is the plural of nafl, which at root means grace, reward, something given beyond obligation — the same word used for voluntary prayer, fasting and charity (nafl acts), which no one is compelled to do. Calling war spoils anfāl already frames them as pure gift, not entitlement.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Qur'an uses three related terms. Ghanīmah (detailed later in ayah 41 of this sūrah) is booty obtained through actual fighting. Fayʼ (treated in Sūrat al-Hashr) is property obtained from the disbelievers without fighting. Anfāl covers both senses and is also used, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas in Tafsir Ibn Jarir, for the extra award a commander gives a fighter for exemplary performance. Ibn Kathir likewise records from the early authorities — Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah and others agreeing with Ibn 'Abbas — that here it means the spoils generally, though some said it refers to the commander's discretionary awards, the khumus (the fifth of the spoils), or the fayʼ.

Why does the word matter? Imam Abu 'Ubayd, in his Kitab al-Amwal, gives what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the best explanation: spoils being lawful at all is a special grace to this Ummah. Among past communities, spoils were unlawful for everyone; they were gathered in one place, and a fire from the heavens consuming them was the sign that the fighting had been accepted in Allah's sight. In a narration of Jabir in Al-Bukhari and Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said he was blessed with five things given to no prophet before him, one being: "made lawful for me are the spoils, though they were not lawful for anyone before me." So the very thing the Companions were disputing over was itself an unearned gift — and its name, anfāl, says so.

## Did ayah 41 abrogate this verse?

A group of leading authorities in tafsir — Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, As-Suddi and others — held that this ruling of total prophetic discretion belonged to the early period, before the detailed law of distribution came down in ayah 41 of this sūrah: one-fifth of the spoils deposited in the treasury for the needs of the Muslims, four-fifths divided among the fighters. On that view the later verse abrogated this one. Other scholars, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, said there is no abrogation here at all: the difference is simply between brevity and detail — ayah 1 states the principle ("for Allah and the Messenger"), and ayah 41 spells out how the Messenger ﷺ distributes under Allah's command. Fayʼ property, by contrast, remained entirely at the Prophet's ﷺ discretion, which is why Sūrat al-Hashr says, "what the Messenger gives you, take it; and what he stops you from, leave it" (59:7). Both positions are attributed in the sources; the practical outcome is the same — distribution is by Allah's law, not by claimants' arguments.

## "Have taqwa of Allah and set your relations right"

The second half of ayah 1 turns from law to hearts: "So have taqwa of Allah, and settle the matters of difference among you, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers." Taqwa — the fear of Allah, the sense of standing answerable before Him — is named first, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why: it is the method by which relations are repaired. Experience bears out, it says, that under a heart filled with the fear of Allah and the Hereafter, major disputes get resolved in no time and deep-rooted hatreds evaporate. Ibn 'Abbas said this ayah is a command from Allah and His Messenger ﷺ that believers have taqwa of Allah and settle their differences; As-Suddi put it with striking simplicity: "Do not curse each other." And Ibn Kathir adds the quiet rebuke folded into the verse: the guidance and knowledge Allah has granted you is better than the thing you are disputing over.

The closing words — "if you are believers" — tie the whole verse together. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, īmān (faith) demands obedience, and obedience is the outcome of taqwa; when people become practitioners of these virtues, their mutual disputes resolve themselves and hearts fill with love rather than hostility. And it is precisely this phrase that the next three ayat unpack.

## Five marks of the true believer (ayat 2–3)

Ayah 2 opens with an exclusive: the believers are only those with these qualities. Ibn 'Abbas (in the report of 'Ali bin Abi Talhah) read this as drawing the line against the hypocrites, into whose hearts no remembrance of Allah enters, who neither trust in Allah, nor pray when alone, nor pay the zakah due on their wealth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the same verses as a mirror: every believer should keep checking whether these attributes are present in him, thank Allah if they are, and set about acquiring or strengthening them if they are not. Five marks follow — three of the heart, two of the limbs and wealth.

**1. Hearts that tremble at His mention.** The Arabic is precise: wajilat qulūbuhum. Mujahid explained, "their hearts become afraid and fearful," and As-Suddi similarly. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why the Qur'an chose wajal rather than the ordinary word for fear (khawf). The fear of a beast or an enemy destroys your peace; this fear does not — for the Qur'an also says, "Hearts find peace through the remembrance of Allah" (13:28). Wajal is awe: the reverent, respectful fear that rises in a heart soaked in the realization of Allah's greatness and love for Him, the way majesty overwhelms. The two verses are not in tension; awe of Allah and rest in Allah live in the same heart. Some commentators (cited from Al-Bahr Al-Muhit) added a concrete case: a man on the verge of a sin remembers Allah, fears His punishment, and pulls back — as in As-Suddi's words reported by Sufyan Ath-Thawri: a man thinking of committing injustice or a sin is told "Have taqwa of Allah," and his heart becomes fearful, and he abstains. The mark of this fear is not emotion but effect: as Ibn Kathir puts it, the true believer feels it and therefore implements Allah's orders and abstains from His prohibitions.

**2. Faith that grows when His verses are recited.** Ibn Kathir records that Al-Bukhari and other scholars relied on this ayah, and those similar to it, as evidence that īmān (faith) increases and varies in strength from heart to heart — the view of the majority of the scholars of Islam, prompting some, such as Ash-Shafi'i, Ahmad bin Hanbal and Abu 'Ubayd, to declare it the consensus of the Ummah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes what that increase feels like in a life: good deeds gain strength and stability, become natural habit, their absence is felt as a pinch, and a natural distaste for sin develops — the great station identified in hadith by the term "the sweetness of īmān." It also draws the sobering corollary: recitation done heedlessly, without the etiquette and reverence due to the Qur'an and without a sense of Allah's greatness, may not be devoid of reward, but it will not produce this result.

**3. Trust in their Lord alone.** Tawakkul is reliance on Allah — and the emphasis in the verse is on "in their Lord" alone. Ibn Kathir: the believers hope in none but Allah, seek refuge with Him alone, ask Him alone, knowing that whatever He wills occurs and whatever He does not will never occurs. Hence Sa'id bin Jubayr's saying: "Tawakkul of Allah is the essence of faith." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān guards against the common misreading: tawakkul does not mean abandoning material means. One gathers and uses the means within one's ability — then entrusts the outcome to the One who created the means and alone makes them bear fruit. As the Prophet ﷺ taught: make a moderate effort to procure what you need, then place your trust in Him — do not let your heart and mind get bogged down with nothing but material ways and means.

**4. They establish the prayer.** Ayah 3 moves from heart to limbs, and again the wording is deliberate. The verse does not say they "perform" or "offer" Salah; it says they establish it — iqāmah, literally "to make something stand straight." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists on the difference: prayer carried out with full regard for its conditions and etiquette, as the Prophet ﷺ taught by word and deed, is established prayer; anything less may be juristically valid, but its blessings shrink by the measure of the shortfall — including the promise that "Salah stops from immodesty and sinfulness" (29:45). Qatadah spelled it out: preserving its times, the ablution, the bowing and prostration. Muqatil bin Hayyan added: perfect purity, perfect bowing and prostration, the recitation, the tashahhud, and invoking blessings on the Prophet ﷺ.

**5. They spend from what We have provided them.** The wording carries its own theology: what you give away was Allah's provision to you in the first place. Ibn Kathir includes under it the zakah and everything else due from the servant, obligatory or recommended, adding: all servants are Allah's dependents, and the most beloved of them to Him are the most beneficial to His creation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān keeps the phrase deliberately wide — zakah, charities, endowments, gifts to relatives, and financial help amiably given to guests, friends and respected elders.

## "It is they who are the believers in truth" (ayah 4)

Ḥaqqan — in truth, in reality. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains: such people are the same outwardly and inwardly; their tongue says what their heart holds. Others pronounce the testimony of faith while their hearts do not throb with Allah's oneness nor burn with obedience to His Prophet ﷺ — what they do contradicts what they say. Every truth has a reality behind it, and one has not reached the truth until one reaches its reality.

The early Muslims took this verse with utter seriousness. Someone asked the famous Hasan al-Basri: "Abu Sa'id, are you a believer?" He answered: there are two kinds of īmān. If you ask whether I believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, Paradise, Hell, and the reckoning of the Last Day — then yes, I am a believer. But if you ask whether I am the perfect believer described in these verses of Sūrat al-Anfāl — I simply do not know whether I am one of them.

Three rewards are then promised: high ranks with their Lord, forgiveness, and a generous (dignified) provision. Tafsir Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, notices an elegant symmetry: the attributes were of three kinds — of the heart (fear, growing faith, trust), of the body (prayer), and of wealth (spending) — and each kind meets its matching reward. High ranks answer the inward, spiritual attributes; forgiveness answers the bodily deeds (prayer, as in hadith, becomes the expiation of sins); and dignified provision answers spending — one receives far better and far more than one gave in this passing life.

On those ranks, Ibn Kathir cites the hadith in the Two Sahihs: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the residents of 'Illiyyin, in Paradise, are seen by those below them as you see a distant planet on the horizon of the sky. The Companions assumed such grades belonged only to the Prophets, but he ﷺ said: "Rather, by He in Whose Hand is my soul, they are for men who have faith in Allah and believed in the Messengers." And in a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad and the collectors of the Sunan, he ﷺ named two of them: Abu Bakr and 'Umar are among them — "and how excellent they are."

## Living the passage

The passage's shape is its lesson. A community fresh from victory nearly fractured over property; Allah removed the property from their hands, commanded taqwa and reconciliation, and then held up the portrait of the believer whose heart trembles, whose faith grows, who trusts, prays and gives. Read together, ayat 1–4 teach that disputes over "mine" are cured not by better arguments but by remembering that everything — the sword, the spoils, the provision you spend from — belongs to Allah; and they leave each reader with Hasan al-Basri's question: the first kind of īmān I have — but am I among the believers in truth?

passages.title: Marched out to Badr against their liking
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat take the believers back to the days just before the battle of Badr, when Allah brought His Prophet ﷺ out of his home in Madinah toward a confrontation that a group of the believers dreaded — and then show why that dread was overruled. What binds ayat 5–8 into one unit is a single contrast: what the Muslims wanted (the easy, unarmed prize) against what Allah willed (the hard meeting that would "firmly establish the truth and wipe out falsehood"). The passage is Allah's own commentary on the march to Badr, teaching the community to trust His planning over their preferences.

## "Just as your Lord brought you out" — what is being compared?

Ayah 5 opens strangely: *kamā akhrajaka rabbuka* — "just as your Lord brought you out." *Just as* what? The word **kamā** is a word of comparison, and the commentators discussed at length what is being compared to what. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Abu Hayyan collected fifteen interpretations, of which three stand out as most probable:

**1. A comparison with the spoils dispute.** This surah opened with the Companions differing over the war spoils (*anfāl*) of Badr; they all then obeyed the command of the Prophet ﷺ under the divine decree, and its blessings and good results became manifest before them. Ayah 5 then says: *just as* that happened, so too with the battle itself — at its beginning some expressed dislike, yet under the divine decree everyone obeyed, and the beneficial outcome and superb rewards it brought were witnessed by all openly. Maʿārif credits this interpretation to al-Farrāʼ and al-Mubarrad (citing Al-Bahr Al-Muhit), and notes that Maulana Ashraf Thanavi preferred it in Bayān al-Qurʼān.

**2. A proof of the promise of the Hereafter.** The previous ayah (8:4) promised the true believers high ranks, forgiveness and dignified provision. On this reading (which Maʿārif cites from Tafsir al-Qurtubi with reference to al-Nahhās), ayah 5 says: that unseen promise is as certain as this seen one — the promise of divine help and victory stands fulfilled at Badr all too manifestly, so take your lesson and be certain that the promise of the Hereafter will be fulfilled just as surely.

**3. A statement of cause.** Abu Hayyan himself was uneasy with all the views he had gathered. Maʿārif relates his remarkable account: pondering the verse one night, he saw in a dream that the elided word is *naṣaraka* — "He helped you." On this reading *kamā* is not used for comparison but gives the reason for the help: Allah's very special help and support came at Badr *because* the Prophet ﷺ had done what he did in this campaign not by some wish or discretion of his own, but by remaining obedient to the divine command exclusively — and divine support always accompanies such a person.

Maʿārif concludes that all three meanings are probable and sound; the ayah is rich enough to carry them together.

Ibn Kathir, for his part, explains the verse this way: after describing the believers as fearing their Lord, resolving their disputes and obeying Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, Allah is saying — since you disputed about dividing the war spoils, Allah took them away from you; He and His Messenger ﷺ then divided them in truth and justice, ensuring continued benefit for all of you. Similarly, you disliked meeting the armed enemy in battle; you disliked fighting, "so Allah decided that battle should occur and made you meet your enemy, without planning to do so on your part" — and the incident "carried guidance, light, victory and triumph."

## The language: why "your Lord brought you out"

The Qurʼan does not say the Prophet ﷺ *went out*; it says his Lord *brought him out* (*akhrajaka*). Maʿārif draws two lessons from this wording.

First, it points to the Prophet's ﷺ perfect servitude: his act was, in reality, the act of Allah flowing through him. Maʿārif cites here a hadith qudsi (a report in which the Prophet ﷺ relates words from his Lord) that when a servant is blessed with nearness to Allah through obedience and servitude, Allah says: "I become his eye. What he sees, he sees through Me. I become his ears. What he hears, he hears through Me. I become his hands and feet..." — which Maʿārif explains to mean that a very special help and support from Allah accompanies such a servant in all he does; what seems to issue from his limbs is, in reality, carried by the power of Allah.

Second, Allah names Himself here with the attribute **Rabb** — the Nurturer and Sustainer. The march to Badr was undertaken, says Maʿārif, in the interest of teaching and training His prophet ﷺ and the Muslim community through him: through this arrangement the oppressed and subdued Muslims were to be made victorious and the arrogant and unjust disbelievers given their first taste of punishment.

And the phrase **bil-ḥaqq** — "with the truth" — declares the motive. This campaign, says Maʿārif, was initiated so that truth would prevail and falsehood be frustrated; it was not driven by "hunger of land or anger of monarch, as customary with other states." The "home" (*baytika*) is, according to the majority of commentators, his home in Madinah, for Badr took place in the second year after the Hijrah.

The ayah closes: "and verily, a party among the believers disliked it." As-Suddī comments simply: what they disliked was meeting the armed idolaters. And Maʿārif explains that this is a hint toward the state of mind some noble Companions were in *while being consulted* on the advisability of the campaign — an aversion, a shortfall of courage, not a refusal. How they came to that state is something the story itself must explain.

## The road to Badr

Both sources tell the story at length, because the whole passage turns on it.

Word reached the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah that Abu Sufyan was returning from Syria with the great trade caravan of Quraysh. This was no ordinary caravan. According to the report narrated by Ibn ʿUqbah and Ibn ʿĀmir (in Maʿārif), all the Quraysh tribes of Makkah were partners in the venture; Ibn ʿUqbah states that there was not a Quraysh man or woman in Makkah without a share in it — even someone owning a single mithqāl of gold (about 4.5 grams) had invested it — and puts its total capital at fifty thousand gold dinars. Seventy strong young men and their chiefs accompanied the caravan to manage its security and business — in real terms, Maʿārif observes, a trading corporation of the Quraysh of Makkah. And Al-Baghawi reports, on the authority of narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās and others, that forty Quraysh chiefs rode with the mounted force accompanying it, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and Mukhramah ibn Nawfal noteworthy among them. This trading wealth was the very base of Quraysh's power — the seemingly "innocent weapon," as Maʿārif puts it, with which they had harassed the Prophet ﷺ and compelled him to leave Makkah. Intercepting it would break their main source of strength.

Ibn Kathir relates from Muhammad bin Ishaq, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ announced: "This is the caravan of Quraysh carrying their property, so march forth to intercept it; Allah might make it as war spoils for you." Note the wording — *might*. It was Ramadan; no battle plans had been made in advance; participation was not made obligatory. Only those whose riding animals were at hand were told to come, and many stayed behind — some because their rides were in outlying villages and there was no time to fetch them, others thinking there would be no fighting anyway. So on Saturday, 12 Ramadan, the Prophet ﷺ moved out of Madinah with preparations suited to confronting a trade caravan, not a war. At Biʼr Suqya he had Qays ibn Saʿṣaʿah count the men: three hundred and thirteen — a number that delighted him, for he said, "This is the number of the companions of Ṭālūt" (the Israelite king Saul), and he took it as a good omen of victory. Between them they had seventy camels, one for every three men, taking turns. The Prophet ﷺ himself shared a camel with Abu Lubabah and ʿAli; when they offered to walk his turns for him, he answered: "Neither are you stronger than me, nor am I need-free of the reward of the Hereafter."

Meanwhile Abu Sufyan, cautiously gathering intelligence from travellers he met, learned of the pursuit. He swerved the caravan toward the coast — and hired Ḍamḍam al-Ghifārī to race to Makkah. Ḍamḍam arrived in the dramatic style of the age's alarm signals — his she-camel's ears and nose cut off, his shirt torn front and back, the camel-seat placed upside down — and the city was electrified. Within three days Quraysh had fielded an army: one thousand armed men, two hundred horses, six hundred coats of mail, with female war-song chanters and their drums, slaughtering ten camels at every stage of the journey to feed the host. Anyone who hesitated was suspected of Muslim sympathies and forced out — including Muslims trapped in Makkah who had been unable to migrate, and members of Banu Hāshim suspected of sympathy, among them al-ʿAbbās, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle, and Ṭālib and ʿAqīl, the sons of Abu Ṭālib.

Near Badr the Prophet ﷺ sent ahead a reconnaissance party of two men. They came back with the report that the caravan, aware of the pursuit, had slipped past along the sea shore — and that an army of one thousand men was coming from Makkah to cover it and fight the Muslims off. The Muslims, equipped to overtake merchants, now faced a transformed situation.

## The consultation — Miqdād and Saʿd

Faced with this news, the Prophet ﷺ consulted his Companions. Some, Maʿārif notes — Abu Ayyub al-Anṣārī among them — submitted honestly that they had neither the force for such a fight nor had they come out for that purpose. Abu Bakr rose and spoke well; then ʿUmar. Then al-Miqdād stood and said: "O Messenger of Allah! March to what Allah has commanded you, for we are with you. By Allah, we will not say to you what the Children of Israel said to Mūsā: 'So go you and your Lord and fight you two, we are sitting right here' (5:24). Rather, go, you and your Lord, and fight — we will be fighting along with you both. By He Who has sent you with Truth! If you decide to take us to Birk-ul-Ghimād, we will fight along with you until you reach it." The Prophet ﷺ said good words to al-Miqdād and invoked Allah for his benefit.

Yet he said again: "Give me your opinion, O people." Ibn Kathir explains why: the majority present were the Anṣār of Madinah, and their pledge at al-ʿAqabah had bound them to protect him within their land, "in the same manner we protect our children and wives." He feared they might consider themselves unbound for a march against an enemy beyond Madinah. Saʿd bin Muʿādh caught the hint: "O Messenger of Allah, is it us whom you meant?" — "Yes." Saʿd answered: "We have faith and believed in you, testified that what you brought is the truth, and gave you our pledges and promises of allegiance and obedience. Therefore, march, O Messenger of Allah, for what Allah has commanded you. Verily, by He Who has sent you in Truth, if you decided to cross this sea, we will follow you in it, and none among us would stay behind. We do not dislike that we meet our enemy tomorrow. Verily, we are patient in war, fierce in battle. May Allah make you witness what makes your eyes pleased with us. Therefore, march with us with the blessing of Allah."

The Prophet ﷺ, pleased and encouraged, proclaimed: "March with the blessing of Allah and receive the good news. For Allah has indeed promised me one of the two camps. By Allah! It is as if I am now looking at the demise of the people." Ibn Kathir notes that al-ʿAwfī reported similar from Ibn ʿAbbās, and that As-Suddī, Qatādah, ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam and several others among the Salaf and later generations mentioned the story similarly.

## Ayah 6 — reluctance, not rebellion

"They disputed with you about the truth after it had been made clear, as if they were being driven to death while they looked on." The wording is severe — but it is essential to understand, as Maʿārif insists, that the Companions concerned **had not disobeyed any command**. What they had done was an expression of their weakness and lack of courage as part of their response *when consulted*. Yet even such an expression of personal opinion, coming from the Companions of the Messengers of Allah and set against the high station they had been blessed with, was unwelcome in the sight of Allah — and so it was set forth in words which spell out displeasure.

Ibn Kathir also records the comment of some that this disputing echoes the surah's opening: they ask and argue with you about the *anfāl* (the spoils) just as they argued with you when you went out for the battle of Badr, saying, "You marched with us to confiscate the caravan. You did not inform us that there will be fighting and that we should prepare for it."

## Ayah 7 — the caravan or the army

Ayah 7 recalls the promise: "Allah promised you one of the two parties would be yours — and you wished the unarmed one would be yours." The narrations name the two: the **ʿīr**, the trade caravan of Abu Sufyan, and the **nafīr**, the armed force that had dashed out of Makkah. Allah had promised His Messenger ﷺ — and all the Muslims through him — that they would totally overcome one of the two groups. The promise was, as Maʿārif puts it, seemingly ambiguous: *one of the two* — and human nature reached instantly for the safe one. Overtaking a trade caravan was easy and danger-free; dealing with an armed force was fraught with all sorts of difficulties and dangers. Maʿārif notes that the Prophet ﷺ and many of his leading Companions, divinely guided, intended otherwise and settled on overcoming the armed force as the better choice.

"But Allah willed to justify the truth by His Words and to cut off the roots of the disbelievers." Ibn Kathir unfolds this: Allah willed for you to meet the armed enemy — rather than the caravan — so that He makes you prevail above them and gain victory over them, making His religion apparent and Islam victorious and dominant above all religions. "He has perfect knowledge of the consequences of all things, you are surrounded by His wise planning, although people only like what appears favorable to them." Twice Ibn Kathir anchors the passage to the master principle of 2:216: "Fighting is ordained for you though you dislike it, and it may be that you dislike a thing which is good for you, and that you like a thing which is bad for you. Allah knows but you do not know."

## Ayah 8 — the purpose beneath the plan

Ayah 8 states the final purpose: *li-yuḥiqqa l-ḥaqqa wa-yubṭila l-bāṭil* — "that He might cause the truth to triumph and bring falsehood to nothing, even though the criminals hate it." Maʿārif explains: the Muslims preferred the unarmed caravan out of a tilt toward personal convenience and a danger-free option, but Allah intended it to be otherwise, so that the real objective of Islam stands achieved — truth established as the ultimate truth, and the very root of the disbelievers cut off. And that objective, as is obvious, could only be achieved when the confrontation is against the armed force itself, and the Muslims overwhelm and overpower it.

## Living it

The passage trains the believer in one discipline: when Allah's command and your comfort point in different directions, the command carries the blessing. The Companions wanted the safe option; Allah chose the hard one, and it became "guidance, light, victory and triumph." What you are averse to may be the very thing your Lord — the Rabb, the Nurturer — is using to raise you: "it may be that you dislike a thing which is good for you... Allah knows but you do not know" (2:216). And the passage models the response Allah loves: not the hesitation of ayah 6, but the words of Miqdād and Saʿd — *march, for we are with you* — spoken before the outcome was visible, trusting that Allah knows and we do not know.

passages.title: Divine reinforcement: angels, rain, and terror
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat relive the night and morning of Badr from heaven's side of the story. A desperate cry rises from three hundred and thirteen mostly unarmed believers; the answer comes down as a thousand angels, a strange sleep, a well-timed rain, and terror cast into the hearts of their enemies. What holds the passage together is the drumbeat of *idh* — "remember when" — as Allah enumerates, favor by favor, what He did for the outnumbered camp, then closes (ayat 13–14) with the verdict on why the other camp fell. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts the chain explicitly: the first blessing was bringing the Muslims out at all (ayah 5), the second the promise of support (ayah 7), the third the answered cry (ayah 9), the fourth the sleep and the rain (ayah 11), and the fifth the command issued to the angels themselves (ayah 12).

## The night before Badr

To feel these ayat you have to stand where the Companions stood. The Quraysh army — a thousand armed men — had already taken the higher ground, with water close at hand. The Prophet ﷺ and his Companions were left the lower part of the valley: soft, sandy, hard to move through. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that Ḥubāb ibn al-Mundhir, who knew the territory, respectfully asked the Prophet ﷺ whether the campsite was divinely commanded or a matter of opinion; told it was open to counsel, he proposed advancing to seize a water source near the enemy. The Prophet ﷺ accepted, moved camp, and had a water tank built and amply filled. Then Saʿd ibn Muʿādh offered to build him a simple shaded shelter, so that if — Allah forbid — the day went badly, he could return to the believers left in Madinah. A modest awning of twigs was set up, in which there was no one but the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr, with a guard standing at its door, sword in hand.

That was the scene: anxiety was natural, and Shaytan was working on it. Ibn ʿAbbas relates (as Ibn Kathir records) that with the sand between the Muslims and the wells, the whisper came: *you claim to be Allah's supporters, with His Messenger among you — yet the idolators hold the water while you cannot even purify yourselves for prayer.*

## "When you cried out to your Lord" — ayah 9

The word in ayah 9 is *tastaghīthūna* — rendered "when you cried out to your Lord for help." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains it as calling upon your Lord and appealing for His help and support: not a calm request but a cry. Seeing his three hundred and thirteen facing a thousand, the Prophet ﷺ raised his hands and prayed. Ibn ʿAbbas preserves the words (as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives them): "O Allah, let the promise You have made to me come true now. O Allah, if this modest group of Muslims were to perish, then, on Your earth, there shall remain no one to worship You." Maʿārif relates that he beseeched so earnestly and plaintively that the sheet around his shoulders slid down; Abu Bakr stepped forward, replaced it, and said, "Ya Rasul Allah, please worry no more — Allah will surely respond to your prayer and fulfill His promise."

Al-Bukhari records his own telling of that imploring, from Ibn ʿAbbas: on the day of Badr the Prophet ﷺ said, "O Allah! I invoke You for Your covenant and promise. O Allah! If You decide so, You will not be worshipped" — until Abu Bakr held his hand and said, "Enough." In that narration, the Prophet ﷺ then went out proclaiming, "Their multitude will be put to flight, and they will show their backs." An-Nasāʾī also collected this hadith.

Notice the plural: "when *you* (all) cried out." Maʿārif explains that the prayer was the Prophet's ﷺ, but every Companion beside him was saying *Āmīn* — so the cry is attributed to the whole group. And the group had earned that attribution. Al-Bukhari records in the book of battles of his Sahih, from Ibn Masʿūd, that al-Miqdād came to the Prophet ﷺ as he was invoking Allah against the idolators and proclaimed: "We will not say as the people of Musa said, 'So go you and your Lord and fight you two.' Rather, we will fight to your right, to your left, before you and behind you." Ibn Masʿūd said he would like, more than almost anything else, to have been the one who did that — for he saw the Prophet's ﷺ face beaming with pleasure at al-Miqdād's words.

## A thousand angels, rank upon rank

The answer: "I am reinforcing you with a thousand of the angels, *murdifīn*." Ibn ʿAbbas explained *murdifīn* as "each behind the other in succession" — wave after wave. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān hears in the very word a hint: there are more coming behind these. That hint matters, because Sūrah Āl ʿImrān mentions three thousand and then five thousand angels at Badr. Maʿārif resolves the apparent tension as three distinct promises made under three different pressures: one thousand in answer to the Prophet's ﷺ prayer; three thousand when the Muslims were shaken by news (reported in Rūḥ al-Maʿānī from a narration of al-Shaʿbī) that Kurz ibn Jābir al-Muḥāribī was bringing reinforcements to Quraysh; and five thousand — a promise which, as some commentators explained, carried three conditions: patience, taqwā (mindful fear of Allah), and a sudden enemy assault. The Companions fulfilled the first two, but no sudden assault came, so the five thousand were never deployed. Even the describing words differ tellingly: *murdifīn* (in succession) here, *munzalīn* (specially sent down from the heavens, not angels already on earth) for the three thousand, *musawwimīn* (bearing distinct marks) for the five thousand — hadith narrations mention that the angels at Badr wore white headgear, and at Ḥunayn red. Ibn ʿAbbas also reported the deployment: five hundred under Jibrīl on one flank, five hundred under Mīkāʾīl on the other.

## "There is no victory except from Allah" — ayah 10

Then comes the theological pivot of the passage. Allah made all of this "only glad tidings, and that your hearts be at rest thereby — and there is no victory except from Allah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān drives the point home with one image: the land of the people of Lūṭ was overturned by Jibrīl with a single flick of his feather. One angel would have been more than enough; a thousand were promised because Allah knows His servants are impressed by numbers, so the promise was kept synchronized with the enemy's count purely to settle human hearts. The angels are means, not the source. Ibn Kathir says plainly: Allah is able to grant victory without sending any angel at all. And Maʿārif draws the standing lesson: all help, open or hidden, issues from Allah alone; even the angels act only by His command — so the believer's gaze must rest on Him, not on the instruments.

Ibn Kathir pauses here on a larger question: why does Allah have believers fight at all, when He destroyed earlier rebellious nations directly — Nūḥ's people by the flood, ʿĀd by the wind, Thamūd by the scream? He answers that after Allah sent Mūsā and drowned Firʿawn, fighting was legislated in the Tawrāh and remained in the successive revealed Laws, and he cites the Qurʼān's own statements of the wisdom in it: "if it had been Allah's will, He Himself could certainly have punished them, but (He lets you fight) in order to test some of you with others" (47:4–6), and the alternation of days by which Allah tests the believers and takes martyrs from among them (3:140–141). Then Ibn Kathir adds a point of his own: it is more humiliating for the disbeliever, and more comforting to the hearts of the faithful, that the believers kill the disbelievers by their own hands — and he grounds it in Allah's words, "Fight against them so that Allah will punish them by your hands, and disgrace them, and give you victory over them, and heal the breasts of a believing people" (9:14). He contrasts two ends: Abu Jahl, killed in battle at Badr — more humiliating for him than dying in his bed, or from lightning or wind — and Abu Lahab, who died of a disease so foul his own relatives washed him by sprinkling water from a distance and buried him under thrown stones. The ayah closes with two names that seal the logic: *ʿAzīz*, the Almighty whose might belongs to Him, His Messengers and the believers, in this life and the Hereafter; *Ḥakīm*, the All-Wise who legislated the fighting though He was able to destroy them by His own will and power.

## Sleep and rain — ayah 11

Ayah 11 recalls two of the tenderest gifts of that night. First, *al-nuʿās* — drowsiness — settled over the camp "as security from Him." The word is precise: Qatādah said slumber (*nuʿās*) affects the head, while sleep affects the heart. Fear should have kept every man awake; instead, Maʿārif describes a drowsiness that overcame each Muslim compulsively, whether he meant to sleep or not, removing anxiety and fatigue. Abu Yaʿlā narrated that ʿAlī said — in the wording Ibn Kathir cites — "Only al-Miqdād had a horse during Badr, and at some point, I found that all of us fell asleep, except the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He was praying under a tree and crying until dawn." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the report in its own telling: no one remained among them who did not go to sleep; only the Prophet ﷺ stayed awake, busy with the Salah of Tahajjud (the late-night prayer) right through dawn. Ibn Masʿūd gave the rule of thumb: slumber in battle is security from Allah; slumber in prayer is from Shaytan. Ibn Kathir notes the same favor returned at Uḥud (3:154), and concludes that this is Allah's pattern for believers in distress — with every hardship, relief (94:5–6). Even the Prophet ﷺ was touched by it: in the narration recorded in the Sahih, as Ibn Kathir cites, slumber overcame him in the shelter while he and Abu Bakr were invoking Allah, and he woke smiling and declared, "Good news, O Abu Bakr! This is Jibril with dust on his shoulders" — then left the shade reciting, "Their multitude will be put to flight, and they will show their backs" (54:45). Maʿārif adds, from narrations cited in Tafsir Mazhari, that as he came out he pointed to spots on the field — this is where Abu Jahl will be killed, this for so-and-so — and events fell out precisely as he indicated.

Second, the rain — and it fell with astonishing discrimination. ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr relates (through Ibn Isḥāq) that the downpour firmed the sandy ground under the Muslims so it no longer hindered their movement, while the ground the Quraysh were camped on became difficult to move in. Ibn ʿAbbas adds that the Muslims drank and used the water for purity — and with that, Shaytan's taunt about the wells simply dissolved. The ayah itself lists four purposes, and Ibn Kathir reads them as two matched pairs of outer and inner: "to purify you thereby" — the outward cleansing for prayer; "to remove from you the *rijz* of Shaytan" — his whispers and evil thoughts, the inward cleansing; "to strengthen your hearts" — inner courage; "and make your feet firm thereby" — outer courage, feet literally planted on solid ground. One rain, and body, heart, battlefield and morale were all set right at once.

## "I am with you" — the command to the angels, ayah 12

Ayah 12 lifts the veil on something no one on the field could see: Allah's revelation to the angels themselves. "Verily, I am with you, so keep firm those who have believed. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who have disbelieved." Ibn Kathir calls this a *hidden* favor now made known, precisely so the believers would thank Allah for it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the angels were given two duties: to steady the believers — whether by visibly swelling their ranks or by unseen influence (*taṣarruf*) upon their hearts — and to fight; and both, it says, actually happened, as hadith narrations documenting eyewitness Companions confirm. Muslim and al-Ṭabarī record from Ibn ʿAbbas, from ʿUmar, that a Muslim pursuing an idolator heard the sound of a whip above him and a rider crying "Come, O Hayzūm!" — and the idolator fell, his nose wounded and his face torn apart as if lashed, the whole face turned green. The Prophet ﷺ told him: "You have said the truth, that was from the reinforcements from the third heaven." Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said that afterwards people could tell whom the angels had slain by the wounds on necks, fingers and toes — as if branded by fire.

The command "strike above the necks, and smite over all their fingers and toes" was explained by the early authorities al-Ḍaḥḥāk and ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī: "above the necks" means the forehead or the neck. And Ibn Jarīr commented that the ayah commands, "O believers! Strike every limb and finger on the hands and feet of your (disbelieving) enemies." Set against it stands Abu Jahl's boast, reported by Ibn ʿAbbas: "Do not kill them, but capture them so that you make known to them what they did — their ridiculing your religion and shunning al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā." Allah's decree to the angels was the answer to that speech. By day's end Abu Jahl lay among seventy dead of Quraysh, with seventy more taken captive.

## Why they fell — ayat 13 and 14

The passage does not end on the marvels but on their cause. "That is because they *shāqqū* Allah and His Messenger" — they set themselves in defiance, joining the camp that defied Allah and His Messenger ﷺ rather than the camp of His Law and faith, as Ibn Kathir puts it. And whoever does that finds Allah severe in punishment: nothing escapes His grasp, and nothing can stand against His anger. Ayah 14 then turns and addresses the defeated directly — "That is yours, so taste it!" — and Maʿārif catches the chilling proportion in the words: Badr was only a *little* punishment, a first taste in this world; for the disbelievers the torment of the Fire still waits, severe, lasting, beyond imagining. Two camps, two outcomes, and the difference was never numbers.

## The honor of Badr

The sources close this scene with the standing Allah gave its people. Al-Bukhari records from Rifāʿah ibn Rāfiʿ al-Zuraqī, himself a veteran of Badr, that Jibrīl came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked, "How honored are those who participated in Badr among you?" He said, "Among the best Muslims." Jibrīl said, "This is the case with the angels who participated in Badr." And in the Two Sahihs, when ʿUmar suggested the execution of Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah, the Prophet ﷺ answered: "He participated in Badr. How do you know that Allah has not looked at the people of Badr and proclaimed, 'Do whatever you want, for I have forgiven you.'"

For the reader, the passage's demand is the one it demonstrates. Take the means seriously — the believers moved camp, seized the wells, formed ranks — but hang the heart on none of it, for "there is no victory except from Allah." When overwhelmed, cry out as they cried out, and know that the answer may come in forms you would never have engineered: sleep when fear should forbid it, rain that hardens your ground and mires your trial, and unseen help beyond counting.

passages.title: Never flee; the victory was Allah's alone
passages.tafsir:
This passage was revealed about the Battle of Badr, and it binds together two teachings that belong to each other: a law for the battlefield — a believer, once battle is joined, may never turn and run — and a correction for the heart — the astonishing victory just won at Badr was not the believers' achievement but Allah's act alone. Ayat 15–16 give the law and its two exceptions; ayat 17–18 strip the victory of any human ownership; and ayah 19 turns to the defeated Quraysh with a devastating irony: the verdict they themselves had prayed for at the Kaʿbah had just been delivered — against them.

## "Never turn your backs" — the law of ayat 15–16

The key word in ayah 15 is *zaḥf*, translated "in a battlefield" or "marching to battle." Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase as meeting the disbelievers "when you get near the enemy and march towards them," and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains that *zaḥf* denotes the confrontation and intermingling of the two armies. The sense, as Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān puts it, is that once a war is on, turning back and deserting the battlefield is not permissible for Muslims. Ibn Kathir spells out what fleeing really means: running away *and leaving your fellow Muslims behind*. Desertion is not only cowardice before Allah; it is betrayal of the brothers left standing.

Ayah 16 then carves out exactly two exceptions, each named with a precise Arabic term:

**1. *Mutaḥarrifan li-qitāl* — "maneuvering for battle."** The word *taḥarruf*, as Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, means turning away obliquely to one side. Saʿīd bin Jubayr and As-Suddī explained it as the feigned retreat: a fighter pretends to flee so the enemy chases him, then wheels round and strikes. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk added the scout who goes ahead of his fellows to probe the enemy's strength. The back is turned, but the heart never left the fight.

**2. *Mutaḥayyizan ilā fiʾah* — "falling back to a troop."** *Taḥayyuz* literally means to join up, and *fiʾah* is a company or group. This covers withdrawing to another Muslim unit to assist or be assisted, falling back to one's commander, or retreating to the head of the Muslims. This is not flight but regrouping — leaving in order to return stronger.

**How far does the ruling reach?** The early authorities discussed this carefully. Ibn Abī Ḥātim records that Nāfiʿ asked Ibn ʿUmar about fighters who are not stationary and may not know where their troop is. Ibn ʿUmar answered, "The troop is Allah's Messenger ﷺ," and then said of the verse: "This Ayah was about Badr, not before it nor after it." ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb, when Abū ʿUbayd was fighting at the bridge in the land of the Persians against the many Zoroastrian soldiers, said, "If he retreated to me then I would be as a troop for him," and in another report declared, "O people! We are your troop" — in Mujāhid's wording, "We are the troop of every Muslim." In other words, the entire Muslim community stands as the *fiʾah* a hard-pressed fighter may fall back upon.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān reconciles these strands. At Badr the command stood in its full severity: 313 believers faced a thousand, three times their number, and were ordered to hold regardless of the odds. Later in this very sūrah (ayat 65–66), Allah lightened the burden: one hundred steadfast believers are expected to overcome two hundred. From this comes the ruling that, per Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān, holds until the Last Day by the consensus of the majority of the Ummah and the Four Imams: so long as the enemy does not exceed **twice** your number, deserting the battlefield is ḥarām (forbidden) and a major sin; beyond that, disengaging is permitted. Ibn ʿAbbās put it memorably: "A person who fled against three did not 'flee'; but one who fled against two is a deserter."

**Why so grave?** Notice the wording of ayah 16: the deserter "has drawn upon himself" — *bāʾa bi-* — wrath from Allah; Ibn Kathir glosses it as he *returned with* wrath. Flight is itself a journey, and its arrival-point is named: "his abode is Hell — and worst indeed is that destination." Al-Bukhari and Muslim record from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Shun the seven great destructive sins," and counted among them — alongside associating partners with Allah, magic, unlawful killing, consuming ribā, and devouring an orphan's wealth — *fleeing the battlefield at the time of fighting*, together with slandering chaste believing women. Desertion sits in the same list as shirk and murder. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān adds that when some Companions retreated early at Ḥunayn, the Qurʼān itself called it a slip caused by Satan — "Satan has but made them slip" (3:155) — confirming how seriously the matter is weighed.

**And yet the law carries mercy inside it.** Tirmidhī and Abū Dāwūd report that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar once left a battlefield, took refuge in Madinah, and presented himself before the Prophet ﷺ, confessing in dismay that he had become a sinning deserter. Far from being displeased, the Prophet ﷺ comforted him: "No — you are not those who flee from battle; you are those who fall back to regroup and return to the attack, and I am your support." Retreating to the Prophet ﷺ himself fell squarely within the exception of the verse. That such a Companion was shaken even by a lawful retreat — Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān attributes it to the intense awe of Allah in his character — shows how the early generation felt the weight of these ayat.

## "You did not kill them" — ayah 17

To understand ayah 17 you must see the scene it answers. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān relates the event as reported by Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarī, al-Bayhaqī and others from narrations of Ibn ʿAbbās and others. When the thousand-man army of Makkah poured into the valley at Badr, it came openly contemptuous of the Muslims' small numbers, swollen with pride in its own strength. The Prophet ﷺ raised his hands: "Yā Allah! Here come Your beliers, the Quraysh of Makkah, all proud and arrogant. The promise of victory You have made to me — let it be fulfilled soon." The angel Jibrāʾīl came and told him to take a handful of dust and throw it toward the enemy. In the report of Ibn Abī Ḥātim from Ibn Zayd, he threw three handfuls — to the army's right, its left, and its center. And then the miracle: those handfuls were spread by Allah over the entire host, until not one man of the force was left without dust and pebbles in his eyes and face. Chaos broke out; the Muslims pursued them; the angels were with them, fighting. Ibn Kathir adds that before this the Prophet ﷺ had been in his shelter invoking Allah humbly, expressing his utter neediness before Him; then he threw the handful saying *"Shāhat al-wujūh"* — "Humiliated be their faces" — and commanded his Companions to fight with sincerity.

The battle won, the Companions returned and — as Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān relates — began recounting their exploits, each telling what he had done on the field. It was then that this verse came down: **"You did not kill them, but Allah killed them. And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw."**

Ibn Kathir draws out the theology plainly: Allah creates the actions the servants perform, and whatever good they do, it is He Who should be praised for it, for He directed them to it and helped them perform it. It was not the believers' power that felled the pagans — many against few — but Allah Who gave the victory, just as He says elsewhere: "Allah has already made you victorious at Badr, when you were a weak little force" (3:123), and warns through Ḥunayn, where great numbers "availed you naught" (9:25). Victory, Ibn Kathir insists, does not depend on numbers or weapons: "How often has a small group overcome a mighty host by Allah's leave? And Allah is with the patient" (2:249).

Notice that the address turns even to the Prophet ﷺ himself: *you* threw — the act was genuinely his — *but Allah threw*. As Ibn Kathir puts it, it is Allah Who made the sand reach their eyes and busied them with it, not the Prophet ﷺ. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains the same point: the specific outcome of the throw — that it reached the eyes of every fighting man in the enemy force and frightened them all — was not the direct effect of his throwing; it was the perfect power of Allah that produced it. The deed belonged to the servant; the effect belonged entirely to Allah. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān quotes Rūmī's couplet on this verse: "'And you did not throw when you did,' said Allah — 'Our Act precedes all other acts.'"

**"That He might test the believers by a fair trial from Him."** The word *balāʾ* literally means a test — and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains that Allah's tests come not only through hardship but also through blessing. A *balāʾ ḥasan*, a "good trial," is a test administered through comfort, wealth, support and victory: will the blessed take it as a favour from Allah and give thanks, or credit their own excellence and swell with pride? ʿUrwah bin az-Zubayr said the trial was "so that the believers know Allah's favor for them by giving them victory over their enemy, even though their enemy was numerous while they were few — that they should know His right and express gratitude." A hadith cited by Ibn Kathir conveys that every trial from Allah is in truth a favour for us.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān then makes a remarkable judgment: this instruction was *more valuable to the Muslims than the victory itself*. It disengaged their minds from the means and fastened them to the Master-Provider of all means, saving them from the pride and arrogance that, in its phrase, "intoxicates victorious nations." Ayah 17 closes: "Verily, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower" — He heard the supplication rising from the shelter at Badr, and He knows who deserves His help.

## The verdict they prayed for — ayat 18–19

Ayah 18 widens the good news: "Allah weakens the deceitful plots of the disbelievers." Ibn Kathir reads it as a promise beyond Badr — Allah will go on undoing their schemes and degrading their cause. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān adds that this was itself one purpose of the victory: to make the disbelievers understand that Divine support is not with them, and no plan succeeds without it.

Then ayah 19 delivers one of the Qurʼān's sharpest ironies. Before the Quraysh army left Makkah, its chiefs — Abū Jahl among them — clung to the drapes of the Kaʿbah and prayed. Strangely, they did not pray for their own victory by name. Their words, as Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān records citing Mazharī (and As-Suddī relates similarly in Ibn Kathir), were: "O Allah, let victory come to the superior-most of the two armies, the better-guided of the two groups, the nobler of the two parties, and to the religion which is more sublime." And on the day of Badr itself, Abū Jahl prayed: "O Allah! Whichever of the two camps severed the relation of the womb and brought us what is not familiar — destroy him this day." This is recorded by Imam Ahmad from ʿAbdullāh bin Thaʿlabah, and by An-Nasāʾī in the Book of Tafsir of his Sunan and Al-Ḥākim in his Mustadrak, who said, "It is Ṣaḥīḥ according to the criteria of the Two Shaykhs, and they did not record it."

They assumed, of course, that *they* were the superior, the better-guided, the nobler — so they thought they were praying for themselves. In reality, as Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān observes, their prayer was a curse upon their own heads and a supplication for the Muslims. So the ayah answers them with their own words: "If you ask for a judgement, then the judgement has come to you." Ibn Kathir explains: you invoked Allah for victory, judgement and a decision between you and your believing opponents — and you got what you asked for. You asked Allah to show which side stood on truth; He has shown you. Truth triumphed, falsehood was routed — by your own requested criterion.

The verse then holds out mercy and warning in a single breath. "If you cease" — Ibn Kathir: cease your disbelief and rejection of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ — "it is better for you," in this life and the Hereafter. "But if you return, We shall return": persist in aggression and Allah will repeat your defeat, as He says elsewhere, "if you return, We shall return" (17:8). And your numbers will avail you nothing, however many you gather — "for those whom Allah is with cannot be defeated." The passage seals itself with the words that explain everything before them: **"and verily, Allah is with the believers."**

## Holding the two halves together

Read as one unit, ayat 15–19 teach a single lesson from opposite directions. When you are weak and outnumbered, do not flee — because victory was never a function of numbers. When you are victorious, do not boast — because the victory was never yours. Ayah 16 forbids despair on the battlefield; ayah 17 forbids pride after it. Both prohibitions rest on the same fact, stated plainly at the passage's close: the outcome belongs to Allah, and Allah is with the believers — steadfastness without despair, gratitude without self-congratulation.

passages.title: Truly listen and obey, unlike the deaf
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are a single sustained appeal to the believers: obey Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and let your hearing of the truth be *real* hearing — the kind that ends in action — not the hollow "we have heard" of the hypocrites and disbelievers. The passage moves in one arc: the command (ayah 20), the warning example not to imitate (ayah 21), Allah's verdict on those who embody that example (ayah 22), and the reason their condition is what it is (ayah 23).

## The Badr backdrop: why obedience is the theme here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The preceding verses recounted the battle of Badr, and earlier in the sūrah Allah had explained the defeat of the Makkan disbelievers — despite their superior numbers and equipment — with the words, "That is because they were hostile to Allah and His Messenger" (8:13). That was the lesson for one side: material strength counts for nothing against the most perfect power of the Creator and Master of the heavens and the earth, and it is self-deception to hope for Allah's help while living in disobedience to Him.

Ayah 20 now turns to the other side of the same truth. The Muslims won at Badr despite their small numbers and poor equipment only through Allah's help — and that help, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, was the outcome of their obedience. So the victory itself becomes the argument for the command: "O believers! Obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you are hearing." Ibn Kathir unpacks "turn not away from him": neither hold back from obeying him and following his commands, nor indulge in what he forbade — and "while you are hearing" means after you have gained knowledge of his Message. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the sense plainly: once you have listened to the Qurʼān, the true word of Allah, do not go about doing things against the norms of genuine obedience.

## The four degrees of listening

The heart of this passage is the word *hearing*, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens it up with a framework worth memorising. Listening to the truth has four degrees:

1. **Sound only.** The words strike the ear, but the hearer neither tries to understand, nor understands, nor believes, nor acts. This, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is the degree of the polytheists and disbelievers, who heard the ayat of the Qurʼān with their own ears but were never moved to think about them.
2. **Hearing and understanding — nothing more.** No belief, no action. This is the degree of the *munāfiqīn* (hypocrites): they listen to the Qurʼān, understand it, even make a feigned show of belief and practice, but in reality do neither.
3. **Hearing, understanding, and belief — but no corresponding action.** This is the state of sinning Muslims. The real purpose of listening is not achieved, yet the belief itself has genuine worth and is not dismissed as useless.
4. **Hearing, understanding, belief, and action.** Only here is the purpose of listening fully realised. This is the station of the perfect believers.

The first three degrees, in a manner of speaking, can be set aside as not really listening at all — which is exactly how the next ayat treat them. And this is the point of ayah 20's address: the believers already possess the first three ingredients — they hear, understand, and believe. What is being demanded of them is the fourth step. They must act, do what must be done, and do it fully and faithfully, so that the purpose of hearing the word of truth is actually achieved.

## Ayah 21: "We hear" — while they do not hear

"Do not be like those who say, 'We hear,' but in fact they are not listening." Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Ishaq: this ayah refers to the hypocrites, who pretend to hear and obey while in fact doing neither. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the reference slightly: it covers the common disbelievers, who claim to be listening without even claiming belief, and the hypocrites, who go further — claiming to understand and believe as well — while both remain deprived of genuine reflection and correct understanding. Their listening therefore falls into the category of not listening, and the believers are forbidden from becoming like them.

Ibn Kathir frames the whole passage in exactly these terms: Allah commands His believing servants to obey Him and His Messenger ﷺ, and warns them against defying him and imitating the disbelievers who reject him. Ayah 21 is that warning made explicit.

## Ayah 22: the worst of all creatures

"Indeed, the worst of all beings in the sight of Allah are the deaf, the dumb — those who do not understand."

**The word dawābb.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the vocabulary. *Dawābb* is the plural of *dābbah*: literally, anything that walks on the earth, though in common usage it refers to four-legged animals. So the verse is saying: the worst of beasts in Allah's sight are those deaf to hearing the truth and dumb when it comes to accepting it. And the ayah adds a third disability: "who do not understand." Even a person who is deaf and dumb can, if he has the least fund of reason, communicate by gestures. But one who is deaf, dumb, *and* devoid of reason — the lines of communication are completely blocked. There is no way in.

**Why "worse than animals" is not rhetoric.** Ibn Kathir gives the reason for this severe judgement: every creature except these people abides by the way Allah created in it. These people were created to worship Allah — and instead disbelieved. That is why the Qurʼān elsewhere likens them to livestock: "the example of those who disbelieve is as that of him who shouts to those that hear nothing but calls and cries" (2:171), and "they are like cattle — nay, even more astray; those, they are the heedless ones" (7:179). An animal fulfils the purpose of its creation; the wilful rejecter does not.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the other side of this: human beings were created with the best of destinies — made superior among created things, with the universe placed at their service — and those great blessings are embedded in, and dependent on, listening to the truth and obeying it. Once a human being turns his back on hearing, understanding, and accepting the truth, those blessings are drawn away and he sinks to something worse than the animals. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relays a view it cites from Tafsir Ruh al-Bayan: in their original creation, human beings are superior to all animals but lower in rank than the angels; when they strive on the pathway of obedience to Allah they rise higher in status than the angels too, and should they turn away from obedience they are condemned to become the lowest of the low, far worse than animals. This is relayed here as that tafsir's position, faithfully attributed, not as a matter the passage itself settles.

**Who was meant?** Ibn Kathir records two views among the early authorities. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Jarir said ayah 22 refers to certain pagans of Quraysh from the tribe of Bani ʿAbd Ad-Dar; Muhammad bin Ishaq said it refers to the hypocrites. Ibn Kathir judges that there is no contradiction: both the disbelievers and the hypocrites are devoid of sound comprehension and have lost the intention to do good, and that shared condition — no sound understanding, no good intention, even if some raw faculty of reason remains — is precisely what the ayah describes.

## Ayah 23: why Allah did not make them hear

"Had Allah known any goodness in them, He would certainly have made them listen; and even if He had made them listen, they would have turned away in aversion."

**What "good" (khayr) means here.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *khayr* in this ayah means the desire to find the truth — the quest for it. It is that quest which opens the doors of reflection and understanding, and that quest which enables a person to believe and act. Whoever has no quest for truth has, in effect, no good in him. Had there been any such receptivity in these people, it would have been within Allah's knowledge, and He would have blessed them with the ability to listen with faith. Now, since Allah's knowledge bears out that no such good is in them, they stand deprived of every possible good in the real sense.

**The second half is not redundant.** A careful reader might feel a logical puzzle here: if Allah would have made them listen had there been good in them, what is added by "and even if He had made them listen, they would have turned away"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān resolves it by distinguishing the two senses of "made them listen." The first (*la-asmaʿahum*) means listening in the full sense — listening to accept and to benefit from. The second (*wa law asmaʿahum*) means bland, bare listening with nothing behind it. So the ayah is saying: real, faith-bearing hearing was withheld because there was no receptivity in them; and had they been given mere exposure to the truth in their present state — with no desire to receive it — they would still have turned away, paying no heed. Ibn Kathir adds the note of character: their turning away would be intentional and out of stubbornness, *even after* they comprehended. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān underlines that their aversion would not be because they had found some flaw in the religion; they simply refused to pay heed to the truth.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with one clear demand. You are not in the position of ayah 22's deaf and dumb — you have heard, understood, and believed. The command of ayah 20 is aimed at the remaining gap: close the distance between hearing and doing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly — do nothing that takes you off the path of obedience, so that the real purpose of listening to the word of truth stands fully realised. And the prohibition of ayah 21 stands as a permanent guard on that path: do not become like those who said "we have heard" while they were not listening.

passages.title: Respond to the call that gives you life
passages.tafsir:
## The call that gives you life

With this passage, Sūrat al-Anfāl turns from narrating the battle of Badr to drawing out its lessons. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that after describing the battle and the Divine favours shown in it, the Qurʼān now offers the believers "words of good counsel" built on its outcome — and that counsel opens in ayah 24 with the summons that names this whole passage: *respond to Allah and the Messenger when he calls you to what gives you life*. The verses that follow continue the same counsel, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān characterises each step: a warning against a particular sin whose punishment does not stay confined to those who commit it (25); a reminder of the believers' past weakness, given to persuade them towards obedience and make the Divine injunctions easy on them (26); a prohibition of betraying trusts (27), followed by a warning about what is usually the cause of such negligence — attachment to property and children (28); and finally the threefold reward of those who hold fast to taqwā (29). Three times the passage begins again with "O you who believe" (24, 27, 29), as if the call keeps being renewed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a striking preliminary point about ayah 24: what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ call you to brings *them* no benefit at all. Every Divine command is prescribed purely for the good of the one commanded. So what is this "life"? The early commentators answered differently — al-Suddī said it is īmān (faith), "because the disbeliever is dead"; Qatādah said it is the Qurʼān, in which lies all life and success of both worlds; Mujāhid said it is truth; Ibn Isḥāq said it is jihād, through which Allah conferred honour on the Muslims — and ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, in Ibn Kathīr, explained it similarly: answer when called to jihād, with which Allah gives you might after meekness and strength after weakness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān rules that there is no contradiction: all of these give **life to the heart**, and the life of the heart means removing every barrier — inertia, desire — that stands between the created and the Creator, so the heart fills with the light of knowing Him. Al-Bukhārī glossed the words simply: "answer" means obey, and "that which will give you life" means "that which will make your affairs good."

**How literally to take "respond"?** Two famous incidents answer that. Al-Bukhārī narrates that Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā was praying when the Prophet ﷺ passed by and called him, and he did not answer until he finished. The Prophet ﷺ said, "What prevented you from answering me? Has not Allah said: *O you who believe! Answer Allah and His Messenger when he calls you to that which will give you life*?" — and then taught him "the greatest sūrah in the Qurʼān": al-Fātiḥah, "the seven oft-repeated verses." Based on a narration from Abū Hurayrah, Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʼī have reported the like of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: the Prophet ﷺ sent for him while he was praying; he finished his prayer sooner than he normally would and presented himself, offering his ṣalāh as his excuse for the delay — and when the Prophet ﷺ reminded him of this very verse, he resolved: "If you call me, even when I am making my ṣalāh, I shall present myself before you immediately." Even the prayer itself does not excuse delaying the Messenger's ﷺ call. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the juristic discussion: some jurists held that obeying the Prophet's ﷺ command during ṣalāh does not interfere with the prayer; others that the prayer is terminated and must be made up later (qaḍāʼ — offering a missed or broken prayer afterwards). This particular obedience is exclusive to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — yet an analogous principle remains: if someone praying sees, say, a blind man about to fall into a well, he should break his prayer to save him and make it up later.

## Allah comes between a person and his heart

Ayah 24 ends with words that deserve to be sat with: *know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart*. Ibn ʿAbbās explained: "Allah prevents the believer from disbelief and the disbeliever from faith" — al-Ḥākim recorded this in his Mustadrak and said, "It is Ṣaḥīḥ and they did not record it"; and Mujāhid, Saʿīd, ʿIkrimah and others said the same. Al-Suddī put it starkly: a person "will neither believe nor disbelieve except by His leave."

Ibn Kathīr notes that several hadiths conform with the meaning of this ayah. Imam Aḥmad records from Anas ibn Mālik that the Prophet ﷺ used to say often, "O You Who changes the hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion." The Companions asked, "We believed in you and in what you brought us — are you afraid for us?" He said, "Yes, for the hearts are between two of Allah's Fingers; He changes them (as He wills)." Al-Tirmidhī recorded this in the Book of Qadar and graded it ḥasan; a similar narration from al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān is recorded by Imam Aḥmad, al-Nasāʼī and Ibn Mājah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws two practical lessons from this sentence, and both are worth living by. **First, urgency.** If you find the door open to a good deed — or the strength to leave a sin — act *now*. Divine decree can intervene between a person and his intention: sickness, death, some sudden preoccupation, and the opportunity is gone. "Refuse to put off until tomorrow what must be done today — for who knows what is going to happen tomorrow?" And even if the chance returns, no one knows "whether or not the surge and urge of this good deed remains active later on." **Second, nearness.** The verse signals how close Allah is to His servant — as the Qurʼān says elsewhere, *closer to him than his jugular vein* (50:16). The heart is at His disposal at every moment: when He wills to protect a servant, He places a barrier between his heart and sin; and hearts can equally be barred from good. That is why the Prophet ﷺ made that prayer for firmness so constantly. The believer answers the call quickly precisely because he cannot take his own heart for granted.

## A fitnah that does not strike the wrongdoers alone

Ayah 25 is one of the Qurʼān's most sobering warnings: *beware of a fitnah* — a trial, an affliction — *that will not strike only the wrongdoers among you*. Ibn Kathīr explains: when sins are not stopped and prevented, the resulting trial engulfs the wicked *and those around them*.

The Companions themselves discovered how directly this applied to them. Imam Aḥmad records that when al-Zubayr was asked at the battle of al-Jamal why he had come, he answered: "We recited this ayah at the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿUthmān — *and we did not think that this Ayah was about us too, until it reached us as it did*." Mujāhid said of the verse simply: "It is for you too!"

Which sin unleashes such a fitnah? Ibn ʿAbbās gave the explanation Ibn Kathīr calls "very good": Allah commanded the believers to stop evil from flourishing among them, so that He does not encompass them all in torment. On this basis, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, many commentators identified the sin as **abandoning al-amr bil-maʿrūf wa'l-nahy ʿani'l-munkar** — bidding the fair and forbidding the unfair. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the obvious objection — does this not contradict *no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another* (35:18)? No: the sinners are seized for their sin, and the "sinless" are seized for a sin genuinely their own — seeing wrong, having the ability to stop it, and staying silent. No one carries anyone else's burden.

The Sunnah presses this hard. The Prophet ﷺ said, in a hadith Imam Aḥmad records from Ḥudhayfah: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! You will enjoin righteousness and forbid evil, or Allah will send a punishment upon you from Him; you will supplicate then to Him, but He will not answer your supplication." Abū Bakr said in a sermon — reported in Tirmidhī, Abū Dāwūd and elsewhere — that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say: when people see an oppressor and do not hold his hand back from injustice, Allah's punishment is near to falling on all of them alike. And there is the unforgettable parable recorded by al-Bukhārī from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr: a people drew lots for places on a ship; those on the lower deck, tired of troubling those above whenever they needed water, decided to make a hole in their own share of the hull. "If the people in the upper part let the others do what they suggested, all the people of the ship would be destroyed, but if they prevented them, both parties would be safe." A community is one hull; private sin is never merely private.

Yet the verse is not a counsel of despair for the righteous caught in such a flood.
