Imam Aḥmad records from Umm Salamah that the Prophet ﷺ said that if sins become apparent in the Ummah, Allah will surround them with punishment; she asked, "Will they have righteous people among them then?" He said yes — "They will be stricken as the people, but they will end up with Allah's forgiveness and pleasure." The worldly trial may engulf everyone; the final outcome does not. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, from Tafsīr Maẓharī, a second reading: the sin may be abandoning jihād when the general call is given, for the consequences of that — enemies overrunning Muslim lands — fall on the innocent as much as the negligent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this reading fits the preceding verses, which condemned forsaking the battlefield — and that at Badr itself, when some Muslims left their security post on the hills, the ill effects did not stay with those who erred but struck the whole army, so much so that the Prophet ﷺ was himself injured.

## Remember when you were few

Ayah 26 grounds the whole appeal in memory. *Remember when you were few, oppressed in the land, fearing that people would snatch you away* — the Makkan years, when the believers practised their religion in secret and feared kidnap from every side. Then Allah gave them refuge in Madīnah, allies in its people, victory at Badr, and good provision. Qatādah's description of the Arabs before Islam is worth quoting: they were "the weakest of the weak... They were being eaten up, but unable to eat up others! By Allah, we do not know of a people on the face of the earth at that time who had a worse life than them. When Allah brought Islam, He made it dominant on the earth... so thank Him for His favours, for your Lord is One Who bestows favours and likes praise. Verily, those who thank Allah enjoy even more bounties from Him."

The verse ends *so that you may be grateful* — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the circle: the finest demonstration of gratitude, in the real sense, is nothing other than obedience to what Allah commands. That, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is exactly why the reminder is given here: remembering the transformation Allah worked is what persuades the heart towards obedience and makes His injunctions easy to carry.

## Do not betray — and the trial of wealth and children

Ayah 27 forbids khiyānah — breach of trust — toward Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and in your amānāt (things entrusted to you). Ibn ʿAbbās explained that the amānah is everything Allah has entrusted His servants with, including the obligations themselves: "do not betray" means "do not abandon the obligations." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens it to both sets of rights — the rights of Allah and the mutual rights people owe one another — whether by neglecting them wholly or fulfilling them defectively; and the closing words *while you know* underline that the believers already know breach of trust to be an evil, so no intelligent person would choose it.

Two stories from the Sīrah illuminate this verse. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs relate that in the year of the conquest of Makkah, **Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah** wrote to Quraysh alerting them that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intended to march towards them. Allah informed His Messenger ﷺ; the letter was retrieved; Ḥāṭib was summoned and admitted what he had done. When ʿUmar asked leave to strike off his head "for he has betrayed Allah, His Messenger and the believers," the Prophet ﷺ said: "Leave him! He participated in Badr. How do you know that Allah has not looked at those who participated in Badr and said: do whatever you want, for I have forgiven you." Ibn Kathīr notes the principle the majority of scholars draw here: a verse revealed about a specific incident is applied by its general wording, not confined to its occasion.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that the majority of commentators tie the revelation to **Abū Lubābah** during the siege of Banū Qurayẓah. Besieged for twenty-one days, the tribe asked to leave for Syria; the Prophet ﷺ refused, and the only option of peace left to them was to accept whatever decision Saʿd ibn Muʿādh gave in their case. They asked instead that Abū Lubābah — whose family and property lay in their territory — be entrusted with the decision, hoping he would be lenient. When their men and women gathered around him weeping and asked whether surrender would bring leniency, he knew it would not — and, moved partly by their wailing and partly by his own love and concern for his family and children, he drew his hand across his throat: a sign that they would be killed, disclosing the Prophet's ﷺ confidence. The remorse was immediate. He went straight to the mosque and tied himself to one of its pillars, swearing to remain until his repentance was accepted, even if he died there. For seven days he stood bound; his wife and daughter attended to him, untying him only for prayer and necessities; he scarcely ate or drank, and would faint from weakness. The Prophet ﷺ said that had Abū Lubābah come to him first he would have sought forgiveness for him; now they must wait for revelation. When, late one night, the verses of his acceptance came down, he refused to be untied by anyone but the Prophet ﷺ — who loosed him with his own hands at Fajr. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states plainly what moved him: the consideration of property and the love of family and children — the very thing the next verse warns about.

That story is the living commentary on ayah 28: *know that your wealth and your children are but a fitnah, and that with Allah is a mighty reward*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that fitnah in the Qurʼān carries three senses — a trial, a punishment, and a cause of punishment — and all three fit here. Wealth and children are Allah's blessings given to test whether we respond with gratitude or absorption; loved immoderately, they become hardship in this world and, where gained or spent against Allah's command, an instrument of punishment in the next. Ibn Kathīr adds the balance: Allah's reward, favour and Paradise are better for you than wealth and children — and cites the hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥ that none has tasted the sweetness of faith until "Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than anyone else," and the Prophet's ﷺ confirmed saying in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "None of you will have faith unless I become dearer to him than himself, his family, his wealth and all people."

## What taqwā buys: the Furqān

Ayah 29 seals the passage with a promise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines the condition: the one who keeps his emotion subservient to his reason in this trial, so that obedience to Allah and love for Him stay ahead of everything — that is **taqwā** in the Qurʼān's terminology. Three things follow.

**First, Furqān.** Furqān and farq share one meaning: a Furqān is what separates two things and makes them clearly distinct — which is why the day of Badr itself is called in the Qurʼān *Yawm al-Furqān*, the Day of Distinction between right and wrong. The early commentators unfolded it richly: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, Mujāhid and others said "a way out" — Mujāhid adding, "in this life and the Hereafter"; other narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās give "salvation" and "aid"; Ibn Isḥāq said "a criterion between truth and falsehood," which Ibn Kathīr judges the most comprehensive, containing all the rest. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the majority view that it means Allah's help and support — no enemy can hurt the people of taqwā, and success goes with them — and the other view that it is inner light: the wisdom and insight to tell the genuine from the fake. Tafsīr Mahāʼimī even hears in it a gentle allusion to Abū Lubābah's slip: the correct and only method of keeping his family and children protected was total obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, under which everything belonging to him would have come within Allah's own security.

**Second and third**, the expiation of misdeeds — the person of taqwā is granted, in this very world, the ability to do good deeds that outshine his slips — and forgiveness, the ultimate pardon in the Hereafter.

And the verse ends: *Allah is the Owner of great bounty*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches the hint: a reward normally follows the measure of the deed, but Allah's grace is bound by no measure. Whoever makes taqwā his way of life should expect from his Lord far more than even these three. The passage that opened with a call thus closes with a guarantee: answer the One who calls you to life, and He gives you a way out, His help and support, and His forgiveness.

passages.title: Meccan plots and mockery at the Sacred Mosque
passages.tafsir:
This passage is an indictment read out over Makkah. In six ayat Allah recounts what the Quraysh actually did with the Prophet ﷺ and with His revelation — they plotted to imprison, kill or expel him (ayah 30), sneered that they could produce the like of the Qur'an (31), dared Allah to rain stones on them (32) — and then answers the question their own dare raises: why has the punishment not come? Ayah 33 names the two shields that held it back, and ayat 34–35 explain why, with those shields gone, their entitlement to punishment became mature and complete. When and how that punishment actually fell — at Badr, at the Conquest of Makkah, or in the Hereafter — is a question the commentators answer in more than one way, and we will meet their discussion below. Ibn Kathir notes that it was after the Messenger ﷺ migrated to Madinah that Allah revealed Sūrat al-Anfāl to him, reminding him of His favours and the bounties He had given him — and this passage recalls the deliverance behind him.

## The night of the plot (ayah 30)

Ibn Kathir relates the scene behind ayah 30 through a chain he gives in full: Muhammad bin Ishaq, the author of al-Maghazi, reported it from 'Abdullah bin Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas. When Islam gained a foothold in Madinah — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this was what alarmed the Quraysh, since the Muslims now had a second centre beyond their control — the chiefs of Quraysh gathered at Dar an-Nadwah, their council house near the Sacred Mosque. Iblis himself joined them in the guise of a venerable old man "from Najd," offering his advice.

Three proposals were tabled, and the ayah records all three. One chief said: imprison him in chains until he dies as the poets before him died. The old man of Najd objected — his companions would storm the prison and free him. Another said: expel him from your land and be rid of his trouble. Again the objection — have you forgotten how his speech captures hearts? Free, he would gather the Arabs and return against you. Then Abu Jahl spoke: take one strong young man from every tribe, arm each with a sword, and let them strike him as one man — his blood would be spread across all the tribes, and Banu Hashim, unable to wage war against all of Quraysh, would have to accept blood-money. "This is it," said the disguised Iblis, and the assembly resolved to act that very night.

But Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ with news of the plot and Allah's permission to migrate. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the night itself: 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, lay in the Prophet's ﷺ bed — gladly risking his life, a merit forever credited to him — while the Prophet ﷺ walked out through the cordon of armed men, casting dust on their heads as Allah turned their sight away from him. They kept their siege until morning, and went home disgraced.

**The word makr.** The ayah ends: "they were plotting and Allah too was plotting; and Allah is the best of plotters." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the Arabic word makr precisely: it means frustrating an adversary's intention through a hidden stratagem. In itself it is neutral — done for an evil end it is blameworthy, done for a good end it is praiseworthy. So the word can be used of Allah, but only in contexts (like this one) where no blameworthy sense could be imagined. Ibn Kathir also cites — through Muhammad bin Ishaq, from Muhammad bin Ja'far bin az-Zubayr — the comment of 'Urwah bin az-Zubayr, paraphrasing the divine speech: "I plotted against them with My sure planning, and I saved you from them." The early authorities also unpack liyuthbitūka: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said it means "to imprison you," and as-Suddi said ithbāt is to confine or shackle — exactly the first proposal at Dar an-Nadwah.

**A verb for present and future.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a subtle grammatical choice: "wa-yamkurūna wa-yamkuru Allāh" is cast in what it calls the indefinite tense — the Arabic verb-form that denotes both present and future. The hint is that this is a standing pattern, not a closed chapter: disbelievers will keep engineering designs against the believers, and Allah's help will keep repulsing them — as it did that night in Makkah.

## Mockery, and a dare flung at heaven (ayat 31–32)

Ayah 31 records the Quraysh's pose of contempt: "We have heard; if we wished we could say the like of this — this is nothing but tales of the ancients." According to Sa'id bin Jubayr, as-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj, the speaker was an-Nadr bin al-Harith, a merchant who had travelled to Persia and collected stories of kings like Rustum and Isphandiyar. Whenever the Prophet ﷺ left a gathering, an-Nadr would retell his Persian tales and ask, "Who has better tales — I or Muhammad?" Ibn Kathir's verdict is withering: they boasted with words, not deeds. The Qur'an had already challenged them to produce even one chapter like it, and they never could. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the Companions confronted an-Nadr directly: if you can say the like of it, why don't you? To go on claiming the ability after failing the open challenge is something no self-respecting person would say. As for "tales of the ancients" (asāṭīr al-awwalīn) — the claim that the Prophet ﷺ had merely copied old books — Ibn Kathir calls it pure falsehood, refuted in the Qur'an itself (25:5–6). An-Nadr was captured at Badr and executed on the Prophet's ﷺ order.

Ayah 32 records something even more brazen — a prayer: "O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones on us from the sky, or bring us a painful torment." Al-Bukhari recorded, from Anas bin Malik, that the one who said this was Abu Jahl bin Hisham — the same man who designed the assassination plot. Ibn Kathir pauses over how ignorant and stubborn this dare is: the honest prayer would have been, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then guide us to it and help us follow it." Instead they invoked judgment on themselves, joining the ancient nations who mocked the same way — the people of Shu'ayb had said, "So cause a piece of the heaven to fall on us, if you are of the truthful" (26:187).

## The two shields (ayah 33)

Allah's answer to the dare is one of the most consoling ayat in the Qur'an: "And Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor will He punish them while they seek forgiveness." Two things stood between Makkah and the stones its chiefs demanded: the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, and istighfār — the seeking of Allah's forgiveness.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that even the pagans, circling the House in tawāf, would cry "O Allah, Your forgiveness, Your forgiveness" — mixed though it was with their shirk. Ibn 'Abbas summed the ayah up: "They had two safety shelters: the Prophet ﷺ, and their seeking forgiveness. The Prophet ﷺ went away, and only seeking forgiveness remained." At-Tirmidhi recorded from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah sent down to me two safe shelters for the benefit of my Ummah… When I die, I will leave the seeking of forgiveness with them, until the Day of Resurrection." And Ahmad in his Musnad and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak recorded from Abu Sa'id that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ related: Shaytan said, "By Your might, O Lord! I will go on luring Your servants as long as their souls are in their bodies," and the Lord replied, "By My might and majesty! I will keep forgiving them as long as they keep invoking Me for forgiveness" — al-Hakim graded its chain sahih.

**How the shields were lifted — two scholarly readings.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out a genuine difference here. Ibn Jarir held that the ayah tracks the events of the Hijrah: the first clause was revealed while the Prophet ﷺ was still in Makkah; after he migrated, the second clause applied, because the weak Muslims left behind in Makkah were still begging Allah's forgiveness, and for their sake the city was spared; and when even they migrated, ayah 34 was revealed — now "what is with them that Allah should not punish them?" — and the punishment came, on this reading, with the Conquest of Makkah at Muslim hands. Others held that the Prophet's ﷺ presence in the world itself is the shield: because his prophethood is universal and lasts until the Last Day — unlike earlier prophets sent to one people, whose departure from a town opened it to destruction — no mass punishment will annihilate his Ummah while his mission endures. On this second reading, the pagans' own istighfār in tawāf was the second shield, rewarded in this world though worthless for the Hereafter (for Allah lets no deed go entirely to waste), and the punishment threatened in ayah 34 is that of the Hereafter. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the comfort out of the second view: this Ummah remains safe from the kind of total destruction that erased the peoples of Nuh, Lut and Shu'ayb — though limited punishments on individuals, as the Prophet ﷺ foretold, are not excluded. Ibn Kathir, for his part, reads the lifting of the shields as fulfilled at Badr, where the chief pagans were killed or captured — and he links it to Allah's word about Hudaybiyyah (48:25), that only the unknown believers still inside Makkah held back a painful torment.

## Why punishment became fully due (ayat 34–35)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads these two ayat as listing three crimes beyond the Quraysh's basic disbelief.

**First, barring the Sacred Mosque.** "Why should Allah not punish them while they hinder people from al-Masjid al-Haram?" The reference is to Hudaybiyah in the sixth year after Hijrah, when the Prophet ﷺ came with his Companions intending only 'Umrah, and the Makkans forced them to release their ihram and turn back — people incapable of true worship themselves, blocking those who sought it.

**Second, a false claim of custodianship.** "They are not its guardians (awliyāʼ); none can be its guardians except those who have taqwā." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān exposes the double error: no disbeliever can be custodian of any mosque at all; and even a legitimate custodian has no right to bar people from a mosque — it is the House of Allah, open to all. The only exceptions the Sharī'ah allows are protective: the Prophet ﷺ taught that mosques should be shielded from small children with no sense of purity, from the insane, and from quarrelling — cases of desecration or harm to worshippers. Beyond that, no custodian may turn a Muslim away. As for who the true awliyāʼ are: 'Urwah, as-Suddi and Muhammad bin Ishaq said the ayah means Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions; Mujahid said it is the mujahidin in Allah's cause wherever they may be; and some commentators read the pronoun as referring to Allah — only those mindful of Him are the friends (awliyāʼ) of Allah — from which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a sharp conclusion: whoever claims to be a walī of Allah while acting against the Sharī'ah is a liar, and those who venerate such a person are deceived.

**Third, worship that was no worship.** "Their prayer at the House was nothing but mukāʼ and taṣdiyah" (ayah 35). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and a long list of early authorities explained: mukāʼ is whistling, taṣdiyah is clapping the hands — and Ibn 'Abbas added that Quraysh would even circle the Ka'bah naked, whistling and clapping. Sa'id bin Jubayr and 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd read taṣdiyah as their hindering from Allah's path. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān remarks that no reasonable person would call this worship — it falls below ordinary human dignity. Hence the sentence that closes the passage: "So taste the punishment, because you used to disbelieve." Ad-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj and Muhammad bin Ishaq said this was the death and capture at Badr; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān allows both Badr and the punishment of the Hereafter.

## Living it

Three threads to carry away. First, the lesson of ayah 30's verb — cast, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, in the tense that speaks of present and future alike: schemes against the believers never stop, and neither does Allah's counter-planning — the believer's task is trust, not panic. Second, ayah 33 hands this Ummah its permanent shelter: the Prophet ﷺ has gone from among us, but he left istighfār with us "until the Day of Resurrection" — as long as the tongue keeps asking, the Lord, by His own oath, keeps forgiving. Third, the contrast the passage builds between two prayers: Abu Jahl's arrogant "rain stones on us" and the humble asking-for-guidance Ibn Kathir says they should have prayed. The passage asks which posture we bring to the truth when it confronts us — and warns that a mosque, any mosque, belongs to Allah and to the people of taqwā, never to those who would turn it into a stage for noise or a gate they control.

passages.title: Wealth spent against Allah, and the ultimatum
passages.tafsir:
# Surah 8, Ayat 36–40 — Wealth spent against Allah, and the ultimatum

These five ayat are the Qur'an's verdict on the enemy's war-chest — and, in the same breath, an open door held out to the very men funding that war. Ayat 36–37 announce that every coin the disbelievers spend to block people from Allah's path is money already lost: it will turn into anguish, then defeat, then Hell. Ayat 38–40 then deliver the ultimatum: stop, and the past is wiped clean; persist, and the fate of earlier nations is already on record — and know that the believers you are fighting have Allah Himself as their Protector. What binds the passage into one unit is a single question: what does wealth actually buy when it is spent against Allah?

## The money behind Uhud

Ibn Kathir opens with the occasion of revelation. Muhammad bin Ishaq narrated that Az-Zuhri, Muhammad bin Yahya bin Hibban, 'Asim bin 'Umar bin Qatadah and Al-Husayn bin 'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Amr bin Sa'id bin Mu'adh said: Quraysh suffered defeat at Badr and their forces went back to Makkah, while Abu Sufyan went back with the trade caravan intact. Then the men who had lost fathers, sons or brothers at Badr — 'Abdullah bin Abi Rabi'ah, 'Ikrimah bin Abi Jahl, Safwan bin Umayyah and other men of Quraysh — went to Abu Sufyan bin Harb and to those among Quraysh who had wealth in that caravan: "O people of Quraysh! Muhammad has grieved you and killed the chiefs among you. Therefore, help us with this wealth so that we can fight him, it may be that we will avenge our losses." They agreed — and that wealth went into fighting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at Uhud. Muhammad bin Ishaq said that this ayah was revealed about them, according to Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Al-Hakam bin 'Uyaynah, Qatadah, As-Suddi and Ibn Abza said it was revealed about Abu Sufyan and his spending money in Uhud to fight the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; Ad-Dahhak said it was revealed about the idolators of Badr. Ibn Kathir concludes: "In any case, the Ayah is general, even though there was a specific incident that accompanied its revelation."

## Four stages of loss

Ayah 36 traces the money through four stages: *they will go on spending it* — then it becomes a **hasrah**, an anguish and grief, for them — *then they will be overcome* — and finally "those who disbelieve will be gathered unto Hell." The punishment does not wait for the Hereafter; the spending itself curdles into grief in this world. Ibn Kathir explains: they seek to extinguish the Light of Allah and make their word higher than the word of truth — "However, Allah will complete His Light, even though the disbelievers hate it." He will aid His religion, make His Word dominant, and His religion will prevail above all religions. Whoever among them lives long will witness with his eyes and hear with his ears what causes him grief; those among them who are killed or die are returned to eternal disgrace and everlasting punishment.

Maarif ul Qur'an extends the ayah's reach to our own time: those who spend enormous wealth in the name of hospitals, educational institutions and charities only to stop people from following Islam and attract them to the false, and those who spend to sow doubts and superstitions against the established beliefs of Islam, fall squarely inside its scope. And, Maarif adds, Allah has His own ways of keeping the faith He revealed protected — it is openly noticed on many occasions that such people fail to achieve their objective despite the huge sums spent.

## Al-khabith and at-tayyib: the great sorting

Ayah 37 gives the divine purpose behind the whole trial: "so that Allah may separate **al-khabith** from **at-tayyib**." Maarif ul Qur'an pauses on this pair of words: *khabith* is whatever is impure, filthy and forbidden; *tayyib* is its exact opposite — pure, clean, nice and lawful. The commentators read the pair in two ways, and both are recorded:

**The wealth reading** (Maarif): the enormous wealth the disbelievers spent was impure and filthy, and its end matched its nature — they suffered the loss of wealth and the loss of lives as well. The Muslims spent very little, but it was pure and lawful, and those who spent it succeeded, with the spoils of war besides. Maarif then offers a striking image: just as a magnet pulls iron and amber pulls grass, deeds and morals have a pull of their own — one bad deed draws in another, impure wealth pulls in more impure wealth into a heap, and Allah will heap all impure wealth into Jahannam, leaving those it belonged to in terrible loss.

**The people reading**, held by "a large number of commentators": the pure means the true believers and the impure means the disbelievers — the true believers gathered together in Jannah, and the disbelievers, all of them at one place, into Jahannam. The battlefield becomes a sieve. Ibn 'Abbas — as 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported from him — said Allah thereby distinguishes "the people of happiness and the people of misery." Ibn Kathir connects this to 3:179 ("Allah will not leave the believers in the state in which you are now, until He distinguishes the wicked from the good") and 3:142, and paraphrases the ayah: 'We tried you with combatant disbelievers whom We made able to spend money in fighting you.' Even the enemy's funding, in other words, was part of the test — and its end is the terrible picture the ayah paints: the wicked put one over another, in a pile on top of each other, heaped together and cast into Hell. "Those! It is they who are the losers" — in this life and the Hereafter.

## The door left open (ayah 38)

Then comes an astonishing pivot. The very men bankrolling the war are offered total amnesty: "Say to those who have disbelieved, if they cease, their past will be forgiven." Ibn Kathir: if they cease the disbelief, defiance and stubbornness they indulge in, and embrace Islam, obedience and repentance, the past is forgiven along with their sins and errors. He anchors this in two hadith. It is recorded in the Sahih Al-Bukhari that Abu Wa'il said that Ibn Mas'ud said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "He who becomes good in his Islam, will not be punished for what he has committed during Jahiliyyah (before Islam). He who becomes bad in his Islam, will face a punishment for his previous and latter deeds." And it is also recorded in the Sahih that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Islam erases what occurred before it, and repentance erases what occurs before it."

The same ayah carries the warning: "But if they return, then the examples of those punished before them have already preceded." Ibn Kathir: Allah's way with the nations of old is that when they disbelieve and rebel, He sends down to them immediate torment and punishment. Maarif captures the tone of the address — persuasion and warning fused in one sentence: Allah does not have to think about making some new law for these people; the law is already there, in force since the disbelievers of earlier times, and the same law would simply come into force against them too — destruction in this world and the punishment of the Hereafter.

## Fitnah and Din: what the fighting was for (ayah 39)

Ayah 39 — "And fight them until there is no more Fitnah, and the religion will all be for Allah alone" — turns on two words, and Maarif notes that both are used in many shades of meaning. Two interpretations come down from the Sahabah (the Companions) and the Tabi'in (their students), and the scholars genuinely differed:

**First, from Ibn 'Abbas:** *fitnah* means kufr and shirk — disbelief and the worship of others alongside Allah — and *din* means the religion of Islam. Muslims must continue fighting until disbelief disintegrates and no religion remains but Islam. Maarif clarifies that on this reading the command is specific to the people of Makkah and of Arabia — because the Arabian Peninsula is "the home of Islam," where the presence of any other religion would be dangerous for Islam; in the rest of the world other religions and faiths could continue to exist, as other verses of the Qur'an and reports from hadith confirm. In Ibn Kathir, Ad-Dahhak reported that Ibn 'Abbas said about the ayah, "So that there is no more Shirk," and similar was said by Abu Al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, As-Suddi, Muqatil bin Hayyan and Zayd bin Aslam. As for "the religion will all be for Allah alone": Ad-Dahhak reported that Ibn 'Abbas said, "So that Tawhid is practiced in sincerity with Allah" — tawhid being the worship of Allah alone; and Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj said, "So that La ilaha illa-llah — 'there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah' — is proclaimed."

**Second, from Ibn 'Umar and others:** *fitnah* means persecution — the chain of pain and suffering the disbelievers of Makkah inflicted on Muslims: tormenting them in Makkah, pursuing, killing and looting them as they migrated, then attacking the city of Madinah itself. Ibn Kathir records the same reading through another chain: Muhammad bin Ishaq said that he was informed from Az-Zuhri, from 'Urwah bin Az-Zubayr and other scholars, that the fitnah here means "until no Muslim is persecuted so that he abandons his religion." On this reading *din* means the state of prevailing over antagonists — Islam's ascendancy, its ability to actually defend and protect Muslims from the injustices inflicted on them.

Ibn 'Umar himself is the living commentary on this ayah, and Al-Bukhari collected several narrations about him. In one, a man came to him and asked why he did not fight, citing first the ayah "And if two parties among the believers fall to fighting..." (49:9); Ibn 'Umar answered that he preferred to be reminded by that ayah rather than by the one that says "And whoever kills a believer intentionally..." (4:93). The man then quoted this very ayah — "And fight them until there is no more Fitnah." Ibn 'Umar said: "We did that during the time of the Messenger of Allah, when Islam was weak and the man would be tried in religion, either tormented to death or being imprisoned. When Islam became stronger and widespread, there was no more Fitnah." In a separate report, also collected by Al-Bukhari, Sa'id bin Jubayr said that Ibn 'Umar came to them and was asked, "What do you say about fighting during Fitnah?" He replied: "Do you know what Fitnah refers to? Muhammad ﷺ was fighting against the idolators, and at that time, attending (or residing with) the idolators was a Fitnah (trial in religion). It is nothing like what you are doing, fighting to gain leadership!"

Maarif adds the scene behind such exchanges: when Hajjaj ibn Yusuf launched an armed attack against 'Abdullah ibn Zubayr in Makkah and Muslim swords swung against Muslims, people came to Ibn 'Umar and urged him to come out and remove this fitnah, quoting this very ayah. His reply: I do recite this verse, and act on it — we continued fighting the disbelievers as it commanded until no fitnah remained and Islam became the dominant din; you now wish to kill each other and plant the fitnah all over again. In such infighting among Muslims, he noted, the Holy Prophet's ﷺ instruction is that the one who keeps sitting is better than the one who stands up. The ayah, in other words, is no license for any sword raised under a religious banner — and intention decides everything. In the Two Sahihs it is recorded that Abu Musa Al-Ash'ari said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about a man who fights because he is courageous, in prejudice with his people, or to show off — which of these is for the cause of Allah? He said: "Whoever fights so that Allah's Word is the supreme, is in the cause of Allah, the Exalted and Most Honored."

Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith collected in the Two Sahihs, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was commanded to fight against the people until they proclaim, 'There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah.' If and when they say it, they will preserve their blood and wealth from me, except for its right (Islamic penal code), and their reckoning is with Allah, the Exalted and Most Honored." Maarif records the same teaching from a hadith of al-Bukhari and Muslim — in its wording, until they accept the Kalimah, establish Salah and pay Zakah — with Muhammad Taqi Usmani's clarifying note: this principle is restricted to the Arabian Peninsula, where no disbeliever is allowed to live as a permanent citizen; in other parts of the world, non-Muslims may opt for jizyah (a tax), continue to profess their own religion, and have the punishment of their disbelief deferred to the Hereafter.

## "Allah is All-Seer": judging by the outward

The closing clause of ayah 39 — "But if they cease, then certainly, Allah is All-Seer of what they do" — carries a whole principle of Islamic dealing. Ibn Kathir glosses the clause: if they desist from their kufr as a result of your fighting them, "even though you do not know the true reasons why they did so" — then Allah is All-Seer of what they do; and he sets beside it the similar ayat 9:5 ("But if they repent and perform the Salah, and give Zakah, then leave their way free"), 9:11 and 2:193. Maarif spells out the anxiety this raised and the practical rule it settles: what if a declaration of Islam or a peace pact is just a strategy of deception usually employed in wars? The answer: Muslims are bound by the deeds they see outwardly; the One who looks into hearts and knows their hidden secrets is none but Allah. When the disbelievers declare their adherence to Islam or make a peace pact, Muslims have no choice but to stop fighting — and whatever deception may lurk falls in Allah's domain, and He will take care of it in some other way. Maarif observes that, in a miraculous manner, Muslims never actually faced such an embarrassing situation in any of their battlefields — while the hundreds of peacetime hypocrites, even spies, had to be treated as Muslims unless they themselves betrayed their hostility or contravened the peace agreement.

The Sunnah drives this home with unforgettable force. It is recorded in the Sahih that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Usamah bin Zayd — when he overpowered a man with his sword after that man proclaimed that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, and killed him: "Have you killed him after he proclaimed, 'La Ilaha Illallah'? What would you do with regard to 'La Ilaha Illallah' on the Day of Resurrection?" Usamah said, "O Allah's Messenger! He only said it to save himself." The Messenger ﷺ replied, "Did you cut his heart open?" — and he kept repeating, "What would you do with regard to 'La Ilaha Illallah' on the Day of Resurrection?" until Usamah said, "I wished I had embraced Islam only that day." And for the non-Muslim who makes peace: Abu Dawud reported from several noble Companions that the Holy Prophet ﷺ said that whoever does any injustice to a peace-pact beneficiary (a person who has entered into a pact of allegiance with the Islamic government), or brings him harm, or makes him do more than he can physically do, or takes something from him without his genuine, heart-felt consent — then on the Day of Judgment he ﷺ will support that person against the Muslim who did it.

## The best of protectors (ayah 40)

The passage closes: "And if they turn away, then know that Allah is your **Mawla** — an excellent protector, and an excellent helper." Ibn Kathir explains *Mawla* here as protector, master and supporter: if the disbelievers persist in defying and fighting you, then Allah is your protector, master and supporter against your enemies. Maarif catches the pastoral point: a command to keep fighting is usually associated with a big army, ample weapons and logistic support, and in those days the Muslims did not have much of any of it — so the command could have felt heavy. Hence the antidote: it does not matter that the enemy has more men and equipment; where in the world will they obtain the unseen support and help of Allah, which the Muslims have with them and have been witnessing on every battlefield? Everyone in the world leans on some helper, Maarif concludes, and a helper's worth depends on his power, strength, knowledge and experience — and a whole world-full of people could never equal, let alone exceed, the power and strength and knowledge of Allah.

So the passage that opened with the enemy's overwhelming war-chest ends by re-pricing everything. Their wealth ends as hasrah, heaped with its owners into Jahannam; the believers' real asset was never money at all, but a Mawla who cannot be outspent.

passages.title: The khums: dividing the spoils of war
passages.tafsir:
# The Khums: Dividing the Spoils of War (8:41)

Sūrat al-Anfāl takes up the injunctions of the spoils of war, and this single ayah lays down the rule of their distribution. Whatever the believers gain in battle, one-fifth (the *khums*) is set aside for Allah, and to the Messenger, and to the near relatives, the orphans, the poor, and the wayfarer — and honouring that division is tied directly to faith itself, sealed by a reference to Badr, "the Day of Criterion."

## A gift no nation before us was given

Ibn Kathir opens by distinguishing two terms. **Ghanimah** is property captured from the disbelievers through actual fighting; **fai'** is property acquired without battle — what they forfeit in return for peace, what they leave behind with no heir, and the *jizyah* (tribute tax) and *khirāj* (property tax). This ayah legislates the first.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān steps back further. In the Qur'anic view, real ownership of everything belongs to Allah alone; human beings own only what He assigns them through His law. When a people persist in rebellion after messengers are sent to them, their claim on the wealth Allah had lent them is forfeited — it passes, so to speak, directly back into the ownership of Allah. Under the ancient divine law that governed such property, no one was allowed to benefit from it: it was gathered on an open spot, and lightning would come from the heavens and burn it up — the sign that the effort of jihad had been accepted. Making ghanimah *lawful* was one of the unique distinctions bestowed upon the Last of the Prophets ﷺ and his Ummah — as Maʿārif notes, this is stated in a hadith of Muslim.

And not merely lawful: Maʿārif calls it "the purest of properties." Ordinary wealth reaches you through long chains of human hands, and somewhere along that chain something doubtful may have crept in. Ghanimah passes from the disbelievers straight into Allah's ownership and from Him to those who receive it — like water drawn from a well or grass growing wild, a provision with no human intermediary to taint it.

## "Whatever you gain, of anything"

The wording is deliberately sweeping. The Arabic *mā ghanimtum* ("whatever you gain") already signifies generality; the added *min shay'in* ("of anything") stresses it further — great or small, everything falls under this law. Ibn Kathir draws the practical conclusion: the fifth must be reserved and paid in full "even a yarn and needle," and he cites Allah's warning elsewhere: "And whosoever deceives (his companions over the booty), he shall bring forth on the Day of Resurrection that which he took" (3:161). The hadith literature names this crime **ghulūl** — misappropriating from the spoils before distribution — and, as Maʿārif observes, treats it as brazenly unlawful, far more serious than common theft.

Maʿārif adds a striking reflection on *why* this law works at all. Battles are fought in wildernesses full of hiding places; no commander could possibly know what each soldier acquired, and to stand guard over that property by the strength of law alone was impossible for anyone. What actually restrained every Muslim from the smallest pilfering was the fear of Allah and the Hereafter. Herein, Maʿārif says, lies the real secret of the effectiveness of the Qur'an's law and what makes it distinct from other laws of the world: it begins by awakening the fear of Allah and concern for the Hereafter, follows that with warnings of consequences, and only then promulgates penal punishments. Its power lies in conscience before courts.

## Where are the other four-fifths?

The ayah names only the fifth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the elegant implication: Allah addresses the fighters — "whatever spoils *you* receive" — hinting that the property belongs to those who took it, and then carves one-fifth out of it. The remaining four-fifths, therefore, belong to the mujāhidīn themselves. The Qur'an uses the same economy of expression in the law of inheritance: "his mother gets the one-third" (4:11), leaving the father's two-thirds understood. The Prophet's ﷺ own word and deed then settled the details of how those four shares were distributed.

The Sunnah states this division explicitly. Ibn Kathir cites a report recorded by Al-Bayhaqi with a sahih chain of narrators, in which ʿAbdullāh ibn Shaqīq relates that a man from Bilqīn said: "I came to the Prophet ﷺ when he was in Wādī al-Qurā inspecting a horse. I asked, 'O Allah's Messenger! What about the ghanimah?'" He replied: "Allah's share is one fifth and four-fifths are for the army." The man pressed — does anyone have more right to it than another? "No. Even if you remove an arrow that pierced your flank, you have no more right to it than your Muslim brother." Even the arrow pulled from your own body belongs to the common pool until it is lawfully divided.

## "For Allah and the Messenger" — one share, and why it is named so

Is Allah's share separate from the Messenger's? Ibn Kathir records that Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, al-Hasan al-Basrī, ash-Shaʿbī, ʿAtā' ibn Abī Rabāh, Qatādah and several other early authorities all held that the share designated for Allah and the Messenger is **one and the same**. Ibn ʿAbbās explained that "for Allah" here is inclusive — just as "To Allah belongs all that is in the heavens and on the earth" (2:284) — so Allah addressed His share and His Messenger's ﷺ in a single statement. Ad-Dahhāk also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās the practice itself: whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent an army, he divided the booty they collected into five shares, reserved one-fifth, and divided that fifth into five shares.

Maʿārif, citing Tafsīr Mazharī, uncovers a beautiful wisdom in opening with *lillāh* ("for Allah"). Charity (*sadaqah*) was forbidden to the Prophet ﷺ and his family — hadith calls such giving *awsākh an-nās*, "the dirt removed from people," since it is taken from people's wealth to purify it, and that does not befit a prophet's station. By heading this list with "for Allah," the Qur'an declares that the shares of the Prophet ﷺ and his kinsmen come not through what people own at all but directly from Allah's own property — grace and reward from Him, not charity from men.

Maʿārif also notes the grammar. Of the six words in the list, the first — *lillāh* — serves as the main heading under which the whole fifth is disbursed: all of it is spent exclusively for the sake of Allah, and the particle *lām* ("for") in *lillāh* denotes exclusivity of ownership, for Allah is the real owner of everything. Then, among the five actual categories of disbursement, the *lām* is affixed to the first two — *lir-rasūl* ("for the Messenger") and *li-dhil-qurbā* ("for the kinsmen") — where it highlights a special entitlement, since Allah bestowed on His Prophet ﷺ the right of disbursing the fifth; the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer are conjoined afterwards without it, indicating differing degrees of entitlement among the recipients.

## Five heads of spending, not five fixed entitlements

Who exactly receives the fifth? Maʿārif, citing Imam Tahāwī and Tafsīr Mazharī, explains that these five are *categories of disbursement*, not five fixed, equal claims. The right of disposal rested with the Prophet ﷺ, who would spend the fifth within these categories — on all of them or some — at his discretion. This is similar, Maʿārif notes, to the sūrah's very first verse, where the disposal of the entire collection of spoils was left to the Prophet's ﷺ discretion. The proof lies in the categories themselves: they overlap. A kinsman may also be an orphan, needy, and a wayfarer; were these separate entitlements, such a person would collect four shares (as actually happens in inheritance law), which no one in the Muslim community holds.

An incident makes this vivid. When Sayyidah Fātimah, physically worn by housework, asked her father ﷺ for a servant, he declined — the People of the Suffah were extremely poor and their need more urgent, and he could not bypass them (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). If any "kinsman" had an automatic entitlement, who could have been more deserving than Fātimah? The fifth was a trust to be directed where need was greatest.

**The recipients defined.** The *kinsmen* are Banū Hāshim **and** Banū al-Muttalib — the Prophet ﷺ himself included the latter because they never separated themselves from Banū Hāshim, in Jāhiliyyah or Islam; when Quraysh boycotted the Muslims for three years, Banū al-Muttalib, though not themselves under the boycott, joined Banū Hāshim in the mountain pass of Abū Tālib and shared the trial. The *orphans* are Muslim orphans; the *wayfarer* is the traveller (or intending traveller, over a distance at which shortening the prayer applies) who lacks resources to spend from. The Prophet ﷺ also had the right to choose some item from the spoils for himself — a servant, a horse, or a sword, according to the reports from Muhammad ibn Sīrīn, ʿĀmir ash-Shaʿbī and many scholars. Imam Ahmad and At-Tirmidhi — who graded it hasan — recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ chose a sword called Dhul-Fiqār on the day of Badr; and ʿĀ'ishah narrated that Safiyyah was among the captured women and that the Prophet ﷺ chose her before the distribution of the booty, as Abu Dawud narrated in the Sunan.

**After the Prophet's ﷺ passing.** According to the majority of Imams, his personal share was tied to his august station as prophet and messenger and lapsed at his death, since there is no prophet after him. On the kinsmen's share, the scholars genuinely differed. Imam Abu Hanifah — and Imam Shāfiʿī took the same position — held that the Prophet ﷺ gave to kinsmen for two reasons, their need and their support of his mission; the second ended with his passing, so what remains is need, and poor kinsmen retain precedence over the other categories (they cannot be helped from Zakah, while the others can). Some jurists held that the kinsmen's share, in their capacity as the Prophet's ﷺ relatives, endures for ever, rich and poor alike, at the ruler's discretion. The practice of the rightly-guided Caliphs is telling: the author of al-Hidāyah records that the four Khulafā' distributed the fifth over three categories only — orphans, needy, and wayfarer — though it stands proved (deduced by Abu Dawud) that ʿUmar used to give to *poor* kinsmen from it.

## Paying the fifth is part of faith

The ayah's condition — "if you have believed in Allah and in that which We sent down to Our servant" — means, as Ibn Kathir puts it: adhere to what Allah legislated for you, including this ruling, if your faith is real. The Prophet ﷺ made the link explicit. In the Two Sahihs, Ibn ʿAbbās narrates the lengthy hadith of the delegation of Banū ʿAbd al-Qays, in which the Prophet ﷺ defined belief in Allah as: testifying that none deserves worship but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, giving Zakah — "and honestly surrendering one-fifth of the war spoils." Al-Bukhari accordingly titled a chapter of his Sahih: "Paying the Khumus (one-fifth) is Part of Faith." Handing over wealth your own hand seized, in the flush of victory, with no one watching — that is where faith shows itself.

Ibn Kathir also records a moving scene from Imam Ahmad's Musnad. Al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib al-Kindī sat with ʿUbādah ibn as-Sāmit, Abū ad-Dardā' and al-Hārith ibn Muʿāwiyah al-Kindī, may Allah be pleased with them, reminding one another of the statements of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Abū ad-Dardā' asked ʿUbādah about the Prophet's ﷺ words concerning the fifth. ʿUbādah recounted: after leading them in prayer facing a camel from the booty, the Prophet ﷺ stood, held a bit of camel hair between his fingers, and said that even this was part of the spoils; that he himself had no share in it except his own share with them, the fifth — "even that fifth will be given to you"; that they must surrender "even the needle and the thread"; and that ghulūl is Fire and a shame on its people in this life and the Hereafter. (Ibn Kathir notes that he did not find this hadith in any of the six collections through this chain, but that Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i recorded similar narrations.) The one to whom the fifth was owed was the first to give his portion away.

## "The Day of Criterion, the day the two forces met"

The ayah closes by anchoring this legislation to Badr — *Yawm al-Furqān*, the Day of Criterion. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is here making His favours and compassion towards His creation known: on that day He distinguished between truth and falsehood, raised the word of faith above the word of falsehood, made His religion apparent, and supported His Prophet ﷺ and his group. Ibn ʿAbbās said, in a statement collected by Al-Hakim: "Badr is Yawm al-Furqān; during it, Allah separated between truth and falsehood" — and the like is reported from Mujāhid, Qatādah, ad-Dahhāk and others. Maʿārif adds that the Muslims scored a clear victory that day and the disbelievers a disgraceful defeat — by extension, the ultimate decision between disbelief and Islam. "And Allah is able to do all things."

The spoils of that victory had passed out of the disbelievers' hands directly into Allah's ownership, and He disposed of them as He willed: four-fifths as His gift to the army who fought, and one-fifth flowing back through His Messenger ﷺ — grace and reward directly from Allah Himself.

passages.title: Allah orchestrated the meeting at Badr
passages.tafsir:
# Ayat 42–44: Allah Orchestrated the Meeting at Badr

This passage is Allah's replay of the day of Badr — *Yawm al-Furqan*, as Ibn Kathir names it, that is, the day of Badr itself — shown from above, after the dust has settled. Twice the same refrain returns, in ayah 42 and again, deliberately repeated, in ayah 44: *so that Allah might accomplish a matter already ordained*. That refrain is what binds the passage together. What looked from the ground like a chain of accidents — two armies stumbling into each other, a dream, a trick of the eyes — is unveiled as a single decree unfolding in layers: Allah arranged the geography (ayah 42), steadied the hearts through a dream (ayah 43), and then governed the very eyesight of both armies on the field (ayah 44).

## The map of the battlefield

Ayah 42 opens with what Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān calls "almost a cartographic view of the war front." Three positions are fixed with precision. The Muslims were *bil-ʿudwat id-dunyā* — on the near side of the valley. The word *ʿudwah* means a side or edge; *dunyā* comes from *adnā*, "nearer" (the same root that names this world *dunyā*, because compared with the Hereafter it is the closer of the two). The idolators were *bil-ʿudwat il-quṣwā*, from *aqṣā*, "farther" — the side of the valley farther from Madinah, towards Makkah. And the caravan of Abu Sufyan — the whole reason anyone had marched out — was *asfala minkum*, on ground lower than you, moving along the seashore about three miles off, safely out of the Muslims' reach.

Why does the Qur'an bother drawing the map? Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān answers: to establish that, humanly speaking, the Muslims could not win — and the map proves it. Their side of the valley was a heavy sandy patch, exhausting to walk through, with no access to water. The disbelievers held smooth terrain with water close by. The two armies stood face to face, so neither side's strength or weakness could be hidden. The Makkans were at ease, knowing their caravan was safe and could even reinforce them if needed; the Muslims could expect help from nowhere. Three hundred and thirteen men, short of mounts and weapons, and hungry, faced a fully equipped force of a thousand. They had not even set out for war — it was an emergency measure against a trade caravan, and suddenly they stood before an army.

## The meeting no one could have planned

Then the remarkable clause: *"Even if you had made a mutual appointment to meet, you would certainly have failed in the appointment."* Muhammad bin Ishaq said that Yahya bin ʿAbbad bin ʿAbdullah bin Az-Zubayr narrated to him from his father the explanation: had a meeting been fixed and you learned of their superior numbers and your few forces, you would not have met them — but Allah had decreed that He would bring glory to Islam and its people while disgracing shirk (polytheism) and its people; you had no knowledge this would happen, but it was out of Allah's compassion that He did it. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws this out: had Badr been arranged like an ordinary war — with surveys, deliberation, negotiation — it would never have been fought. The Muslims, seeing themselves few and weak, would have hesitated; and the disbelievers, in whose hearts Allah had already cast awe of the Muslims, would have been scared off despite their superiority. So the divine plan created conditions on both sides that left no time to calculate: Makkah was swept out by the alarm raised for Abu Sufyan's caravan, and the Muslims marched thinking they were intercepting merchants, not meeting an army. As Kaʿb bin Malik said, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Muslims marched to intercept the Quraysh caravan, but Allah made them meet their armed enemy without appointment.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān lifts a universal principle from this: what happens "accidentally" in this world is, in the sight of its Creator, a well-set link in a formidable system. Nothing in that system is abrupt or out of place; only when the whole unravels does man glimpse the wisdom hidden behind what seemed a mere accident. Badr is the test case the Qur'an itself dissects.

## The two water-carriers: how the Prophet ﷺ read the enemy

Ibn Kathir records that Muhammad bin Ishaq said that Yazid bin Ruwman narrated to him that ʿUrwah bin Az-Zubayr related a scene from the approach to Badr that shows this "accidental" meeting taking shape on the ground. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent ʿAli bin Abi Talib, Saʿd bin Abi Waqqas, Az-Zubayr bin Al-ʿAwwam and several other Companions to scout. They captured two boys bringing water — and brought them back while the Prophet ﷺ was praying. Under interrogation the boys truthfully said they were carrying water for the Quraysh army; the Companions, hoping they belonged to Abu Sufyan's caravan, beat them until they said what was wanted. When the Prophet ﷺ finished his prayer he said: "When they tell you the truth you beat them, but when they lie you let them go? They have said the truth, by Allah! They belong to the Quraysh."

Then he questioned the boys himself. How many are they? *Many.* How many exactly? *We do not know.* How many camels do they slaughter each day? *Nine or ten.* From that single figure he ﷺ concluded: "They are between nine hundred and a thousand" — Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains the arithmetic of the age: one camel fed about a hundred men. Then he asked which chiefs of Quraysh had come, and the boys recited the roll — Abu Jahl, ʿUtbah and Shaybah the sons of Rabiʿah, Umayyah bin Khalaf, and the rest of Makkah's leading men. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the people: "This is Makkah! She has brought you her most precious sons." The enemy's own elite had been drawn, unwitting, to the appointed place.

## "That whoever perishes, perishes upon clear evidence"

Ayah 42 gives the purpose of it all: *so that those who were to be destroyed might be destroyed after a clear evidence, and those who were to live might live after a clear evidence*. Both commentaries insist that death and life here are not bodily. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān states it plainly: *halākah* (destruction) in this verse means kufr — disbelief — and *ḥayāt* (life) means Islam; the Qur'an uses the words this way elsewhere, as in 8:24, "respond to Allah and the Messenger when He calls you to what gives you life." Ibn Kathir says the same: "faith is the life of the heart," citing 6:122 — "Is he who was dead and We gave him life and set for him a light whereby he can walk among men…"

So the *bayyinah*, the clear evidence, is Badr itself. Muhammad bin Ishaq comments — and Ibn Kathir calls this a sound explanation — that those who disbelieve do so after witnessing clear proof and lessons, and those who believe, likewise. When three hundred and thirteen ill-equipped, hunger-stricken men ram themselves against what was, for them, a mountain — and the mountain shatters — Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān says this is an all-too-visible demonstration that some great power was operating behind them which the thousand-strong army lacked. The Muslims were supported because of Islam; the disbelievers deprived because of disbelief. After that, no plea of misunderstanding remains: whoever chooses kufr walks to destruction with open eyes, and whoever chooses Islam takes hold of eternal life knowingly and deliberately. The ayah closes with two of Allah's names that seal the scene: *All-Hearing* — of your invocations, your humility, your pleas for help, says Ibn Kathir — and *All-Knowing* of you, and that you deserved victory over your enemies.

## The dream and the governed eyes (ayat 43–44)

Having shown the orchestration of place, the passage turns to the orchestration of perception — and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes it happened twice: once in a dream (ayah 43), once wide awake on the field (ayah 44). Its stated purpose was to make sure neither army abandoned the battlefield before the encounter that was destined to manifest the truth of Islam.

**The dream.** Mujahid said: "In a dream, Allah showed the Prophet ﷺ the enemy as few. The Prophet ﷺ conveyed this news to his Companions and their resolve strengthened." The ayah itself states the alternative: had He shown them as many, *you would surely have been discouraged and disputed in making a decision* — Ibn Kathir glosses: you would have abstained from meeting them and fallen into dispute among yourselves. *But Allah saved you* from all that. And the closing clause — *He is the All-Knower of what is in the breasts* — Ibn Kathir connects to Allah's knowledge of all that hearts and inner selves conceal, citing 40:19: "Allah knows the fraud of the eyes, and all that the breasts conceal."

**On the field.** In ayah 44 the miracle moves from dream to waking sight, and becomes mutual: *He showed them to you as few in your eyes, and He made you appear as few in their eyes*. Of the first half — the enemy shown as few to the believers — Ibn Kathir writes that it "demonstrates Allah's compassion towards the believers": Allah made them see few disbelievers so that they would be encouraged and eager to meet them. Abu Ishaq As-Subaiʿi said that Abu ʿUbaydah said that ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud said: "They were made to seem few in our eyes during Badr, so that I said to a man next to me, 'Do you think they are seventy?' He said, 'Rather, they are a hundred.' However, when we captured one of them, we asked him and he said, 'We were a thousand.'" Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir recorded it. The other half had its own wisdom. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān relates — as it appears in many narrations — that Abu Jahl, surveying the Muslim line, told his companions they looked no more numerous than the men who would eat a single camel as a day's ration — about a hundred; and the wisdom of this reduction was that the awe of the Muslims should not so affect the disbelievers' hearts before the confrontation that they bolt from the battlefield. Ibn Kathir gathers both halves in one sentence: Allah encouraged each group against the other and made them look few in each other's eyes, so that they were eager to meet — echoing the words of ʿIkrimah, in a report recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim with a sahih chain: "He encouraged each of the two groups against the other."

**Reconciling this with 3:13.** A reader may recall Surah Aal ʿImran, where the disbelievers at Badr saw the believers as *twice their number*. Ibn Kathir resolves the apparent contradiction by sequence: the diminishing happened *before* the fighting began, so both sides would be eager to meet; but once battle was joined and Allah supported the believers with a thousand angels in succession, the disbelieving army saw the believers as double their number. "This is how we combine these two Ayat," he writes, "and certainly, each one of them is true."

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān appends a "Special Note" worth pausing on: this verse teaches that there are occasions when, as a matter of miracle and supernatural happening, even direct optical observation may prove incorrect — as it did here.

## "And to Allah all matters are returned"

The refrain *so that Allah might accomplish a matter already ordained* is deliberately repeated in ayah 44 — Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains: the overriding of the eyes served the same single decree as the geography and the dream, that Islam's truth and the reality of unseen divine support be established forever. Muhammad bin Ishaq relates — Yahya bin ʿAbbad bin ʿAbdullah bin Az-Zubayr narrating to him from his father — the two faces of that decree: that the war would start so that Allah would take revenge on those He had decided to requite, and grant and complete His favour upon those He had decided to favour, His supporters. And the passage closes on the note that gathers everything: *to Allah all matters are returned*. He does what He wills and commands as He wills — He can make a minority overcome a majority, weakness overtake strength, the less become more and the more become less.

For the believer scrolling through this passage today, its demand is the one Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān drew from it: learn to read the "accidents" of your own life as links in that same well-set system. And its warning is the one ayah 42 states outright: after evidence this clear, no one perishes or lives except knowingly — so let nothing be chosen in heedlessness.

passages.title: Battle ethics: firmness, unity, humility
passages.tafsir:
This short passage is the Qur'an's code of conduct for the battlefield — what Ibn Kathir titles the "Manners of War". In ayat 45–46 Allah gives the believers five articles of battle discipline: stand firm, remember Allah much, obey Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, do not fall into dispute, and be patient. Then ayah 47 completes the lesson by painting the exact opposite — the arrogant, showy march of the Quraysh towards Badr — and telling the believers: do not be like them. Positive instruction, then a living counter-example; that pairing is what holds the passage together.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls these instructions "the master prescription of success" — and locates in them the secret of the early Muslims' extraordinary victories: wherever they followed these guidelines precisely, they overcame far superior forces.

## Ayah 45 — Firmness of feet, firmness of heart

The first command is **fa-thbutū** — "take a firm stand". The Arabic word is *thibat*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains as standing firm and holding one's ground — and it stresses that this includes **firmness of the feet and firmness of the heart both**, because a person whose heart is not firm can hardly keep the rest of his body holding the line. Every nation, believer or disbeliever, understands this much: the first weapon in war is not steel but steadiness; without a firm heart, all other weapons are rendered useless.

The second command is unique to this ummah: **remember Allah much**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls dhikr (the remembrance of Allah) "a weapon in its own right, special and spiritual" — something the rest of the world, for all its state-of-the-art weaponry and morale-boosting techniques, simply does not possess. Remembering Allah with confidence is, in its words, like a highly charged energy that "makes a weak person run through mountains": it steadies the heart and plants the feet.

To feel the force of this command, consider the moment it addresses. The heat of battle is a time when, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, no one remembers anyone — everyone is consumed with self-preservation. The poets of pagan Arabia boasted that they remembered their beloved even amid swinging spears, and took that as the ultimate proof of a strong heart. The Qur'an asks the believer for something higher: to remember *Allah* in that same terror — and not merely to remember Him, but **kathira, "much"**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on that word. Nowhere in the entire Qur'an is any other act of worship commanded with "much" — there is no "pray much" or "fast much" phrased this way. Why is dhikr singled out? Because it is the easiest of all worship: it needs no wudu (ablution), no state of purity, no facing the qiblah (the direction of the Ka'bah); it can be done standing, sitting or lying down, and it does not stop you from whatever else your hands are doing. It goes further, citing the approach of Imam al-Jazri in Hisn Hasin, the famous collection of authentic Islamic prayers: any permissible act performed within obedience to the Prophet ﷺ counts as dhikr — so broad that some narrations even count the sleep of the practising scholar as worship. Nor is dhikr on the battlefield an extra burden piled onto the fighter: just as labourers hum a beat to carry them through hard work, dhikr brings a pleasure and energy that helps a person do everything else. One familiar form of it is the battle cry itself — *Allāhu-Akbar*, the cry of Takbir — a positively voiced declaration of Allah's greatness in the setting of a battlefield; but dhikr also includes keeping the thought of Allah always in sight, trusting Him, and remembering Him with the whole heart.

The ayah ends: **"so that you may be successful"**. Master these two techniques — firm feet and a remembering heart — and, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, success is yours.

## From the Sunnah — do not wish for war

Ibn Kathir brings the hadith that captures the spirit of this passage. It is recorded in the Two Sahihs from ʿAbdullah bin Abi Awfa that during one battle the Messenger of Allah ﷺ waited until the sun declined, then stood among the people and said: "O people! Do not wish to face the enemy (in a battle) and ask Allah to save you (from calamities). But if you should face the enemy, then be patient and let it be known to you that Paradise is under the shadows of the swords." He then stood and said: "O Allah! Revealer of the (Holy) Book, Mover of the clouds, and Defeater of the Confederates, defeat them and grant us victory over them."

Notice how perfectly this mirrors the ayah: no eagerness for bloodshed, but once the meeting is unavoidable, firmness and patience — and the turning to Allah in duʿāʾ (supplication), which is the dhikr the ayah commands. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the Prophet ﷺ delivered this very sermon on the site of combat during many battles, precisely so that these instructions would become the believers' ever-present response.

## Ayah 46 — Obedience, and why disputing drains an army

The third article is **obey Allah and His Messenger** — because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, Allah's help can only be expected through obedience to Him, while disobedience invites His displeasure and cuts a people off from His grace.

Then comes the warning: **"do not dispute with one another, lest you lose courage and your strength departs"**. The word rendered "strength" is *rīḥ* — and Ibn Kathir explains it as your strength, endurance and courage departing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the mechanism with striking psychological insight. Disputation has two end-products: you become personally weak and cowardly, and you lose your aura of dominance in the enemy's eyes. The second is obvious — quarrelling people look small. But why does discord make an individual *himself* weaker? Because when a group is united in trust, every member carries within himself the strength of the whole group; once that unity is gone, each man is left with only his own solitary strength — "which, obviously, means nothing in a killing field".

The final command, **"and be patient"**, is not a loose addition. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it, in context, as the practical prescription for avoiding disputes in the first place. However united a group's goals, temperaments differ, and among informed and experienced people divergence of opinion is inevitable. So the only way to stay together is to train oneself to bear patiently what goes against one's own temperament — to not be so rigid over a personal opinion that its rejection makes one explode and fight. That resilience is what *sabr* (patience) means here. And it offers a piercing observation: everyone today says disputes are bad, but very few have learnt the actual technique of avoiding them — training yourself to be patient with what you dislike, and to stop worrying about making people say yes to your view. Without that training, "all sermons of unity and harmony are rendered useless." You usually cannot force another person to surrender to your view — but two things always remain in your power: accept what he says, or, if reason and justice will not let you, simply stay silent to avert the dispute.

Note the precision of the Qur'an's wording: it forbids **tanāzuʿ** — disputation — not difference of opinion itself. Honest, sincere disagreement never becomes a quarrel; quarrels are born when disagreement is gripped by the emotional need to make the other person accept your word while refusing his. It is exactly that emotion which "be patient" removes.

And whatever is bitter in patience is sweetened by the ending: **"Surely, Allah is with the patient."** To have the company of Allah at all times and in all conditions is, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, a wealth beside which everything in this world and beyond is nothing.

Ibn Kathir closes his comment on these two ayat with history as proof: through their courage and obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, the Companions — few in number against Romans, Persians, Turks and the rest — opened hearts and lands east and west, until Allah's Word became the highest, and the Islamic state spread across the known world in less than thirty years.

## Ayah 47 — The march of Abu Jahl: how not to go to war

Having given the believers their code, Allah now shows them its photographic negative: **"Do not be like those who came out of their homes boastfully and to be seen of men, and hinder people from the path of Allah."** Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and As-Suddi all say these were the idolators who fought the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at Badr.

The story, as Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tell it: the Quraysh marched out of Makkah with heavy backing of men and materials to protect Abu Sufyan's trade caravan. But when the caravan slipped safely beyond any possible Muslim attack, Abu Sufyan sent a courier to Abu Jahl: there is no need to go further — turn back. Many Quraysh chiefs agreed. Abu Jahl, driven by pride and the hunger for recognition, swore: "No, by Allah! We will not go back until we proceed to the well of Badr, slaughter camels, drink alcohol and female singers sing to us. This way, the Arabs will always talk about our stance and what we did on that day." Muhammad bin Kaʿb adds that when the Quraysh left Makkah towards Badr, they brought female singers and drums along — and Allah revealed this verse about it.

Two words in the ayah diagnose their disease. **Baṭaran** — "boastfully", the intoxication of pride in one's own strength and numbers. And **riʾāʾ al-nās** — "to be seen of men", doing a deed for the eyes of spectators rather than for any sincere purpose. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distils the warning into two vices believers must never carry into their mission: waxing proud over strength and numbers, and nursing a personal agenda instead of sincerity to the task at hand — for these two, it says, are precisely what bring the great powers of the world to their knees.

The ayah closes: **"and Allah is Muhīt (encompassing and thoroughly comprehending) all that they do."** Nothing of their motives was hidden from Him — Ibn Kathir says He knew how and what they came for, and so made them taste the worst of punishments. The irony was total: Abu Jahl swore to feast at the well of Badr so the Arabs would talk about him forever, and in the aftermath of the battle he and his accomplices were thrown into that same well — dead, disgraced and humiliated. The Arabs do still talk about that day, but not as he intended.

## Living it

The passage's five articles are given for battle, but the sources themselves show how far they reach. Dhikr is deliberately the easiest worship there is — no ablution, no fixed posture, no time cost — so the command to do it "much" belongs to every state of life, not only the trench. And the discipline of ayah 46 is the discipline of every family, community and team: distinguish honest difference of opinion from ego-driven dispute; train yourself to bear what goes against your temperament; when you cannot win someone over, either accept his view or hold your peace. That patience is not weakness — it is the thing Allah has attached His company to: "Surely, Allah is with the patient." And whatever the endeavour, go out like the believers, not like Abu Jahl: without swagger, without performing for an audience — knowing that Allah encompasses what you do and, above all, why you do it.

passages.title: Satan flees and the hypocrites scoff
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are a matched pair of portraits from the day of Badr. In ayah 48, Satan pumps the Quraysh full of false confidence, marches them to the battlefield, then abandons them the instant he sees what is really there. In ayah 49, the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease scoff that the Muslims must be "deceived by their religion" — and Allah answers both delusions with one truth: whoever trusts in Allah has behind him the All-Mighty, the All-Wise. What holds the passage together is a single contrast: the counterfeit assurance Satan offers his followers, against the real assurance Allah gives those who rely on Him. One evaporates at first contact with reality; the other never fails.

## The scene: a frightened army needing a push

To feel the force of ayah 48, you need to know the state of the Quraysh army as it left Makkah — and the sources tell that story vividly. The previous ayah (47) had already described them coming out of their homes "boastfully and to be seen of men": Ibn Kathir records that when Abu Jahl was told the trade caravan had escaped safely and they could all go home, he swore, "No, by Allah! We will not go back until we proceed to the well of Badr, slaughter camels, drink alcohol and female singers sing to us. This way, the Arabs will always talk about our stance and what we did on that day." Muhammad bin Kaʿb adds that they brought female singers and drums along. It was a march staged for an audience — and Ibn Kathir notes the grim irony: in the aftermath of Badr they were thrown into that very well, dead, disgraced and humiliated.

But beneath the swagger there was fear. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing a narration of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas reported by Imam Ibn Jarir, explains that the Quraysh were "terribly worried" about their neighbouring tribe of Banu Bakr — also their enemy. If the fighting men marched out to face the Muslims, Banu Bakr might seize the moment to attack Makkah and harm their women and children left behind. They had answered Abu Sufyan's appeal for help, but they were dragging their feet.

That hesitation is the door Satan walked through.

## Satan in human form: the two assurances

Ayah 48 says Satan "made their (evil) deeds seem fair to them" — the translation elsewhere renders the same verb "made their deeds appealing," and Maʿārif describes the method as making evil deeds "appear handsome, desirable and beneficial." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question directly: was this a whispering of scruples into their hearts, or did Satan actually appear and speak to them? Both are possible in principle, it says, but the wording of the Qurʼān supports the second — and the narrations fill in the picture. Satan appeared in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Juʿshum, chief of Bani Mudlij — a real, known and influential chief who, Maʿārif notes, controlled the very tribal area from which the feared attack was expected — holding a flag, flanked by what looked like a regiment of tough fighting men.

Notice how surgically his speech in ayah 48 targets their two anxieties:

- **"No one of mankind can overcome you today"** — answering their fear of the Muslims. He assured them he had a good idea of the enemy's strength and could see their own numerical and physical superiority: stop worrying, march, prevail.
- **"Verily, I am your *jār*"** — a *jār* is a neighbour; Ibn Kathir's translation carries the sense "I am your neighbor (for each and every help)," and Maʿārif renders the same words "I am a protector for you." Either way, the target was the second fear. Coming from "Suraqah," this meant: Banu Bakr will not touch your homes — I take responsibility, as your supporter and caretaker, that nothing of the sort will happen. Hearing this from the chief of the very region they feared, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, "they became emotionally stable" — the threat was dismissed from their hearts, and they were all set to march.

Two fears, two lies, and an army walks to its killing field. Ibn Kathir links this to Allah's description of Satan elsewhere: "He makes promises to them, and arouses in them false desires; and Shaytan's promises are nothing but deceptions" (4:120).

## The flight: "I see what you see not"

Then the Qurʼān's cinematic turn: "But when the two forces came in sight of each other, *nakasa ʿalā ʿaqibayhi* — he turned back on his heels." Not a dignified withdrawal; a spinning-around and bolting.

What did he see? Both commentaries answer from the narrations of Ibn ʿAbbas: the angels. Because a force of devils had assembled in support of the Makkan army, Allah sent a force of angels under Jibraʾil and Mikaʾil to meet them.
