Ibn Kathir relates (through Ali bin Abi Talhah, from Ibn ʿAbbas) that when the two armies stood face to face, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took a handful of sand and threw it at the faces of the idolators, causing them to retreat; and when Jibril, peace be upon him, came towards Satan — who at that moment was holding the hand of a man from the idolators — he withdrew his hand and ran away with his soldiers. The man called after him, "O Suraqah! You claimed that you are our neighbor?" and his answer was the ayah's closing words: "Verily, I see what you see not. Verily, I fear Allah for Allah is severe in punishment."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, from a narration of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas reported by Imam Ibn Jarir and others, preserves the almost comic human detail of the same flight — and names the man. When the Satan commanding his force in Suraqah's guise saw Jibraʾil and the force of angels, "he lost his nerves." He was standing hand in hand with a Qurayshi warrior, Harith ibn Hisham. Suddenly he tried to wrench his hand free, and when Harith asked why, he struck him in the chest, knocked him down, and bolted from the battlefield. Harith — still under the impression that this was Suraqah — shouted after him: O Suraqah, chief of Arabia, you said you would support us, and you do this to us in the middle of a battle! The reply, in Maʿārif's rendering of the ayah: "I have nothing to do with you. I am seeing what you do not see. I am scared of Allah."

The epilogue seals the deception. On the Quraysh's return, one of them met the real Suraqah ibn Malik and scolded him for causing the defeat by deserting mid-battle. Suraqah answered: I never went with you, nor took part in anything you were doing there — I only heard of your defeat after you had reached Makkah. And Abu Jahl, seeing weakness spread through his army when "Suraqah" withdrew, had tried to spin even that — appealing to his men not to be affected, for Suraqah had a secret understanding with Muhammad ﷺ to do it. The deceived defending their deceiver to the end.

## Did Satan really "fear Allah"?

The commentators pause over his parting words, "I fear Allah." Qatadah, an authority in tafsir, said this was simply a lie he forged — had he truly feared Allah, why would he disobey Him? Other commentators, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, held that the fear itself is justified in its own place: Satan is fully aware of Allah's perfect power and that He is severe in punishment, so there is no reason for him not to fear — and indeed, when he saw the force of angels he saw real trouble for himself, for he knew their power. But both readings converge on the same lesson, stated plainly in Maʿārif: "bland fear without faith and obedience is useless." Trembling before Allah while refusing to submit to Him saves no one.

## Satan's standing method

Ibn Kathir, after gathering these narrations, draws out the general rule: it is the customary practice of Satan to get a person deeply involved in evil and then abandon him in the middle of it. The Qurʼān mentions this habit repeatedly; one such verse: "It is like the Shaytan when he tells man: 'Disbelieve.' Then, after he becomes a disbeliever, he says: 'I have nothing to do with you. I am scared of Allah, the Lord of all the worlds'" (59:16) — the same disavowal he made at Badr.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distils further lessons from the episode:

**He attacks in more than one way.** Sometimes he simply injects a scruple into the heart to harass his victim; sometimes, as here, he deceives by appearing in a convincing outward form. Allah has given him the ability to appear before man in various guises — a matter proved in detail, Maʿārif notes, in the well-known book of Hanafi jurisprudence *Akam al-Marjan fi Ahkam al-Jann*. For this reason, authorities among the mystic scholars — those recognized as masters of *kashf* (illumination, perception beyond the ordinary senses) and *shuhūd* (eye-witness) — have warned that it is dangerous to start following a person simply because of what you saw of him or heard him say, without taking the trouble to find out who he really is. Maʿārif adds that satanic inputs can be couched even in what is known as *kashf* (illumination) and *ilhām* (inspiration). The one reliable safeguard against every disguise is to follow Divine Revelation faithfully — the standard no impersonation can counterfeit.

**Sincerity alone is not enough.** This may be the passage's most sobering point. Maʿārif observes that the most frequent way people fall into disbelief and wrong is precisely this: Satan making evil deeds look handsome, desirable, beneficial, turning hearts away from truth as it is — until a person takes his falsehood for the epitome of truth and, very much like a lover of truth, stands ready to lay down his life for it. The proof is startling: as the army and chiefs of Quraysh departed from the Baytullah (the House of Allah), they supplicated before it, "O Allah, help the better-guided group between the two of us" — sincerely convinced that they were the better-guided side, marching to sacrifice lives and possessions for a false stand with all the "sincerity" at their command. From this, Maʿārif concludes: bland sincerity is never sufficient unless the direction of deeds is correct. Being earnest about the wrong thing is still being wrong.

## Ayah 49: "Their religion has deluded them"

The second portrait. As the armies drew close, a remark went around — from the hypocrites (*munāfiqūn*) and "those in whose hearts is a disease," a disease which the translation explicitly glosses as disbelief: "These people are deceived by their religion." Maʿārif identifies it as a common saying of the hypocrites of Madinah and the polytheists of Makkah, spoken in a strain of combined sympathy and contempt: this handful of Muslims has come all the way to challenge so powerful and well-equipped an army — surely their faith has deluded them and thrown them into the jaws of death.

Why did the Muslims look so easy to dismiss? Ibn ʿAbbas (as related by Ali bin Abi Talhah) explains that when the two armies drew near, Allah made the Muslims look few in the eyes of the idolators, and the idolators look few in the eyes of the Muslims — so the idolators believed, without doubt, that they would defeat the Muslims. Al-Shaʿbi adds a third group of speakers: some Makkans who had been considering Islam, but who, seeing how few the Muslims were at Badr, said the same words — faith abandoned on the strength of a headcount. And Qatadah relates the ugliest version of the sentiment: when Abu Jahl saw Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions, he said, "By Allah! After this day, they will never worship Allah!" — spoken, Qatadah says, in viciousness and transgression.

## The answer: whoever trusts in Allah

Allah does not answer the scoffers with numbers. He answers with a sentence that closes the passage and settles the whole question: "But whoever puts his trust in Allah — then surely Allah is All-Mighty, All-Wise."

This is *tawakkul* — placing one's reliance on Allah while acting. Ibn Kathir unfolds the two names. **ʿAzīz, All-Mighty:** those who take Allah's side are never overwhelmed, for His side is mighty and His authority supreme. **Ḥakīm, All-Wise:** He places everything in its rightful place, giving victory to those who deserve it and defeat to those who deserve it — Badr itself being the proof. Maʿārif adds the deeper diagnosis of the scoffers: those who know no more than what is material will place their trust in nothing but the material. How could they know the secret power that lies in the treasures of the One who created everything material — the power that accompanies those who believe in Allah and place their total trust in Him? One who places his total trust in Allah, it says, never runs into disgrace: Allah is all-dominating, and no plan, intelligence, or insight into the future can hold before His wisdom.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with three working principles, each drawn straight from the sources. First, examine what looks attractive: Satan's signature is making a bad course seem fair, and his signature ending is desertion at the moment of crisis — so a project that flatters your fears and promises easy triumph deserves the hardest scrutiny. Second, measure guidance by Revelation, not by impressive appearances or even spiritual experiences; the disguise of "Suraqah" fooled an army, and only the standard of Allah's guidance exposes such fraud. Third, expect the scoffing. Maʿārif notes that even in our day, religiously observant Muslims become ready targets for those who claim to have advanced rationally and intellectually, and who benignly dismiss them as old-timers — the same "deluded by their religion" in modern dress. The answer now is what it was at Badr: armed with perfect faith and trust in Allah, no harm can touch them, even if intended and tried.

passages.title: Death of deniers and the pattern of Pharaoh
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These five ayat pull back the curtain on two things the eye cannot normally reach: what happens to a denier at the moment of death, and the fixed pattern by which Allah deals with nations that reject Him. The unit is held together by a repeated phrase — **"like the way of the people of Pharaoh and of those before them"** — which appears in ayah 52 and again in ayah 54, framing ayah 53 like two arms around a centre. Ayah 53 is the centre: the standing rule that Allah does not withdraw a favour from a people until they themselves change what is within them.

---

## Ayah 50: a scene the eye does not reach

The ayah opens with a conditional that is left hanging. Ibn Kathir's rendering: *"And if you could see when the angels take away the souls of those who disbelieve (at death); they smite their faces and their backs, (saying): 'Taste the punishment of the blazing Fire.'"* Notice that the sentence never says what you would see. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the form of address to the Prophet ﷺ is *"And only if you were to see"* — had he seen it, he would have seen a scene full of sobering lessons. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: if you witnessed the angels capturing the souls of the disbelievers, "you would witness a tremendous, terrible, momentous and awful matter." The reality is beyond describing, so the description is withheld and the imagination is left to stand at the edge of it.

**Why the faces and the backs.** Ibn Jurayj reported from Mujahid that "their backs" refers to their back sides, as happened on the day of Badr. Ibn Jurayj also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "When the idolators faced the Muslims [in Badr], the Muslims smote their faces with swords. When they gave flight, the angels smote their rear ends." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some leading commentators took the ayah to be about those particular disbelievers of the Quraysh who came out to confront the Muslims at Badr, where Allah had sent an army of angels to help the Muslims — the Quraysh chiefs killed that day were killed at the hands of angels, while giving them the dark tidings of the punishment of Hell in the Hereafter.

**But it is not only about Badr.** Ibn Kathir: "Although these Ayat are describing Badr, they are general in the case of every disbeliever. This is why Allah did not make His statement here restrictive to the disbelievers at Badr." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same second view, held by commentators who kept the sense general: when a disbeliever dies, the angel of death beats his face and back while taking out his soul, and in some narrations it appears that they have lashes of fire and maces of iron in their hands.

**Why we do not see it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds: this punishment is not related to this world of elements but to the universe of the grave, known as **Barzakh** — the state after death and before resurrection. That is why it is not generally seen by the eye. The punishment of the grave finds mention in several other verses of the Qur'an as well, while hadith narrations on this subject abound.

**The soul that refuses to leave.** Ibn Kathir places this ayah alongside a parallel scene in Surat al-Anʿam: *"And if you could but see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, while the angels are stretching forth their hands (saying): 'Deliver your souls!'"* (6:93). The angels stretch out their hands and smite the disbelievers by Allah's command, he explains, since their souls refuse to leave their bodies, so they are taken out by force. This occurs at the very moment the angels are giving them the news of torment and of Allah's anger.

Ibn Kathir then relates a hadith narrated from **al-Baraʾ**: when the angel of death attends the disbeliever at the time of death, he comes to him in a terrifying and disgusting shape, saying: *"Get out, O wicked soul, to fierce hot wind, boiling water and a shadow of black smoke."* The disbeliever's soul then scatters throughout his body, but the angels retrieve it just as a needle is retrieved from wet wool — with veins and nerve cells still attached to it.

The angels do not only strike; they speak: **"Taste the punishment of the blazing Fire."** Before the Fire is reached, its taste has already been announced.

---

## Ayah 51: what your hands forwarded

Then comes the explanation, addressed directly to them: *"This is because of that which your hands forwarded. And verily, Allah is not unjust to His servants."*

Ibn Kathir reads it simply: this punishment is the recompense of the evil deeds committed in the life of this world. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a linguistic observation: **why "hands"?** Because things done usually take their shape through the work of hands, so mention was made of hands.

**"And verily, Allah is not unjust to His servants."** Ibn Kathir affirms: certainly, Allah does not wrong any of His creatures, "for He is the Just, who never puts anything in an inappropriate place." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point from the other side: Allah was not the kind of authority who would bring injustice upon His servants and go about subjecting someone to punishment just for no reason.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here what **Muslim** recorded from Abu Dharr, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah, the Exalted, said: *"O My servants! I have prohibited injustice for Myself, and made it prohibited to you between each other. Therefore, do not commit injustice against each other. O My servants! It is your deeds that I am keeping count of, so whoever found something good, let him praise Allah for it. Whoever found other than that, has only himself to blame."*

That last line is the whole of ayah 51 in miniature.

---

## Ayah 52: the pattern — *daʾb*

*"Similar to the behavior of the people of Firʿawn, and of those before them — they rejected the Ayat of Allah, so Allah punished them for their sins. Verily, Allah is All-Strong, severe in punishment."*

The key word is **daʾb**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines it as *habit or way*; Ibn Kathir glosses it as "Our behavior [or custom] and way" — what Allah characteristically does with people of this type. Ibn Kathir paraphrases the whole ayah as a divine statement: the behaviour of these rebellious disbelievers against what I sent you with, O Muhammad ﷺ, is similar to the behaviour of earlier disbelieving nations.

The ayah refuses to treat Badr as news. It files it under a heading that already existed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the full sequence of that customary practice: Allah gives His servants reason and understanding so they can act as guided; all around them He places countless things they can think about, so that they come to know Him and recognise His great power, and do not stoop to taking the weak ones among His creation as His partners; then, for additional warning, He sends His Books and His Messengers, who leave no stone unturned in making people understand, going as far as demonstrating the manifestations of His subduing power in the form of miracles. **After all of that** — if a person or a people were to close their eyes to all these things, then the inevitable practice of Allah with such people is that they are visited by punishment in this world too, and subjected to the everlasting punishment of the Hereafter as well. The world has already seen this practice worked out, the commentary says: Pharaoh was made to drown in the sea with all his power and people, and similar was the fate of those before him, the people of ʿAd and Thamud.

**"Verily, Allah is All-Strong, severe in punishment."** Ibn Kathir: "none can resist Him or escape His grasp." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why: no one claiming any kind of strength and valour can, on that basis alone, get away from His punishment.

---

## Ayah 53: the rule at the heart of the passage

*"That is so because Allah will never change a grace which He has bestowed on a people until they change what is in themselves. And verily, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower."*

Ibn Kathir reads this as an affirmation of Allah's perfect justice and fairness in His decisions: He decided that He will not change a bounty that He has granted someone, except on account of an evil that they committed. He brings the parallel from Surah ar-Raʿd: *"Verily, Allah will not change the (good) condition of a people as long as they do not change their state (of goodness) themselves. But when Allah wills a people's punishment, there can be no turning it back, and they will find besides Him no protector."* (13:11)

**A distinction worth pausing on.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a point here: Allah has set forth *no* rule as to the **bestowal** of blessing and favour — no restriction, no condition, no dependence on some good deed. The foremost favour bestowed on us is our very existence, and placed in this marvellous display of His power are thousands upon thousands of additional blessings, all conferred at a time when we did not exist, nor did any deed of ours. Blessing and mercy are there all by themselves, as an outcome of His being the Lord of all the worlds, the All-Merciful, the Very-Merciful.

What ayah 53 states is a rule governing not the *giving* but the **continuity** of that favour and mercy. Once Allah has favoured a people with His blessing, He does not take it back until they themselves bring about changes in their conditions of living and their ways of doing things, and thus become the very agency that invites His punishment. And the "change" meant here, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies, is a shift from good deeds to bad and from good states of being to bad — or that someone already involved in sins when the blessing arrived stoops lower afterwards.

**Pharaoh's people as the first case.** Ibn Kathir lists what was taken from them when the change came: gardens, springs, plants, treasures and pleasant dwellings, as well as all of the delights they enjoyed. "Allah did not wrong them, but it is they who wronged themselves." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces their downward turn: they started inflicting all sorts of injustices against the Bani Israʾil, then rose in hostility against Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) — a grave addition to their past crimes. They changed; the blessing was changed into retribution and punishment.

**The Quraysh as the second — and the one being addressed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān becomes devastatingly specific. The Quraysh were involved in polytheism and other evil practices, yet they did have a few good deeds to their credit: regard for kinship, hospitality, service of the Hajj pilgrims, and respect for the Baytullah. And Allah showered on them many material and spiritual blessings anyway. Materially: in a country where no trading caravan belonging to anyone could pass through safely, theirs went to Syria in the north and Yemen in the south and returned in safety and with success — the very favour the Qur'an mentions in Surah al-Quraysh, "they used to make alternate trading visits in winter and summer" (106:2). Spiritually: they were blessed with a favour so great as was never conferred upon any of the past peoples — that the foremost among prophets, the last of the line ﷺ, was destined to rise among them, and that the Qur'an, the last and comprehensive Book of Allah, was sent to them through him.

Then look at what they did with each of those virtues:

- **Kinship** — they stopped treating their near relations well and started inflicting savage injustices against their own brothers and nephews who chose to embrace Islam.
- **Hospitality** — rather than keep to that tradition, pledges were written and promulgated that a total boycott of such Muslims be made, even to the limit of holding back the supply of food and water to them.
- **Service to pilgrims** — instead of providing the essential services for Hajj pilgrims which they once considered their duty, they started preventing Muslims from entering the Haram.
- **The faith itself** — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Tafsir Mazhari that Kilab ibn Murrah, an ancestor of the Prophet ﷺ, was a staunch adherent of the faith of Sayyidna Ibrahim and Ismaʿil (peace be upon them) right from the beginning, and that he retained the role of leadership in this faith generation after generation. It was during the period of Qusayy ibn Kilab that idol-worship started as a practice among the people. Before him, Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy was their religious leader; he used to deliver a sermon on the day of Jumuʿah — called *ʿArubah* in their dialect — telling his audience that the last among prophets ﷺ would rise from among their progeny, and that everyone would be bound to follow him. Given this historical perspective, the commentary says, the "change" which affected the mass behaviour of the Quraysh may as well mean precisely this: that they had forsaken the faith of Sayyidna Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and taken to idol-worship.

These were the standing conditions which brought about a change in the disbelievers of Quraysh — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, as a result came the counter-change from Allah: He transformed His favours and blessings into retribution and punishment, making them taste disgrace in this mortal world too; and it was through the noble person sent as a mercy for all the worlds that they invited their own destruction.

**"All-Hearer, All-Knower."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the ending: Allah is the One who hears everything they say and knows everything they do — therefore there is no probability of some error or misunderstanding in the decision He finally takes.

---

## Ayah 54: the same refrain, deliberately altered

*"Similar to the behavior of the people of Firʿawn, and those before them. They belied the Ayat of their Lord, so We destroyed them for their sins, and We drowned the people of Firʿawn for they were all wrongdoers."*

Almost the same words as ayah 52 — but Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows that the purpose behind the two statements differs. In ayah 52 the purpose was to state that the **disbelief** of those people became the cause of their punishment. In ayah 54 the purpose is the rule just stated: when the blessings of Allah descend upon a people and they fail to recognise their worth and value and refuse to bow down before Him, His blessings are transformed into misfortunes and punishments.

Three deliberate changes carry that shift:

**1. "The signs of Allah" (52) becomes "the signs of their Lord" (54).** By mentioning the attribute **Rabb** — sustainer, nourisher, cherisher — instead of the name Allah, a hint is given that these people were terribly unjust and insensate against truth: people who would just go ahead and start belying the signs of the very Being who was their Rabb.

**2. "So Allah seized them for their sins" (52) becomes "so We destroyed them for their sins" (54).** Being *seized* is deliberately broad — such punishment could take different forms: perhaps they are overtaken by misfortunes within their lifetime on this earth, or their very existence is eliminated outright. Saying *We destroyed them* makes it clear that the punishment all those peoples deserved was the punishment of death.

**3. Pharaoh's people are singled out for drowning.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why he is mentioned particularly among all the destroyed nations: because the Pharaoh from among them claimed godhood and his people attested to his claim. The forms destruction took for the other peoples are not described here, though details appear in other verses — some were overrun by an earthquake, some made to sink into the earth, some transformed into animals, some seized by wind storms. And finally, the commentary adds, came the punishment for the disbelievers of Makkah at the hands of the Muslims in the battle of Badr.

Ayah 50 showed angels striking faces and backs on the day of Badr; ayah 54 files Badr into the same ledger as the drowning of Pharaoh's people.

---

## Living it

The passage is aimed at deniers, but ayah 53 states a standing rule, and rules do not check whose door they are at.

**Blessing arrives unearned; it stays or goes by conduct.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says as much directly: there are occasions when Allah bestows His favour even on people who, judged by their deeds, do not seem to deserve it — but if, having received it, they take to committing excesses and indulging in evil deeds more frequently rather than turning their deeds towards correction and betterment, the favour is taken away and they become deserving of divine punishment. So the question a believer should carry is not "what did I do to deserve this" but "since receiving this, have I moved towards Him or away from Him?"

**Watch for the specific inversion.** The Quraysh did not lose their blessings by becoming vaguely worse. They lost them by turning each particular virtue into its opposite. The audit that ayah 53 invites is that precise — take the good you are actually known for, and ask whether you have begun doing its opposite.

**And the closing of ayah 51 is a mercy as much as a warning.** Nothing arrives in your account that you did not send ahead — and what you did send ahead, Allah Himself is keeping count of.

passages.title: Treaty-breakers and the answer to treachery
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat form a single argument about one problem: people who sign a treaty and then break it, again and again. Allah first names what such people are in His sight, then identifies them by their behaviour, then tells the Prophet ﷺ what to do if they are met in war — and then, before the passage closes, turns the whole instruction around and forbids the Muslims from ever doing to anyone what was done to them. The last ayah is the counterweight that holds the other three in balance, and none of the four can be read honestly without it.

## The setting: Madinah, and a treaty that kept being torn up

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the verses just before this described the punishment that came down on the disbelievers of Makkah at Badr, and how they resembled the rejecting communities of the past. Now the focus shifts from the open enemy in Makkah to a danger closer to home — a group who, in Maʿārif's vivid phrase, became "like serpents in the sleeves of Muslims" soon after the migration to Madinah: outwardly at peace with the Muslims, inwardly conspiring with the Makkans against them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies these ayat as being about the Jews of Madinah, and those of Banū Qurayẓah and Banū Naḍīr. Just as Abū Jahl was the top anti-Islam leader among the disbelievers of Makkah, their leading figure in Madinah was Kaʿb ibn Ashraf. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah after the Hijrah they saw the rise of Muslim power and were impressed, even somewhat overawed by it — but the fire of their anti-Muslim feeling kept burning underneath.

To feel the weight of what follows, you have to know what the treaty was. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the Prophet's ﷺ political work in Madinah in two steps.

**Step one — a new brotherhood.** He ﷺ first eliminated the prejudices of country and tribe from the Muhājirīn (those who had emigrated from Makkah) and the Anṣār (the people of Madinah who received and helped them), and put in their place a new nationhood in the name of Islam itself. Different tribes among the Muhājirīn and Anṣār became brothers to one another; through him, Allah also removed the mutual differences that had divided the Anṣār among themselves for centuries. The two groups then became brothers across the divide as well.

**Step two — the treaty.** The Muslims faced two adversaries: the Makkans whose persecution had driven them out, and the Jews of Madinah who were now their neighbours. With the second, a treaty was concluded and documented in detail, binding on all Jews living in and around Madinah and on all the Muhājirīn and Anṣār alike. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that its full text can be seen in Ibn Kathīr's *Al-Bidāyah wa an-Nihāyah*, in the *Sīrah* of Ibn Hishām, and elsewhere. Its most significant article: in the event of any mutual difference, the decision of the Prophet ﷺ would be binding on all. Another stipulated that they would not provide assistance to any enemy against the Muslims, overtly or covertly.

**The first breach.** At the time of Badr they committed a breach of trust, supporting the disbelievers of Makkah by supplying weapons and other war materials. When Badr ended in a clear victory for the Muslims and a disgraceful defeat for the Makkans, they felt cowed once more. They came before the Prophet ﷺ, apologised for what they had done, and sought his forgiveness on the promise that there would be no breach of trust in future. Because Islamic forbearance and generosity was his way, he ﷺ accepted, and the treaty was renewed.

**The second breach.** When word reached them of the Muslims' initial losses at Uḥud, their ambitions rose again. Their chief Kaʿb ibn Ashraf travelled to Makkah himself and urged the Makkans to mount another attack with fresh and full preparation, in which the Jews of Madinah would be with them. That is the "each time" the Qurʼān is pointing at. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records how it ended: like Abū Jahl, the chief of the disbelievers, Kaʿb ibn Ashraf the chief of the Jews was killed, and the rest of the Jews of Madinah were expelled from the city.

## The verdict, and the reason for it

Of these people Allah says, in Maʿārif's rendering: *Surely, the worst of all the living, in the sight of Allah, are those who reject Faith*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word دَوَابّ (*dawābb*), the plural of *dābbah*, which literally means creatures who walk on the earth — a word wide enough to cover human beings and every animal that walks, though in common usage it is applied particularly to four-footed animals. The Qurʼān's choice is deliberate. Because these people had sunk so far in their state of insensitiveness that they were below animals, they were identified by that expression and then ranked at the bottom of it: the worst of animals from among all animals and human beings together. Ibn Kathīr reads it the same way — the worst moving creatures on the face of the earth are those who disbelieve, who do not embrace the faith, and who break promises whenever they make a covenant, even when they vow to keep them.

The closing words, *so they do not believe*, are not a taunt but a diagnosis. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that such people have allowed the abilities Allah gave them to go to waste by making the satisfaction of their physical needs the very purpose of their life — and once that is the whole aim of a life, access to the refinements of faith was simply not possible for them.

Who exactly was meant? Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said this verse was revealed about six men from the Jews, about whom Allah declared in advance that they would never enter the fold of faith. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something merciful in the very wording: through it, the aim is to grant exemption from the punishment to people who were at that time engaged in tandem with the disbelievers in their struggle against the Muslims and Islam, but of whom it was likely that a time would come when they would repent their past mistakes and embrace Islam. That is exactly how it came to be. A very large group from among them, by embracing Islam, became not only personally pious and righteous but rose to be — in word and deed alike — leaders among the men and women of the world, heralds of moral betterment and paradigms of responsible conduct of life before the Creator. The condemnation lands on a settled disposition, and the door was deliberately left open for anyone who would walk through it.

The next ayah identifies them by what they do rather than what they are: *those from whom you have taken a pledge, then they break their pledge each time, and they do not fear Allah*. Notice the shape of the accusation. **You** made the treaty with them, and **they** broke it — every time. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this is precisely where their wickedness comes into focus: they were the ones who themselves made a treaty with the Prophet ﷺ, and they were the ones who each time kept breaking their pledge to abide by it. The wrong is not merely political; it is a repeated betrayal of a bond they had entered of their own accord.

Ibn Kathīr's comment on **وَهُمْ لَا يَتَّقُونَ** (*wa hum lā yattaqūn*) is short and searching: it means they do not fear Allah regarding any of the sins they commit. *Taqwā* — that awareness of Allah which makes a person hesitate before a wrong — is exactly the faculty a treaty rests on, since an agreement is only ever as good as the conscience behind the signature. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two possible readings of the phrase, and both are worth holding together: that these ill-fated people, drunk with worldly greed and with no concern for the life to come, do not fear the punishment of the Hereafter; and that even at the worldly level, characterless people who break pledges do meet their evil end here — yet through negligence and ignorance these people do not fear even that.

## The answer to treachery, and the mercy inside it

Then comes the instruction, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes as a standing one given by Allah to His Messenger ﷺ concerning such evil breakers of solemn pledges: *So, if you find them in war, make them an example (deterrent) for those behind them, so that they take a lesson.*

Maʿārif explains the two key words. **تَثْقَفَنَّهُمْ** (*tathqafannahum*) means to get the upper hand against them; Ibn Kathīr glosses the phrase as defeating them and having victory over them in war. **شرّد** (*sharrada*) derives from *tashrīd*, whose essential sense is to drive out or scatter away. So the command is not simply "defeat them" but "let the defeat of these people scatter the ones standing behind them."

Ibn Kathīr reports that **فَشَرِّدْ بِهِم مَّنْ خَلْفَهُمْ** — "then disperse those who are behind them" — was understood as severely punishing the captured, and he names Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, as-Suddī, ʿAṭāʼ al-Khurāsānī and Ibn ʿUyaynah among those who said so. The ayah commands punishing them harshly and inflicting casualties on them, so that other enemies, Arabs and non-Arabs alike, will be afraid and take a lesson from their end. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it in the same direction: the punishment should make such an impression on the disbelievers of Makkah and other hostile tribes that it sucks away any courage they had to come back and confront the Muslims again, and those busy bashing Islam from behind such people, using them as their agents, should understand that no alternative remains for them but to run for their lives.

But the verse does not end with the blow. It ends with a purpose — *laʿallahum yadhdhakkarūn*, "so that they take a lesson." As-Suddī commented on it: "They might be careful not to break treaties, so that they do not meet the same end." And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees in that closing phrase a hint towards the universal mercy of the Lord of all the worlds. It makes clear that the real purpose of this exemplary punishment was not to take revenge or to release personal anger; it was being awarded in the wrongdoers' own interest, so that they might perhaps review the conditions before them, regain some of their sanity, feel ashamed of what they did, and go on to correct themselves. A punishment aimed at producing repentance is a different thing from one aimed at satisfying a grudge, even when the outward act looks similar.

## The line the Muslims may not cross

Having authorised a hard response to treachery, the passage immediately fences the Muslims in. The final ayah addresses the reverse case: what if *you* hold a valid treaty with a people and you begin to fear betrayal from their side? *And if you apprehend a breach from a people, then, throw (the treaty) towards them being right forward. Surely, Allah does not like those who breach trust.*

Ibn Kathīr walks through it phrase by phrase. **وَإِمَّا تَخَافَنَّ مِن قَوْمٍ** — if you fear from a people with whom you have a treaty of peace — **خِيَانَةً**, treachery and betrayal of the peace treaties and agreements you have conducted with them, **فَانبِذْ إِلَيْهِمْ**, then throw back their treaty of peace to them, **عَلَىٰ سَوَاءٍ**, on equal terms: informing them that you are severing the treaty, so that you and they alike are aware that a state of war exists and the bilateral peace treaty is null and void. Then: **إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ الْخَائِنِينَ** — "Certainly Allah likes not the treacherous." And Ibn Kathīr adds the crucial extension: *this even includes treachery against the disbelievers.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the resulting article in the Islamic law of war and peace. After placing due stress on the importance of complying with the terms of a treaty, an alternative is laid out for a situation in which a danger of breach of trust arises from the other party during the treaty's legal tenure. In that case it is no longer necessary that the Muslims continue to abide by their allegiance to it. But no initiative — no pre-emptive action of any kind — is permissible against the other party **before** the treaty has been clearly terminated. Taking military initiative against a people with whom a peace treaty has been signed is itself included under breach of trust, and Allah does not like those guilty of *khiyānah*, even where that treachery would cause loss to hostile disbelievers; that too is impermissible.

The correct approach, Maʿārif says, is to pick a peaceful and convenient occasion and let them know that their ill intentions or their contraventions of the treaty are no secret, or that their dealings appear dubious, and that for this reason the Muslims will not consider themselves bound by the treaty — and that they too are consequently free to take whatever action they wish. And the proclamation has to leave both sides on the same footing. Nothing should be done to create a situation in which preparations to confront the other party are completed in advance of the warning while they are caught unawares and unable to make counter-preparations for their own defence. Make whatever preparations must be made — but only after the proclamation and the warning.

This, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, is the justice of Islam: that the rights even of enemies who themselves commit breach of trust are guarded, and that the restriction is placed on the Muslims and not on their adversaries. (Mazharī and others)

## An army that turned back

Ibn Kathīr records that Imām Aḥmad reported from Sālim bin ʿĀmir: Muʿāwiyah was leading an army in Roman lands at a time when the bilateral peace treaty was still valid. He wanted to move closer to their forces so that when the treaty of peace ended he could invade them. An old man riding on his animal called out, "Allāhu Akbar, Allāhu Akbar! Be honest and stay away from betrayal." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Whoever has a treaty of peace with a people, then he should not untie any part of it or tie it harder until the treaty reaches its appointed term. Or, he should declare the treaty null and void so that they are both on equal terms."

When Muʿāwiyah was informed of the Prophet's ﷺ statement, he retreated. They found that man to be ʿAmr bin ʿAnbasah, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn Kathīr notes that this hadith was also collected by Abū Dāwūd aṭ-Ṭayālisī, Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʼī and Ibn Ḥibbān in his *Ṣaḥīḥ*, and that at-Tirmidhī said, "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the same episode, based on a narration of Sālim ibn ʿĀmir reported by Abū Dāwūd, Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʼī and Imām Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, and fills in the scene: Muʿāwiyah had a no-war pact with a group of people for a specified period, and it occurred to him to move his army and equipment close to them so that his forces could move the moment the pact expired. Exactly as the army was getting ready to march, an aged man on horseback was noticed shouting a slogan at the top of his voice — *Allāhu Akbar, Allāhu Akbar*, we should fulfil the pledge, we should not contravene it — carrying the famous cry of takbīr, which lent the matter its full religious gravity. He was ʿAmr ibn ʿAnbasah, a Companion. Muʿāwiyah lost no time and ordered the army to march back, so that he would not become one of those who commit a breach of trust by initiating war action while still inside the time frame of a no-war pact.

Sit with that image: an army already forming up to move, halted because one old man rode across its front calling out the takbīr and a plea for faithfulness over betrayal — and because the Prophet's ﷺ teaching, once it reached the commander, outweighed every advantage the manoeuvre promised. Note what the manoeuvre actually was. Muʿāwiyah intended to strike only after the pact expired; the letter of the agreement would not have been broken. Yet the teaching that one must "not untie any part of it or tie it harder" until its appointed term reaches even the positioning of troops. A treaty, on this reading, is not a document to be technically satisfied. It is a trust, and a trust can be spoiled by intention as surely as by act.

## Living it

**A treaty is a trust before it is a tactic.** This passage's harshest words are reserved for people who make agreements they never meant to keep, and who keep breaking them each time. Whatever you have given your word to — a contract, a debt, an arrangement with someone you do not even like — the standard set here is that you do not manoeuvre against it while it stands.

**Your enemy's rights are still rights.** Ibn Kathīr's line that Allah's dislike of treachery "even includes treachery against the disbelievers" is the heart of the final ayah, and Maʿārif states the principle just as plainly: the restriction falls on the Muslims, not on their adversaries. Being wronged first does not licence you to become the wrongdoer.

**If you must end an agreement, end it in the open.** No quiet completion of preparations, no advantage taken of the other side's unreadiness. Say it plainly, leave both parties on the same footing, and let them know exactly where they stand. Then prepare.

**Even severity has a purpose beyond itself.** The instruction to make an example closes on *laʿallahum yadhdhakkarūn* — that they may take a lesson. Where a believer is entitled to be firm, the aim is still correction rather than the pleasure of revenge. That single closing phrase, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, is where the mercy of the Lord of all the worlds shows itself even inside a command to strike hard.

passages.title: Prepare deterrent strength, yet incline to peace
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Ayah 59 tells the disbelievers who survived Badr that survival is not escape. Ayah 60 gives the believers real work: prepare whatever strength you can, aimed at deterrence. Ayah 61 tells the Prophet ﷺ that when the other side leans toward peace, he may lean back — and hand his fears to Allah. Ayah 62 tells him that even if the peace is a trick, Allah is enough. Ayah 63 points to the strength that was never his equipment at all: the hearts Allah joined together for him. What holds the unit together is a single argument about where power actually comes from.

---

## 1. "Surely, they will not frustrate [the Divine will]" (ayah 59)

**The occasion.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this ayah addresses the disbelievers who came out of Badr alive: those who never turned up to the battle at all, and those who showed up and then deserted the field, saving their lives. Badr was divine punishment for disbelief, and escaping from its grip was not possible for anyone.

**The words.** Of the first half, Ibn Kathir writes: "Do not think that such disbelievers have escaped Us or that We are unable to grasp them. Rather, they are under the power of Our ability and in the grasp of Our will; they will never escape Us." Of the second — *innahum lā yuʿjizūn* — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says: "these people cannot outsmart the will and power of Allah by their cleverness. If He decides to seize them, they would be unable to move even one step." And it adds the wider frame: perhaps they are seized here in this mortal world; otherwise their detention in the Hereafter is all too obvious.

**What it means for you, not only for them.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a lesson: a sinner who finds himself delivered from some hardship and then, instead of repenting, stands adamant over his sin, must never take that escape as a sign of everlasting deliverance. He is in the grip of Allah the whole time, and the respite given to him is in reality adding to his punishment and distress. Survival is not the same as safety.

---

## 2. "Prepare against them whatever you can" (ayah 60)

**The mercy hidden in a qualifier.** The command is *wa aʿiddū lahum mā istaṭaʿtum* — prepare for them whatever you are able. Ibn Kathir: Allah commands the Muslims to prepare for war "as much as possible, according to affordability and availability." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses on the qualifier: the ayah hints that success does not require acquiring the same quantity and quality of equipment as your adversary has; put together whatever supplies you can possibly acquire, and the help and support of Allah will be with you. The duty is maximum effort, not parity.

**Why the word is *quwwah* and not "swords".** The ayah says *min quwwah* — "of power". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this the heart of the ayah: the word covers everything in the form of military equipment, weapons and means of transport — and also staying physically fit and training in fighting skills and strategy. Because *quwwah* is a general word, its reference differs by age and place: the weapons of those days were arrows, swords and spears; then came the age of guns and cannon; and now is the time of bombs and rockets. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states plainly that Muslims of today should therefore acquire, as far as they can, capability of the modern kind — it names nuclear capability, tanks, fighter planes and submarines — because all of it is included within the sense of this one word. It adds: if reaching that end requires learning some art or science, and the effort is made with the intention that it will be used to defend Islam and the Muslims, then that study itself falls under the procedure of jihad and carries reward.

Ibn Kathir records the Prophet's ﷺ own words spoken over this ayah. Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿUqbah bin ʿĀmir heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, while standing on the minbar, reciting "And make ready against them all you can of power": **"Verily, Power is shooting! Power is shooting."** Muslim collected this hadith.

**And *ribāṭ al-khayl*.** After the general term comes one specific: the tethering of horses. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *ribāṭ* covers both the act of tying horses and horses tied up, and the outcome of either is the same — to breed, break and train horses and hold them in readiness with the intention of using them in jihad. Horses were mentioned particularly because in those times they were the most effective means of winning a war. The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah has placed *barakah* — blessing — on the forehead of horses.

Ibn Kathir gathers the sunnah on this, and its thrust is that the *intention* behind the preparation is what is being weighed:

- Imam Malik recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said horses are kept for one of three purposes: for some people a source of reward, for others a means of shelter, for others a source of sin. Reward for the man who keeps a horse for Allah's cause, tying it with a long tether on a meadow or in a garden — whatever it eats there is counted as good deeds for him; if it breaks its rope and jumps over one or two hillocks, its dung and footmarks are written as good deeds for him; if it passes a river and drinks, he is rewarded for that drinking though he had no intention of watering it. Shelter for the man who tied his horse maintaining self-sufficiency and abstinence from begging, while not forgetting Allah's right concerning it. And sin for the man who tied a horse for the sake of pride, pretence and showing enmity to Muslims. Al-Bukhari and Muslim collected this hadith; this is the wording of Al-Bukhari.
- Al-Bukhari recorded that ʿUrwah bin Abi al-Jaʿd al-Bāriqi said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Good will remain in the forelocks of horses until the Day of Resurrection — reward, and the spoils of war."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens "power" beyond hardware with a hadith reported by Abu Dawud, an-Nasa'i and ad-Darimi from Anas: **"Carry out jihad against the Mushrikin with your belongings, and your own selves and your eloquence (of speech or writing)."** Its comment: jihad is waged with weapons, and at times with the power of speech — and the jihad carried out with the pen falls under the same ruling as speech.

**The purpose: to be feared, not to kill.** Ibn Kathir glosses *turhibūn* as "to threaten", or to strike fear. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point sharply: the real purpose of acquiring and storing this strength "is not to indulge in an exercise of killing and being killed." The purpose is to bring down the force of disbelief and idolatry and fill the hearts of its protagonists with awe so that they stay suppressed. On some occasions the spoken or written word alone achieves that; on others fighting becomes necessary — defence is obligatory as the prevailing condition dictates.

**"And others besides them, whom you do not know."** Ibn Kathir records the early views: Mujahid said this refers to Banu Qurayzah; as-Suddi said the Persians; Muqatil bin Hayyan and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said the hypocrites. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it more broadly: the known enemies were those in ongoing confrontation with the Muslims — the disbelievers of Makkah and the Jews of Madinah — while the unknown were the disbelievers and polytheists of the wider world. And it notes what history then showed: full preparation against a present adversary casts its shadow over disbelievers in distant lands, as happened in the case of Cyrus and Caesar, who were deterred and suppressed during the age of the rightly guided caliphs. Notice what this half-ayah quietly affirms: there are enemies whose existence you cannot know, and He knows them.

**Paying for it.** All of this must be paid for, so the ayah closes: whatever you spend in the way of Allah will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be treated unjustly. Ibn Kathir recalls the parable of the grain that grows seven ears, each ear a hundred grains, "and Allah gives manifold increase to whom He wills" (2:261). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this return sometimes comes in the form of war spoils here in this world; otherwise the return laid up in the Hereafter is already determined — and that, obviously, is the more praiseworthy.

---

## 3. "If they incline to peace, incline to it" (ayah 61)

**The verb.** *Janaḥū* — to tilt, to incline toward. The picture is of two sides tilting: if theirs tilts your way, let yours tilt back.

**Is it a command or a permission?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is precise here: the imperative form is used to carry the sense of *choice*. At a time when the disbelievers are inclined toward peace, the Prophet ﷺ also has the choice of making peace, if he feels peace is in the best interest of the Muslims. Ibn Kathir reads it as the command to facilitate peace: if they resort to reconciliation and seek a treaty of non-hostility, accept their offers of peace.

**Hudaybiyah.** Ibn Kathir points to the living precedent: when the pagans inclined to peace in the year of Hudaybiyah and sought a cessation of hostilities for nine years, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ accepted this from them. Preparation and peace are not opposites here; they are two obediences.

Ibn Kathir records that ʿAbdullah bin al-Imam Ahmad reported from ʿAli bin Abi Talib that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"There will be disputes after me, so if you have a way to end them in peace, then do so."**

**Who may propose it.** From the restriction *in janaḥū* ("if they tilt"), Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives a point of policy: peace can normally be made only when the desire for it comes from the other side, since Muslims proposing peace unbidden would be taken as a sign of their weakness. But it adds the jurists' ruling for the hard case — if the Muslims are totally encircled and find no way out except a peace-for-security arrangement, then initiating a peace proposal is also permissible.

**And the worry that comes with it.** A peace proposed by the enemy carries the probability that they mean it as a strategy of deceit — to make you negligent and then strike. So the ayah ends: *wa tawakkal ʿala'llāh, innahu huwa as-Samīʿ al-ʿAlīm* — "and place your trust in Allah. Surely, He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the two names to the situation exactly: Allah hears what they say and also knows the intentions and designs concealed in their hearts. He is sufficient to help you — so do not base your decisions on probabilities that cannot be proved; the safest policy is to entrust all such apprehensions to Allah.

---

## 4. "And if they intend to deceive you" (ayah 62)

The passage now names the fear and dissolves it: *fa-inna ḥasbaka'llāh* — Allah is All-Sufficient for you. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paraphrases: should that probability turn out to be the reality — their intention bad, stopping at nothing short of a deceptive strike — even then you need not be troubled. Then the ayah points to the visible means: "He it is Who has supported you with His help and with the believers." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the group of Muslims Allah raised around him were the outward causes of the phenomena; the real and absolute Master who fused all the causes of victory together will never leave him alone to be deceived by the enemy.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then records what followed: under this divine promise, after the revelation of this ayah it never happened throughout his life that any deceit or ambush from his enemies brought him harm. The scholars of tafsir have therefore said that this promise is very much like the promise in "and Allah shall keep you protected from the people" (5:67) — after whose revelation the Prophet ﷺ told the noble Companions who had been guarding him that they could now set aside their concerns for his safety. And the commentary is careful to add the limit: this promise was special to the Prophet ﷺ. As for others, they should make proper practical arrangements after assessing the conditions prevailing around them. Trust in Allah does not cancel the taking of means — ayah 60 already commanded the means.

---

## 5. "He joined their hearts" (ayah 63)

**The favour being pointed at.** Ibn Kathir: it is Allah who gathered the believers' hearts — the Muhajirin and the Ansar — into believing, obeying, aiding and supporting the Prophet ﷺ. And then the staggering counterfactual: "If you had spent all that is in the earth, you could not have united their hearts." Why not? Ibn Kathir answers from history: because of the enmity and hatred that existed between them. Before Islam there were many wars between the Ansar tribes of Aws and Khazraj. However, Allah ended all that evil with the light of faith. He recalls the parallel address: "And remember Allah's favour on you, for you were enemies one to another, but He united your hearts, so that by His grace you became brethren" (3:103).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this ayah the explanation of the previous one. Ayah 62 said Allah supported him "with the believers" — but help from a community can only be available when that community is united as one. It was the *barakah*, the blessing, of the Prophet ﷺ that Allah made sworn enemies into loving brothers. So the real cause of the establishment and survival of the new Islamic state at Madinah, and of its dominance over its enemies, was nothing but the help and support of Allah; and the apparent cause was the mutual love and unity among the Muslims. Note where this leaves ayah 60: hardware without hearts is nothing.

Ibn Kathir cites what is recorded in the Two Sahihs — that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave a speech to the Ansar about the division of the war booty collected at Hunayn, he said to them: **"O Ansar! Did I not find you misguided and Allah guided you by me, poor and Allah enriched you by me, and divided and Allah united you by me?"** To every question he asked, they said, "Truly, the favour is from Allah and His Messenger."

**Beyond human reach.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle baldly: uniting the hearts of different people is something beyond human control. This can be done only by the One who created them all — the inner life of a human being answers to its Maker, not to a budget.

**ʿAzīz, Ḥakīm.** The ayah seals with two names. Ibn Kathir: He is the Most Formidable, and the hopes of those who have trust in Him never end unanswered; and He is All-Wise in all of His decisions and actions. Set against ayah 61's instruction to trust, the pairing is exact.

**Unity has a price, and it is obedience.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the practical consequence. Since the uniting of hearts is a blessing from Allah, that blessing cannot be hoped for in the presence of disobedience to Him; obedience and the seeking of His pleasure are binding conditions for it. The Qur'an's method is: "Hold the cord of Allah firmly, all of you, and do not be divided" (3:103) — the cord being the Qur'an, the Sharīʿah of Islam. The commentary's diagnosis: everyone loves to harp on unity, but the meaning each person takes is "if people agree to what I say, everyone will stand united" — and since normal difference of opinion among reasonable, honest people is inevitable and even necessary, unity on those terms cannot materialise until the Day of Doom. There is no sound and natural format of unity other than the one the Qur'an gives: both parties sit together and agree to what a third party has to say, a party whose decision is certainly free of error — and Allah alone can be that decision-maker. It also cites Sūrah Maryam: "Surely, among those who believe and do good deeds, the All-Merciful generates love" (19:96). Dispute and disorder erupt only when the limits of the Sharīʿah are crossed.

---

## Living it

**Prepare with what you actually have.** The command is bounded by *mā istaṭaʿtum*: you are not asked to match anyone; you are asked not to be idle. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's extension is a live one for a student today — an art or science learned with the intention of defending Islam and the Muslims falls under the procedure of jihad.

**Aim at deterrence, not destruction.** The stated purpose of strength in ayah 60 is that the enemy be filled with awe and stay suppressed.

**Take the peace when it is offered.** Hudaybiyah is the precedent Ibn Kathir chose, and the report from ʿAli that he cites carries the principle forward into the disputes that came after the Prophet ﷺ.

**Do not let suspicion govern you.** Ayah 61 hands your unprovable fears to as-Samīʿ al-ʿAlīm; ayah 62 tells you Allah is All-Sufficient. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that the guarantee against deceit was special to the Prophet ﷺ, so take sensible practical measures — and then stop turning the fear over.

**Guard the unity you were given.** Ayah 59 says the disbelievers cannot outstrip Allah; ayah 63 says the believers could not, with all the wealth of the earth, have manufactured their own brotherhood. Both ends of the passage take the outcome out of human hands and place it in His — which is why the response to both is the same: obey Him, prepare honestly, and trust.

passages.title: Allah suffices; rouse the believers to fight
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat are the Qur'an steadying a small, under-equipped community on the edge of its first battle. Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ that He is sufficient for him (64), commands him to rouse the believers for the fight (65), and then fixes the odds a believer is required to hold against — first one against ten, then, made easy, one against two (65–66). What holds the three together is a single movement: **sufficiency, then courage, then a burden measured to the strength of the people carrying it** — the whole of it sealed with the promise that "Allah is with the patient."

## The moment: the eve of Badr

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that the commentators say ayah 64 was revealed *before actual fighting started* at the battle of Badr, precisely so that the Muslims — small in numbers and, in its words, "virtually unequipped" — would not be overawed by the heavy numerical and technical superiority of their adversary.

Maʿārif fills in the picture. Badr was "the very first battle Muslims had ever fought," and at that time "they were in a terrible condition." The total number of Muslims was itself insignificant; not even all of them had gone to the war front; the "army" of that battle was simply those who could get ready on the spot. Into that situation comes a revelation that does not deny the odds — it reframes who is actually on the field.

## Ayah 64: "Allah is sufficient for you"

The ayah reads: **"O Prophet! Allah is sufficient for you and for the believers."** The Arabic word at its centre is *ḥasbuka* — "your sufficiency," rendered here as "Allah is sufficient for you."

There is a fine difference in how the two commentators read the rest of the ayah, and it is worth seeing both:

- **Ibn Kathir's rendering:** "Allah is sufficient for you *and for the believers who follow you*." Allah's sufficiency covers the Prophet ﷺ and everyone who follows him.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading:** the Prophet ﷺ is comforted by being told that "sufficient for him is Allah Taʿālā in the real sense, and the group of believers in the physical sense." That is, Allah is the true and ultimate sufficiency, and the believers around him are the physical means.

On either reading, Maʿārif draws the same conclusion: "he should have no fear of an enemy, no matter how big, strong, numerous or well-equipped."

Ibn Kathir puts the same guarantee in his own words. Allah, he says, "will suffice, aid, support, and help the believers against their enemies, even if their enemies are numerous and have sufficient supplies, while the believers are few." Both commentators land in the same place: the smallness of the believers' numbers and equipment is simply not the decisive fact on that field.

## Ayah 65: *ḥarriḍ* — the Prophet ﷺ is told to rouse them

The command in ayah 65 is **ḥarriḍ al-muʼminīna ʿalā l-qitāl** — "Motivate the believers to fight," or in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "Urge the believers to fight." He glosses the word simply: he "encouraged and called them to fight."

This is worth pausing on. Allah has just said He is sufficient — and the very next thing in the passage is a task given to the Prophet ﷺ. Divine sufficiency does not cancel human effort; it is the ground on which human effort is asked for. And what is asked for here is not a matter of tactics or supplies. It is **the work of raising hearts.**

Ibn Kathir then shows us what that rousing actually sounded like. He relates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to encourage the Companions to fight when they faced the enemy, and that on the day of Badr, when the idolators came with their forces and supplies, he ﷺ said to his Companions:

> "Get ready and march forth towards a Paradise as wide as the heavens and earth."

ʿUmayr bin al-Humām said, "As wide as the heavens and earth?" The Messenger ﷺ said, "Yes." ʿUmayr said, "Excellent! Excellent!" The Messenger ﷺ asked him, "What makes you say, 'Excellent! Excellent!'?" He said, "The hope that I might be one of its dwellers." The Prophet ﷺ said, **"You are one of its people."**

ʿUmayr went ahead, broke the scabbard of his sword, took some dates and started eating from them. He then threw the dates from his hand, saying: "Verily, if I lived until I finished eating these dates, then it is indeed a long life." He went ahead, fought and was killed, may Allah be pleased with him.

That is the whole passage acted out by one man. Notice the order in his own words: he hears the promise, weighs the rest of his life against it, and finds that even the time it would take to finish a handful of dates is a long life to wait.

## Why the ruling arrives as good news, not as an order

Read ayah 65 again and notice its style. It does not say "twenty of you *must* stand against two hundred." It says: **"If there are twenty steadfast persons among you, they will overcome two hundred."** It is phrased as an announcement of victory.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out beautifully. The style of expression used here, it says, "is that of a welcome news flash — that one hundred Muslims shall overcome one thousand disbelievers. But, the purpose is to order" that a hundred Muslims may not avoid fighting a thousand disbelievers. So why announce a duty as a bulletin? "The wisdom behind using the style of news is to make the hearts of Muslims become strong with this glad tidings telling them that Allah is promising their safety and victory. Had this order been announced in the imperative mood as a law, it would have naturally weighed heavy on temperaments."

This is a teaching about how Allah legislates for people He knows. The same content — *do not run* — lands as crushing weight in one form and as confidence in another, and He chose the form that strengthens the heart that has to carry it. Maʿārif notes the setting again here: because Badr was the first battle, fought in that condition, "one hundred Muslims were commanded to confront one thousand disbelievers in a style which carried the promise of Divine help and support."

Ayah 65 also supplies its own reason for the lopsided arithmetic: **"because they (the disbelievers) are people who do not understand."** Maʿārif approaches the same imbalance from the side of the believers: the Muslims' "matter is different, not like that of the peoples of the world at large," for the unseen help of Allah is with them. He cites the principle from elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"There are many smaller groups which overcome larger groups with the will of Allah"* (2:249). On that basis, Maʿārif says, "ten Muslims were declared to be equal to one hundred men in the first Jihad of Islam at the famous battle of Badr."

## The lightening: from one-against-ten to one-against-two

Ayah 65 set the bar at ten to one. Ayah 66 lowers it: **"Now Allah has lightened your burden, for He knows that there is weakness in you."**

Ibn Kathir states it plainly: the earlier ayah means "one Muslim should endure ten disbelievers"; "Allah abrogated this part later on, **but the good news remained**." The obligation shrank; the promise did not.

He supports this with two narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās:

1. ʿAbdullāh bin al-Mubārak said that Jarīr bin Ḥāzim narrated to them, that az-Zubayr bin al-Khirrīt narrated to him, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās: when the ayah about twenty overcoming two hundred was revealed, "it became difficult for the Muslims, when Allah commanded that one Muslim is required to endure ten idolators. Soon after, this matter was made easy" by *"Now Allah has lightened your (task)."* Ibn ʿAbbās explains the mechanism: "Allah lowered the number, and thus, made the required patience less, compatible to the decrease in numbers." **Al-Bukhari recorded a similar narration from Ibn al-Mubārak.**
2. Muhammad bin Isḥāq recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said the ruling "was difficult for the Muslims, for they thought it was burdensome since twenty should fight two hundred, and a hundred against a thousand. Allah made this ruling easy for them and abrogated this Ayah with another Ayah."

Ibn Kathir then states the settled outcome: **thereafter, if the Muslims were half as many as their enemy, they were not allowed to run away from them; if they were fewer than that, they were not obligated to fight the disbelievers and were thus allowed to avoid hostilities.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reaches the same place from the legal side: in ayah 65 the avoidance of one Muslim fighting against ten was declared forbidden; in ayah 66 "the avoidance of one against two was all that remained forbidden. And this is the last and final injunction which is operative forever and shall continue as such." Maʿārif also notes that ayah 66 keeps the *same* gentle style: "here too, the command does not appear in the usual style of a command. Instead, the manner used is that of glad tidings," which indicates that asking one Muslim to stand firm against two was in no way an injustice or a coercion — because Allah has Himself placed in a Muslim, because of his īmān (faith), "a special power that one of them turns out to be equal to two."

## "For He knows that there is weakness in you"

This clause is the heart of the passage's tenderness. Allah does not say *you failed*, or *you complained*. He says **He knows.**

The narrations do record that the first ruling "became difficult for the Muslims" and that "they thought it was burdensome." But the reason the ayah itself gives for the lightening is not their difficulty; it is His knowledge — *for He knows that there is weakness in you.* He knows the weakness, and knowing it, He legislates around it. Ibn ʿAbbās's phrasing captures the proportion exactly: the numbers came down, and with them the amount of patience required came down to match. The obligation was re-cut to fit the person wearing it.

## The condition attached to the promise: *ṣabr*

Both ayat make the good news conditional, and the condition is one word — **ṣābirūn / ṣābirah**, the steadfast, the patient. Twenty *steadfast* men overcome two hundred; a hundred *steadfast* overcome two hundred. Ayah 66 adds another qualifier the reader should not skim past: they overcome **"by the leave of Allah" (bi-idhni-llāh)**. The victory is never a mechanical output of the ratio; it is granted.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the condition explicit: "at both places, the glad tidings about this support and victory has been made subject to the condition that these Muslims should be observers of patience and fortitude." And it explains why patience is the hinge: "standing steadfast while endangering one's dear life in fighting and killing on a battlefield is a feat which can be performed only by a person whose 'Iman is perfect — because, perfect 'Iman generates enthusiasm for surrendering one's life in the way of Allah and this enthusiasm multiplies his combat strength a lot more." Faith is not a supplement to fighting strength. In Maʿārif's account, it *is* the multiplier.

## "And Allah is with the patient"

The passage closes on a sentence far wider than the battlefield it was revealed for: **wa-llāhu maʿa ṣ-ṣābirīn** — "And Allah is with the patient."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this comes "in the manner of a general principle," and that those included in it are not only "those who remain steadfast in the battlefield" but also those "who keep following the usual injunctions of the Sharīʿah strictly. The promise of Divine company stands good for all of them."

And what Maʿārif draws from it is the practical heart of the matter: "in this state of His being with one and all of them lies the real secret of their victory — because, whoever has the good fortune of having the company of the Absolute Master simply cannot be moved away from the station of duty by anyone, not even by the whole world in unison."

So the passage ends where it began. Ayah 64 said *Allah is sufficient for you*. Ayah 66 says *Allah is with the patient*. Sufficiency at the start, companionship at the end, and in between a duty carefully sized to human weakness.

## Living it

- **Begin from sufficiency, not from the odds.** Ayah 64 settles the question of who suffices before ayah 65 issues the command to fight. Counting the opposition first and looking for Allah afterwards inverts the order of the passage.
- **Sufficiency does not excuse you from effort.** The very next ayah is a command to act. Ibn Kathir's note that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "used to encourage the Companions to fight when they faced the enemy" makes the rousing of others' courage part of the work, not a preface to it.
- **Expect Allah's law to fit your actual strength.** Ayah 66 is the proof that "He knows that there is weakness in you" is written into how you are commanded. The One who lightened this burden did so because He knew the weakness of those carrying it.
- **Steadfastness is the condition of the promise, and it is broader than war.** Maʿārif extends "Allah is with the patient" to everyone who keeps following the injunctions of the Sharīʿah strictly. Wherever holding your ground is hard, that ayah is addressed to you.
- **Keep ʿUmayr's arithmetic.** He measured the remainder of his life against a Paradise as wide as the heavens and the earth, and called even the time to finish a handful of dates "a long life." Most of us are not asked for his battlefield — but we are asked for his sense of proportion.

passages.title: The rebuke over the captives of Badr
passages.tafsir:
# The rebuke over the captives of Badr (8:67–69)

These three ayat address one moment: the aftermath of Badr, when the Muslims took seventy of the enemy's chiefs prisoner and gathered the property the enemy left behind — before Allah had yet revealed any ruling permitting either. Ayah 67 delivers the rebuke, ayah 68 explains why the punishment it deserved never fell, and ayah 69 lifts the matter entirely, declaring the spoils lawful and pure and closing with forgiveness and mercy. Read together, they are a single arc: **censure, reprieve, permission.**

## The day the question had no answer yet

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene carefully. Badr was the first jihad in Islam, and it came upon the Muslims all of a sudden. Until then, the detailed injunctions of jihad had not been revealed. Live questions hung in the air: if spoils come to hand during jihad, what should be done with them? If enemy soldiers fall under your control, is it even permissible to arrest them?

The law of spoils operative in the religious codes of the past prophets was that the gains of battle were **not lawful** for the believers to use for their own benefit. The whole of it was to be collected and placed in some open field, and by a Divine practice a fire would come from the skies and burn it. That was taken as the sign that the particular jihad was approved of. If the fire did not come, it was taken as a sign that there was some shortcoming in the effort, and that it was not acceptable with Allah.

That spoils would be particularly lawful for this Ummah — this community of believers — already existed in the infinite knowledge of Allah, but no revelation attesting to it had yet come down to the Prophet ﷺ. Then Allah blessed the Muslims at Badr with an extraordinary victory. The enemy left behind its belongings, which fell into Muslim hands as spoils, and seventy of their big chiefs were taken as prisoners. The necessary clarification of whether those two actions were permissible was still to come through revelation. It is this haste that these ayat address.

## The consultation over the prisoners

Imam Ahmad recorded that Anas said that the Prophet ﷺ asked the people for their opinion about the prisoners of war of Badr, saying, *"Allah has made you prevail above them."* ʿUmar bin Al-Khaṭṭāb stood up and said, "O Allah's Messenger! Cut off their necks" — but the Prophet ﷺ turned away from him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked again: *"O people! Allah has made you prevail over them, and only yesterday, they were your brothers."* ʿUmar again stood up with the same answer, and again the Prophet ﷺ ignored him and asked the same question, and he repeated the same answer. Then Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq stood up and said, "O Allah's Messenger! I think you should pardon them and set them free in return for ransom." Thereupon the grief on the face of Allah's Messenger ﷺ vanished. He pardoned them and accepted ransom for their release — and Allah revealed ayah 68.

**The two options offered from above.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a crucial layer, reporting on the authority of Sayyidunā ʿAlī al-Murtaḍā (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) in Jāmiʿ Tirmidhī, Sunan al-Nasāʼī and Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān: Jibrāʼīl al-Amīn (ʿalayhi as-salām) came to the Prophet ﷺ on this occasion with the command that he give his Companions a choice between two courses — (1) that they kill these prisoners and destroy the image of enemy power for ever, or (2) that they be released against some payment of *fidyah* (ransom), **but** with it Divinely ordained that in the coming year the number of Muslims who would fall as martyrs would match the number of prisoners released today against ransom. Yet in the second, where mention was made of the martyrdom of seventy Muslims, there existed a delicate indication of that option's undesirability in the sight of Allah — because had it been desirable, the killing of seventy Muslims would not have been made binding as its result.

**How the Companions reasoned.** Some thought that if these men were released against ransom, it was quite possible that all or some of them might become Muslims at a later stage — which would be the real gain, and the very objective of jihad itself. They also thought that the Muslims were poor at that time, so a financial gain through ransom for seventy men would remove their hardship and contribute to their preparations for jihad in future. As for the martyrdom of seventy Muslims, that was a standing blessing and good fortune — why worry about something so welcome? It was for these reasons that Abū Bakr and most of the Companions tilted toward ransom. Only ʿUmar, Saʿd ibn Muʿādh and some other Companions differed, recommending that they be killed: it was a good chance, they argued, since the Quraysh chiefs who sponsored the entire force arrayed against the Muslims had fallen into their hands at one time. That these men would embrace Islam was a figment of the imagination; what was more likely was that once released they would become the cause of hostility more pronounced than ever before.

**And the Prophet ﷺ.** He looked at the two opinions and accepted the one that provided mercy and ease for the prisoners. Addressing Abū Bakr and ʿUmar he said: *"Had you two agreed upon any one opinion, I would have not acted against the opinion given by you two"* (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, from Maẓharī). And the outcome was that the next year, at the battle of Uḥud, the martyrdom of seventy Muslims came to pass as Divinely indicated.

## "Until he has had a thorough bloodshed in the land"

The pivot of ayah 67 is the word **يُثْخِن (yuthkhin)**, from **اِثخان (ithkhān)**.
