Lexically, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, it means to demolish someone's might and power *exhaustively and conclusively* — not to wound but to break. The words **فِي الْأَرْضِ (fi'l-arḍ, "in the land")** were made to follow precisely in order to intensify that sense of total termination. So the ayah is not a general prohibition on taking captives; it is a statement about *sequence*. Captives come after the enemy's power has been broken, not instead of breaking it.

This is why the verse tells those Companions that their advice was improper: it did not match the august station of any prophet that, once he overpowers his enemies, he should leave their power and its image undemolished and instead grant relief to a wicked and conspiratorial enemy, only to commit the Muslims to everlasting trouble.

## "You want the goods of this world, but Allah wants the Hereafter"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that in ayah 67 the address — تُرِيدُونَ عَرَضَ الدُّنْيَا — is to the noble Companions who had suggested release for ransom. Part of their view was, no doubt, purely religious: the hope that once free these people might embrace Islam. But part was motivated by personal interest as well — that they would have spoils to bring back — although until that time there was no decisive textual authority proving spoils to be permissible property for Muslims. The ayah names only the second strand.

Maʿārif draws the lesson out: in view of the high standards being set for a society under the education and training of the Prophet ﷺ — standards aiming to take them to ranks even higher than the angels — the slightest turn of thought toward material acquisition was counted a kind of disobedience; and the sum total of a mixture of deeds both permissible and impermissible will, after all, be called impermissible. As for the Prophet ﷺ, by accepting their opinion he had gone along with them in a certain way, but that act of his was purely a demonstration of his being universally merciful.

**عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ — Mighty, Wise.** The closing of ayah 67 is not decoration. Maʿārif reads it as a promise embedded in a rebuke: Allah, being the source of all might and wisdom, would have provided them wealth and properties in their future victories through His infinite grace — only if they had not acted in a hurry.

## Ayah 68: the decree that arrived before the mistake

**لَّوْلَا كِتَابٌ مِّنَ اللَّهِ سَبَقَ** — "Were it not a previous ordainment from Allah, a severe torment would have touched you for what you took."

What was that prior writ? ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās said it was "in the Preserved Book, that war spoils and prisoners of war will be made allowed for you" — and that the torment "would have touched you for what you took" was because of the captives. So the punishment was withheld not because the act was small, but because Allah had already inscribed the permission that was about to be revealed. Al-ʿAwfī also reported this statement from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Ibn Kathīr notes that a similar statement was collected from Abū Hurayrah, Ibn Masʿūd, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿAṭāʼ, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Qatādah and al-Aʿmash — all stating that the "previous ordainment" refers to the allowing of the spoils of war for this Ummah.

Supporting this view, Ibn Kathīr cites what the Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded that Jābir bin ʿAbdullāh said, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *I have been given five things which were not given to any Prophet before me. (They are:) Allah made me victorious by awe, (by His frightening my enemies) for a distance of one month's journey. The earth has been made a place for praying and a purifyer for me. The booty has been made lawful for me, yet it was not lawful for anyone else before me. I have been given the right of intercession (on the Day of Resurrection). Every Prophet used to be sent to his people only, but I have been sent to all mankind.*

Ibn Kathīr then reports: al-Aʿmash narrated that Abū Ṣāliḥ said that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"War booty was never allowed for any among mankind except us."* The text adds — attributing the remark to Abū Hurayrah — that this is why Allah said, "So enjoy what you have gotten of booty in war, lawful and good."

**How close it came.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that it appears in hadith narrations that, after this ayah was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said that the Divine punishment was almost about to descend when Allah in His grace held it back — and had it come, no one except ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Saʿd ibn Muʿādh would have remained safe from it. (The bundle reports this without naming a collection, so it is given here as it stands, unattributed to any book.)

**Which act was rebuked — the ransom, or the spoils?** According to a narration from Abū Hurayrah reported in Tirmidhī, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Spoils were not lawful for any community before you." Maʿārif (citing Maẓharī) explains that when, on the occasion of Badr, the Muslims went after collecting spoils — though spoils had not been made lawful for them until that time — this ayah was revealed. So one report ties the admonition to the release of prisoners against ransom, while the Tirmidhī narration points to the collecting of spoils. Maʿārif sees no contradiction between the two: **taking ransom from prisoners is also nothing but a part of spoils.**

## Ayah 69: made lawful, and made pure

What remained unclear was the future course Muslims were to take in such matters. So the next ayah settles it: **فَكُلُوا مِمَّا غَنِمْتُمْ** — "So, eat of the spoils you have got." From now on it is lawful for you.

The injunction making spoils lawful came at *this* stage; what of the spoils collected in error *before* it — might some element of undesirability cling to them? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the very next words remove exactly that doubt: **حَلَالًا طَيِّبًا — "lawful and pure."** Taking the initiative in collecting spoils before the Divine guideline came was not correct; but now that the injunction has been revealed, all that was collected earlier is lawful too, without any shade of repugnance or reprehensibility — *karāhah*, the quality of being disliked — attached to it.

**A principle of fiqh worth keeping.** Maʿārif draws out the rule and, importantly, its limit. When some impermissible initiative is regularized through a standing verse, no effect of the previous initiative remains operative in it: the property becomes lawful and pure, as here. But take the contrasting case, where an injunction had *already* been revealed and people contravened it, discovering only later that their deed was contrary to such and such injunction of the Qurʼān and Sunnah — there the property does not become lawful, even though the previous error is forgiven (*Nūr al-Anwār*, Mullā Jīwan).

**And then a restraint.** The ayah does not end with permission; it ends with **وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ** — "and fear Allah. Surely, Allah is Most-Forgiving, Very-Merciful." The hint given here, says Maʿārif, is that though spoils have been made lawful, they have been made lawful under a particular law: taking against that law, or taking more than one's due, shall still not be permissible. A permission from Allah is never a licence — hence *taqwā*, that mindful fear of Allah which keeps a person inside the limits He sets.

## What the scholars derived about captives

Ibn Kathīr records that the Muslims then took the ransom for their captives: in his *Sunan*, Imām Abū Dāwūd recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ fixed four hundred dirhams in ransom from the people of Jāhiliyyah — the age of ignorance before Islam — in the aftermath of Badr.

**The majority position**, as Ibn Kathīr states it, is that the matter of prisoners of war is up to the Imām, the Muslim ruler or commander. If he decides, he can have them killed, as in the case of Banū Qurayẓah; he can accept a ransom for them, as with the prisoners of Badr; or exchange them for Muslim prisoners — the Messenger ﷺ exchanged a woman and her daughter who were captured by Salamah bin al-Akwaʿ for some Muslims who were captured by the idolators; or, if he decides, he can take them as captives.

**The question of abrogation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out a genuine difference. Ibn ʿAbbās said that the Divine admonition came over releasing prisoners against ransom at Badr, when the might and power of the disbelievers was yet to break apart; when Islam and the Muslims went on to achieve total ascendency, Allah revealed 47:4 in Sūrah Muḥammad, in which the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims were given four options over prisoners: kill them, put them in bondage, release them against ransom, or free them without taking any ransom. The Ummah is agreed on the first two — that the Amīr of the Muslims has the right to kill prisoners or hold them in bondage. On the other two, the jurists differ:

- **Imām Mālik, Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, Thawrī, Isḥāq**, and, from among the Tābiʿīn — the generation that followed the Companions — **al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and ʿAṭāʼ**: both forms are permissible for the Amīr of the Muslims — release against compensation, release without it, or exchange for Muslim prisoners.
- **Imām Abū Ḥanīfah, Abū Yūsuf, Muḥammad, Awzāʿī**, and **Qatādah, Ḍaḥḥāk, Suddiyy, Ibn Jurayj**: setting them free without compensation is simply not permissible; and even releasing them against ransom is not permissible in the well-known view of Imām Abū Ḥanīfah — though it appears in a report of *al-Siyar al-Kabīr* that if the Muslims are in need of financial support they may release prisoners against ransom. Releasing them in exchange for Muslim prisoners is permissible with Abū Ḥanīfah and his two companions, Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad.

Those who permit release, with or without ransom, regard — as Ibn ʿAbbās said — the verse of Sūrah Muḥammad as the abrogator (*nāsikh*) of this verse of al-Anfāl. The Ḥanafī jurists reverse it: for them 47:4 is what stands abrogated (*mansūkh*), its abrogators being 8:57 ("make them an example, for those behind them") and 9:5. **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own reading** is that careful deliberation over the wording of the two passages leaves the impression that neither can be called abrogator or abrogated: they are **two injunctions for two different situations.** Al-Anfāl states the pivotal objective — *ithkhān fi'l-arḍ*, breaking the power of the disbelievers. Sūrah Muḥammad grants the option of release, as a favour or against ransom, *once* that power has been broken. On this reading, the report of *al-Siyar al-Kabīr* from Abū Ḥanīfah could itself be intended to establish that either kind of ruling may be given in view of the conditions and needs the Muslims face.

## Living it

The passage is astonishingly gentle with the people it is correcting. Yet Allah still weighed the intention beneath the reasoning, and it was the strand of personal interest woven into an otherwise religious argument that drew the words *"You want the goods of this world."*

Three things follow. **First**, motives are audited, not just actions — a good deed can be entered into for mixed reasons, and Allah sees which strand is which. **Second**, do not run ahead of the ruling; the error at Badr was not wickedness but haste. **Third**, when Allah permits something, receive it as *ḥalālan ṭayyiban* without lingering unease — and receive it with *taqwā*, within the limits He sets. The passage that opens with a warning of severe torment closes on **Ghafūr, Raḥīm**, and that ordering is the mercy of it.

passages.title: Hope and warning for the captives
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These two ayat are a message Allah gives the Prophet ﷺ to deliver to the prisoners of Badr — men who had come out against him and were now in his custody, released against ransom. Ayah 70 offers them hope: if Allah knows any good in their hearts, He will give them something better than what was taken from them, and forgive them on top of it. Ayah 71 closes the other side of the door: if they mean to betray, they should remember they already betrayed Allah before, and He is the One who brought about their capture.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the unity of the two exactly: in ayah 70 the call to Islam is given to the released prisoners **in the mode of persuasion**, and in ayah 71 **in the mode of warning** — that their success in this world and the next depends on Islam and faith. One invitation, two voices. The closings differ too: ayah 70 ends *Ghafūr Raḥīm* — Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful — while ayah 71 ends *ʿAlīm Ḥakīm* — All-Knowing, All-Wise.

## The situation behind the words

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks us to feel the strangeness of the scene. These captives were sworn enemies of Islam who "had left nothing undone when it came to harassing, torturing, beating and killing" the Muslims whenever they got the chance. Now they were prisoners in Muslim hands — and they were merely being released against ransom. Simply being granted a lease of life, Maʿārif notes, was no small thing; it was "virtually touching the outside limits of kindness under given circumstances," and the ransom taken from them was far too ordinary.

And then comes the astonishing part. Allah does not stop at sparing them. Maʿārif invites us to imagine the consideration shown even for the discomfort caused to them in paying that paltry sum for freedom — and to see how it is removed. That is the door ayah 70 opens.

## Before the battle: the Prophet ﷺ marks out who must not be killed

Muhammad bin Ishaq reported that ʿAbdullah bin ʿAbbas said that before Badr the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told his men that some people from Bani Hashim and others had been forced to accompany the pagans although they had no desire to fight the Muslims — so whoever met any of them should not kill him. He named Abu Al-Bukhtari bin Hisham, and his own uncle Al-ʿAbbas bin ʿAbdul-Muttalib, "for he was forced to come (with the pagan army)."

Abu Hudhayfah bin ʿUtbah objected out loud: "Shall we kill our fathers, children, brothers and tribesmen, and leave Al-ʿAbbas? By Allah! If I meet him, I will kill him with the sword." When this reached the Prophet ﷺ he turned to ʿUmar bin Al-Khattab and said, *"O Abu Hafs!"* — and ʿUmar said, "By Allah that was the first time that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called me Abu Hafs." Then he said: **"Will the face of the Messenger of Allah's uncle be struck with the sword?"** ʿUmar said, "O Allah's Messenger! Give me permission to cut off his neck" — meaning Abu Hudhayfah — "for he has fallen into hypocrisy, by Allah!" Abu Hudhayfah never stopped fearing that sentence afterwards; he used to say he would not feel safe from it coming back to haunt him unless Allah forgave him for it through martyrdom. He was martyred at Al-Yamamah, may Allah be pleased with him.

Keep that scene in mind when you reach ayah 70. Long before the prisoners were told "if Allah knows any good in your hearts," the Prophet ﷺ had already drawn a line between the men dragged out against their will and the men who had come to fight.

## The night after Badr

Ibn ʿAbbas said that on the eve after Badr the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spent the first part of the night awake while the prisoners lay bound. His Companions asked why he was not sleeping. Al-ʿAbbas had been captured by a man from the Ansar, and the Prophet ﷺ said: **"I heard the cries of pain from my uncle Al-ʿAbbas, because of his shackles, so untie him."** When his uncle stopped crying from pain, he went to sleep.

And yet the ransom itself was not waived for him. In his *Sahih*, Al-Bukhari recorded a hadith from Musa bin ʿUqbah, from Ibn Shihab, from Anas bin Malik, that some men from the Ansar asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission to set free their maternal cousin Al-ʿAbbas without taking ransom from him. He said: **"No, by Allah! Do not leave any Dirham of it."** Compassion for a man's pain, and no relaxation of what was due from him. The two do not cancel each other.

## The ransom, in two tellings

Both commentaries dwell on Al-ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that most commentators say this ayah was revealed about him, since he too was one of the prisoners of Badr and ransom was taken from him too.

His case was special. Maʿārif explains that he had left Makkah for Badr with almost seven hundred guineas of gold on his person — twenty *Uqiyah*, a unit of weight — which was meant to be spent on the army of the disbelievers. Before it could be spent, he was taken prisoner with the gold.

The two commentaries preserve the ransom negotiation in two separate accounts. They overlap in substance but are not one continuous scene, and it is worth hearing each in its own voice.

**Ibn Kathir's account.** The Quraysh sent to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning ransoming their prisoners, and each tribe paid what was required for their own. Al-ʿAbbas said, "O Allah's Messenger! I became a Muslim before." The Prophet ﷺ replied: **"Allah knows if you are Muslim! If what you are claiming is true, then Allah will compensate you. As for your outward appearance, it was against us. Therefore, ransom yourself, as well as your nephews Nawfal bin Al-Harith bin ʿAbdul-Muttalib and ʿAqil bin Abu Talib bin ʿAbdul-Muttalib, and also your ally ʿUtbah bin ʿAmr, from Bani Al-Harith bin Fihr."**

Al-ʿAbbas said, "I do not have that (money), O Allah's Messenger!" The Prophet ﷺ said: **"What about the wealth that you and Umm Al-Fadl buried, and you said to her, 'If I am killed in this battle, then this money that I buried is for my children Al-Fadl, ʿAbdullah and Quthm?'"**

Al-ʿAbbas answered, "By Allah, O Allah's Messenger! I know that you are Allah's Messenger, for this is a thing that none except Umm Al-Fadl and I knew." He then asked whether the twenty *Uwqiyah* taken from him in the battle could be counted towards his ransom. The answer was: **"No, for that was money that Allah made as war spoils for us from you."** So Al-ʿAbbas ransomed himself, his two nephews and an ally — and Allah revealed this ayah.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account.** When the time came to pay ransom, Al-ʿAbbas asked that the gold he had carried be applied to cover his ransom. The Prophet ﷺ said that the wealth he had brought to support disbelief had become war spoils for the Muslims, and ransom had to be in addition to that — and that he should also pay the ransom for his two nephews, ʿAqil ibn Abi Talib and Nawfil ibn Harith. Al-ʿAbbas protested that so much financial burden would leave him begging before the Quraysh like a pauper. The Prophet ﷺ said: Why? What about the wealth you entrusted to your wife, Umm al-Fadl, on leaving Makkah? Al-ʿAbbas asked how he could possibly know this, when he had entrusted it to her in the darkness of night, personally and in private, with no third person aware of it. He said: **"My Rabb has told me everything about it."**

Maʿārif tells us what that moment did to him. His heart became certain that the Prophet ﷺ was a true messenger of Allah. He had held him in esteem even before this, but there were some doubts as well — which Allah removed at that moment. In reality, he had become a Muslim right then. But he had a great deal of money loaned out to the Quraysh of Makkah, and an immediate public declaration would have cost him all of it; so he did not announce it, and the Prophet ﷺ said nothing about it to anyone either. Later, before the Conquest of Makkah, he asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to migrate from Makkah to Madinah, and the Prophet ﷺ advised him not to do that yet.

Maʿārif adds that following this conversation, the Prophet ﷺ also told him about the promise appearing in this very ayah: that if he embraced Islam with unalloyed sincerity of heart, the money he had spent in ransom would be returned to him by Allah, made much more and much better for him.

## Reading ayah 70 closely

**"Say to the captives that are in your hands."** Notice who is told to speak: *Yā ayyuhā an-Nabī*, "O Prophet." The very Messenger of Allah ﷺ they had come out against is the one commanded to bring them the offer.

**"If Allah knows any good in your hearts."** The condition is not a public declaration or a display; it is what Allah knows is inside. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *khayr* — "good" — here means **īmān (faith) and ikhlāṣ (sincerity)**: prisoners who, once free, take to faith and Islam with sincerity will receive more and better than what they gave in ransom. Maʿārif's own comment on the whole arrangement is the right response to it: "Certainly great is the kindness of Allah Taʿālā."

**"He will give you something better than what has been taken from you."** Not repayment — *khayr*, better. Maʿārif draws out the invitation: made free and independent, the prisoners are being asked to consider their profit and loss as free individuals.

**"And He will forgive you; and Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** The compensation is worldly; the forgiveness is what actually matters. Maʿārif observes that events proved it out: those of them who embraced Islam were heavily rewarded by Allah right here in this mortal world with wealth and property far higher than what they had paid as ransom — "not to mention the forgiveness they were blessed with and the high ranks of Paradise they received in the Hereafter."

## The promise, visibly kept

Al-ʿAbbas himself became the proof. Ibn Kathir records his words: **"After I became Muslim, Allah gave me twenty servants in place of the twenty Uwqiyah I lost. And I hope for Allah's forgiveness."** Maʿārif fills in his fuller testimony, from after his adherence to Islam had become public knowledge: he used to say he was seeing the manifestation of this promise with his own eyes — twenty of his slaves running businesses in several places, no venture worth any less than twenty thousand dirhams each; and on top of all this, the blessing of serving the visiting pilgrims with drinking water from the sacred well of Zamzam, a service he considered so valuable as would pale out the possession of the entire wealth of the people of Makkah. Note where he stopped: the wealth he counted, but forgiveness he only *hoped* for. That is the posture of a believer.

Ibn Kathir adds a scene recorded by Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Al-Bayhaqi from Anas bin Malik — and also collected by Al-Bukhari in several places of his *Sahih* with an abridged chain, in a manner indicating his approval of it. Wealth was brought to the Prophet ﷺ from Bahrain, the biggest amount of goods he had ever received, and he said, **"Distribute it in my Masjid."** He left for prayer and did not even look at it. Afterwards he sat by the goods and gave to everybody he saw. Al-ʿAbbas came and said, "O Allah's Messenger! Give me (something) too, because I gave ransom for myself and ʿAqil." He was told to take. He stuffed his garment until he could not carry it, asked for someone to help him lift it and was refused, asked the Prophet ﷺ himself and was refused again, then dropped some of it and hauled the rest away on his shoulders — and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept watching him until he disappeared from sight, astonished at his greediness. He did not get up until the last coin was distributed. The ransom he had paid was the very reason Al-ʿAbbas gave for asking — and he left with more than he could lift.

## Ayah 71: the warning behind the offer

**"But if they intend to betray you..."** Ibn Kathir explains the betrayal (*khiyāna*) precisely: it means intending to betray "in contradiction to what they declare to you by words." It is the gap between the tongue and the intention — exactly the danger in a prisoner who says whatever buys his freedom.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the worry this answers: about some Badr prisoners who had become Muslims, a doubt lingered that once back in Makkah they might turn away from Islam and start hurting the Muslims afterwards. Ayah 71 removes that apprehension.

**"...they indeed betrayed Allah before."** On what this earlier betrayal was, the two commentaries take different routes. **Ibn Kathir** reads it as their disbelief in Allah before the battle of Badr. **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reaches further back: they had admitted Allah to be the Lord of all the worlds at the time of the original Covenant, and then became hostile to it. Either way the logic holds — this would not be their first betrayal, and the first one did not go well for them.

**"So He gave [you] power over them."** Note who does the giving. Ibn Kathir: this means Allah caused them to be captured at Badr. Maʿārif renders it "so Allah has given [you] power over them," and adds that their breach of trust turned out to be fatal for none but themselves, ending in their disgrace and detention. Should these people decide to commit a breach of trust with the Prophet ﷺ, Maʿārif says, it will bring him no hurt or loss; and if they start opposing him even now, there is nowhere they can go outside the range of Allah's power and control, and He shall inevitably seize them as before.

**"And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise."** Ibn Kathir: "He is Ever Aware of his actions and All-Wise in what He decides." Maʿārif says the same of this closing: He is the knower of secrets hidden in hearts, and the possessor of great wisdom. The hidden intention is already seen; the outcome is already wisely arranged. So the Prophet ﷺ is not being asked to gamble on their sincerity — he is being told he never had anything at risk.

## Living it

**Nobody's past disqualifies them.** The men addressed here had done everything a person can do against Islam, and the ayah still says *if Allah knows any good in your hearts*. Never write off a person, and never let anyone write you off — including yourself.

**What is being examined is the heart, not the performance.** Al-ʿAbbas's claim, "I became a Muslim before," was met with "Allah knows if you are Muslim... as for your outward appearance, it was against us." Outward conduct is judged outwardly and carries real consequences; what Allah rewards is settled by what He knows within. Both are true at once.

**Compassion and firmness are not rivals.** Ibn Kathir preserves two moments concerning the same uncle: the Prophet ﷺ would not sleep while Al-ʿAbbas groaned in his bonds, and had him untied; and when the Ansar offered to release him without ransom, he answered, "No, by Allah! Do not leave any Dirham of it." Personal kindness is not a licence to be loose with what is owed to others.

**Give up something for Allah and you are not the poorer for it.** Twenty *Uwqiyah* went out; twenty servants came back — with forgiveness hoped for beyond that.

**A believer does not live in fear of other people's treachery.** Ayah 71 is not a security policy; it is a settling of the heart. As Maʿārif puts it, there is nowhere the schemer can go outside the range of Allah's power and control.

## Where the surah goes from here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the turn at this point. Up to here the text has dealt with fighting the disbelievers, taking them prisoner, setting them free and carrying on peace negotiations with them. From the following ayat right up to the end of the surah, a related chapter is taken up: the injunctions of *Hijrah*, emigration — because situations can arise in a confrontation with disbelievers in which the Muslims have neither the power to attack nor the willingness to make peace. In such a state of weakness, the only course through which Islam and the Muslims can be salvaged is to leave that city or country for some other land where acting freely in accordance with Allah's injunctions is possible.

passages.title: Bonds of alliance: emigrants, helpers, kin
passages.tafsir:
These are the last four verses of Sūrah al-Anfāl, and they answer a question the young community could not avoid: now that faith has cut straight through families and cities, who belongs to whom? The passage sorts people into groups, attaches rights and duties to each, and in its last line puts blood kinship back at the centre of the law of inheritance.

*Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* states the objective plainly: these verses describe the rulings of Hijrah (emigration) as they bear on the inheritance of the Muhājir Muslims, and alongside that, the inheritance of non-Muhājir Muslims and of non-Muslims. Ibn Kathīr reads the same verses under the heading of *walāyah* — mutual support, loyalty and protection.

## Four groups

Ayah 72 names three kinds of believers; ayah 73 names a fourth group:

1. **The Muhājirūn** — "those who believed, and emigrated and strove hard and fought with their property and their lives in the cause of Allah." Ibn Kathīr: they left their homes and estates to give support to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and to establish His religion.
2. **The Anṣār** — "those who gave asylum and help": the Muslims of Madinah who took their emigrant brothers into their own homes, comforted them with their wealth, and gave aid by fighting alongside them.
3. **Believers who did not emigrate** — those who accepted Islam but remained where they were, in Makkah.
4. **Those who disbelieved**, who are "allies of one another" (ayah 73).

Of the first two Allah says *baʿḍuhum awliyāʾu baʿḍ* — "they are allies of one another." Ibn Kathīr's gloss is plain: each one of them has more right to the other than anyone else does.

## The word the passage turns on: *waliyy*

Everything hinges on *waliyy* (plural *awliyāʾ*) and its noun *walāyah/wilāyah*. *Maʿārif* says the Qurʼān uses these words here for friendship and close relations in the real sense; and, commenting on ayah 73, that *waliyy* carries a general sense in which inheritance is included, along with guardianship and charge of a person's affairs.

*Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* records a genuine difference among the early authorities. **The early authorities of tafsīr — Sayyidunā Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Mujāhid and others — said that *wilāyah* here means *wirāthah*, inheritance, so that *waliyy* means *wārith*, heir.** Some others took *wilāyah* in its usual lexical sense: friendship, help and support. On the first reading ayah 72 legislates who inherits from whom; on the second, who defends whom. The two readings lie close together: *Maʿārif* speaks of the Muhājir and the Anṣār being friends to one another in a way that includes mutual help and support as well as inheritance.

## The brotherhood of Madinah

This is why Allah's Messenger ﷺ forged ties of brotherhood between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār — Ibn Kathīr cites al-Bukhārī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, for this. And that brotherhood was not symbolic. **They used to inherit from one another, having more right to the inheritance than the deceased man's own relatives** — until Allah abrogated that practice with the fixed share for near relatives.

He then gathers the ayat in which Allah praised these two groups (9:100, 9:117), including the portrait of the people of Madinah who "love those who emigrate to them, and have no jealousy in their breasts for that which they have been given, and give them preference over themselves even though they were in need" (59:8–9). The best comment on "no jealousy in their breasts," says Ibn Kathīr, is that **they do not envy the Muhājirūn the rewards Allah gave them for their emigration**. These ayat, he adds, indicate that the Muhājirūn are better in grade than the Anṣār — a ruling on which he reports a consensus among the scholars.

## "You owe them no protection until they emigrate"

Then the hard clause of ayah 72: *"And as to those who believed but did not emigrate, you owe no duty of protection to them until they emigrate."*

Why so severe towards fellow believers? *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* explains: before the conquest of Makkah, emigration was an absolute obligation on every Muslim man and woman, and in obedience to it most Muslims, with the exception of only a few, had left Makkah for Madinah. In those conditions **staying behind had itself become a sign of not being a Muslim** — the Islam professed by a non-Muhājir was therefore taken to be doubtful, and it was for that reason that the bond of mutual inheritance with him was severed. Yet he was *not* classed as a disbeliever on the basis of that sign alone, unless he betrayed open, clear and decisive proof of disbelief.

Ibn Kathīr adds the practical consequence: this third category has no share in the war booty, nor in the fifth of it, unless they attend the battle. He supports this with the hadith of Buraydah bin al-Ḥaṣīb al-Aslamī — recorded by Imām Aḥmad, and, Ibn Kathīr notes, collected by **Muslim** — in which the Prophet ﷺ would advise a commander sent out with an expedition to have taqwā of Allah and be kind to the Muslims under his command, and instructed him to call the enemy to Islam; then to call them to leave their own area and come to the areas in which the Muhājirūn reside, making known to them that if they do so they will have the rights and the duties of the Muhājirūn. If they refuse and choose to remain where they are, they are to be told that they will be just like the Muslim bedouins: Allah's law applies to them just as it does to all believers, but they will have no share in the war booty or in *fayʾ* (booty without war) unless they perform jihād along with the Muslims. If they refuse all of this, they are called to pay the jizyah; and only if they refuse that too is there fighting.

**Was this ruling abrogated?** *Maʿārif* gives both positions. After the conquest the Prophet ﷺ himself declared *lā hijrata baʿd al-fatḥ* — "there is no hijrah after the Conquest" — so the obligation of Hijrah was no longer operative, and with it the question of severing relations with those who did not migrate terminated automatically. **Most commentators therefore say this injunction stands abrogated by the Conquest of Makkah.** But **according to the investigative scholars of the field it too is everlasting and unabrogated — only changed under specific conditions**: if the conditions in which it was revealed were to reappear in some period or some country — that it becomes altogether impossible to fulfil Islamic obligations while living there, so that not emigrating without a strong excuse becomes an unmistakable sign of disbelief — the same ruling would come into force once again.

## "But if they seek your help in religion"

The severity is at once softened: *"but if they seek your help in religion, it is your duty to help them — except against a people with whom you have a treaty."*

Ibn Kathīr, reporting this from Ibn ʿAbbās: if these Muslims who did not perform Hijrah ask you to aid them against their enemy, then aid them; it is incumbent upon you, **because they are your brothers in Islam** — unless they ask you to aid them against disbelievers with whom you have a fixed-term treaty of peace. In that case, do not betray your treaties or break your promises. *Maʿārif* draws out the purpose of the first half: their Islamic right to be helped when in need was retained.

*Maʿārif* puts the exception directly: the religious bond is indeed formidable, and yet standing by the terms of a treaty comes first and is more preferable. Contravention of a treaty is not permissible under the heat of religious partisanship.

### Abū Jandal at Ḥudaybiyah

*Maʿārif* illustrates this with an incident from the Peace Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah, among whose terms was the condition that the Prophet ﷺ would send back anyone who came to Madinah thereafter. Just as the treaty was being concluded, Sayyidunā Abū Jandal (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) appeared — a Muslim whom the disbelievers of Makkah had put in detention and tortured. He presented himself before the Prophet ﷺ, told him how oppressed he had been, and sought his help.

Muhammad Shafi asks us to consider before whom that plea was being made: none but the one who had come to this world as the universal mercy. Yet, bound by the injunction in this very verse, he ﷺ excused himself from helping him and let him go back. His return in that manner was heart-rending for all the Muslims present. But the Prophet ﷺ, guided by divine words, preferred the treaty obligation to the personal misfortune of Sayyidunā Abū Jandal — as if already seeing that the years of oppression would not last, that Makkah would soon be conquered, and that a few more days of patience would be added to Abū Jandal's reward.

## Ayah 73: the other side of the line

*"And those who disbelieve are allies of one another."*

Ibn Kathīr: after Allah mentioned that the believers are supporters of one another, He severed all ties of support between them and the disbelievers. Ibn Kathīr cites al-Ḥākim, who recorded in his *Mustadrak* from Usāmah that the Prophet ﷺ said that no followers of two religions inherit from each other — neither a Muslim from a disbeliever nor a disbeliever from a Muslim — and then recited this very ayah; al-Ḥākim said its chain is authentic.

*Maʿārif* draws out the easily missed half of this ayah. Since *waliyy* here carries its general sense — inheritance together with guardianship and the patronage of affairs — we learn from this verse that **disbelievers are to be considered inheritors of one another, and the law of inheritance in force in their own religion is what is implemented in their inheritance matters**. Likewise the guardian responsible for the upbringing of their orphaned children and for the marriage of their girls is to be from among themselves. In short: in family matters, the religious law of non-Muslims stands duly protected in an Islamic state.

**The warning.** *"If you do not do so, there will be fitnah on the earth and great corruption."* Ibn Kathīr: if you do not shun the idolaters and offer your loyalty to the believers, fitnah will overcome the people, believers will be mixed with disbelievers, and tremendous, widespread trials will follow. *Maʿārif* attaches the warning to the whole cluster of rulings just given. On the surface these look like a few subsidiary injunctions, says Muhammad Shafi, but they are in reality comprehensive basic principles of equity and justice for all, which guarantee world peace — which is why the warning here is worded as it is not generally worded for other injunctions.

## Ayah 74: "the believers in truth"

Ayah 74 repeats the description of the emigrants and the helpers and gives the verdict: *"these are the believers in truth; for them is forgiveness and a generous provision."*

Ibn Kathīr: after Allah affirmed the ruling of loyalty and protection between the believers in this life, He mentioned their destination in the Hereafter. He affirmed their faith, just as at the beginning of this surah, and promised to reward them with forgiveness and by erasing their sins if they have any, and with honourable provision — abundant, pure, everlasting and eternal, delightful and coming in great varieties.

*Maʿārif* catches the force of "in truth": the hint given is that those who did not emigrate were Muslims, but their Islam was neither perfect nor certain. On "for them is forgiveness," Muhammad Shafi points to what has been explained in sound (ṣaḥīḥ) ahadith: that Islam demolishes what was before it, and that Hijrah razes what was before it — becoming a Muslim demolishes the whole edifice of past sins, and so likewise does emigration.

**"One will be with whom he loves."** Ibn Kathīr adds that those who follow the path of the believers in faith and good deeds will be with them in the Hereafter, as Allah says in 9:100 and 59:10. He cites a hadith that he describes as being in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, *mutawātir* (transmitted by so many chains that its authenticity is beyond doubt): "One will be in the company of those whom he loves." Another hadith states, "He who loves a people is one of them," and in another narration, that he will be gathered with them on the Day of Resurrection. For anyone reading these ayat centuries later and feeling shut out of the honour described in ayah 74, this is where Ibn Kathīr leaves the way open.

## Ayah 75: latecomers, and the return of blood kinship

*"And those who believed afterwards, and emigrated and strove hard along with you — they are of you."*

*Maʿārif* explains that the Muhājirūn fell into two categories: those who migrated before the Peace Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah, and those who migrated after it. **Because of this there will be a difference in the ranks they are to have in the Hereafter — but in the rulings of this world they are covered by the same injunction**, in that they inherit from one another. Hence Allah says of the later ones: *fa-ulāʾika minkum* — "they are of you," a part of your group.

Then the final line of the surah: *"But kindred by blood are nearer to one another in the decree ordained by Allah."*

*Maʿārif* takes the phrase apart. *Ulū* carries the sense of being the possessor or the people of something — as in "people of wisdom" for *ulū al-ʿaql*. *Arḥām* is the plural of *raḥim*, the part of the body where the creative process of the human child takes place; since the bond of relationship is established through that link, *ulū al-arḥām*, literally "womb-relatives," is used for relatives generally. And *fī kitābi'llāh*, "as in the Book of Allah," is used here in the sense of *fī ḥukmi'llāh*: Allah has made this law by His special command. Ibn Kathīr says the same: it means in Allah's decision.

**This is where the brotherhood-inheritance of early Madinah is set aside.** Ibn Kathīr reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and several others that this ayah abrogated inheriting from those with whom one had ties of treaty or brotherhood, as was the case at the beginning of Islam; *Maʿārif* likewise says the earlier arrangement was abrogated because it was an emergency-oriented injunction given during the initial period of the Hijrah. Ibn Kathīr also settles the scope: this ayah encompasses **all** relatives, not only those degrees of relative who have no fixed, designated share, as some people claim and argue from this verse — supported by the hadith that Allah has allotted every right to the one who deserves it, so there may be no will for an heir. And Allah knows best.

*Maʿārif* sketches how the distribution works. The shares of particular relatives have already been determined by the Qurʼān in Sūrah al-Nisāʾ; these are the *Aṣḥāb al-Furūḍ* or *Dhawū al-Furūḍ*, popularly called the "Qurʼānic heirs." What remains is distributed over the other relatives. Of that remainder the Prophet ﷺ said, in a hadith reported by **al-Bukhārī**, that after giving the shares identified in the Qurʼān, what remains is to be given to the males nearer to the deceased — those known in the terminology of inheritance as the *ʿaṣabāt* (agnates, the paternal relatives), taken degree by degree, the nearer excluding the more distant. And if no agnate is alive, distribution is made over the rest of the relatives — technically the *Dhawū al-Arḥām*, such as the maternal uncle or maternal aunt. Nearness has to do the excluding for a simple reason: some kind of distant relationship definitely exists among all the human beings of the world, since all owe their birth to one father and one mother, Sayyidunā Ādam and Sayyidah Ḥawwāʾ, peace be upon them.

**Why relatives inherit at all.** Whatever a person receives in this mortal life is, in the real sense, owned entirely by Allah; a man is only made its temporary owner for a lifetime. By all canons of logic and justice, then, an estate should have reverted to Him. But Muhammad Shafi observes that everyone would naturally have been hurt to learn that after death his wealth would reach neither his children nor his parents nor his spouse — and the natural consequence would be that no one would bother to work for more than his basic needs, which would have meant disaster for human beings and their cities. So Allah, in His perfect mercy and profound wisdom, made inheritance the right of relatives, especially those relatives for whose benefit a person has been working hard and putting assets together all his life.

## Living it

- **Test loyalty by Ibn Kathīr's phrase.** Does this brother have more right on me than anyone else does?
- **Help the Muslim who seeks help in his religion** — that duty was written into the very ayah that cut him off from inheritance.
- **Keep your word even when your sympathies pull hard the other way.** Abū Jandal walking back to Makkah, with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ letting him go, is *Maʿārif*'s measure of how seriously Islam takes a treaty.
- **Leave other communities their own family law.** Ayah 73 severs alliance with the disbelievers, and in the same breath, as *Maʿārif* reads it, protects their law of guardianship and inheritance from interference.
- **Love the people of ayah 74**, and give blood relatives their due.
